title: Latin American Fashion Gifts and Souvenirs Worth Buying, Country by Country
dek: Rebozos, mochilas, alpaca, toquilla hats and more: the Latin American fashion souvenirs worth buying, how to buy well and how to pack them.
body:
The best souvenirs are the ones you actually wear. Latin America is full of artisan pieces that look as good in your hometown as they do on the trip, provided you buy well and pack carefully. Here is what to look for, country by country, with more designers to discover in our Latin American fashion designers hub.

Mexico: Rebozos, Embroidery and Silver

The rebozo, Mexico’s traditional shawl, is the most versatile gift you can buy: a scarf, a wrap and a statement in one. Embroidered blouses and huipiles from Oaxaca and Chiapas carry regional designs worth asking about, and silver from Taxco remains a classic; look for the .925 stamp that indicates sterling.

  • Gift idea — a silk scarf from Pineda Covalin, printed with Mexican cultural motifs
  • Plan it — browse more in our Oaxaca guide

Colombia: Mochilas, Hats and Filigree

A Wayuu mochila, crocheted by Wayuu women in La Guajira, is the quintessential Colombian gift. The sombrero vueltiao, woven from caña flecha fiber by Zenú artisans, is a national symbol, and gold and silver filigree from Santa Cruz de Mompox is exquisitely fine. In Cartagena, you will find all three.

Peru: Alpaca and Andean Textiles

Alpaca is Peru’s signature fiber, warm, light and soft. Note that baby alpaca refers to a grade of especially fine fiber, not to the age of the animal. Woven textiles from Andean communities around Cusco, chullo hats and silver filigree are also lovely gifts. Buy from makers or cooperatives who can tell you where the fiber came from.

Ecuador: Toquilla Straw and Tagua

The Panama hat is woven in Ecuador from toquilla palm fiber, with Montecristi and Cuenca as its two great centers. Grades range widely, so set a budget and compare weaves. Tagua, the nut known as vegetable ivory, is carved into colorful jewelry and buttons. Near Quito, Otavalo’s market is a good place to find woven scarves and textiles.

Brazil: Flip-Flops and Golden Grass

Havaianas are the easy, crowd-pleasing gift, available in almost every color. For something rarer, look for capim dourado, the naturally gold-toned grass from the Jalapão region of Tocantins, woven into bracelets, earrings and small bags. Straw bags and beachwear also travel well.

Argentina and Uruguay: Leather and Wool

Argentina is the place for leather: belts, wallets, gloves and jackets. A poncho, or a mate gourd with silver detailing, makes a more traditional gift. In Uruguay, Manos del Uruguay, an artisan cooperative, is known for hand-dyed yarns and knitwear, ideal for anyone who knits or simply loves good wool.

Chile and Panama: Lapis and Molas

Chile is a renowned source of lapis lazuli, beautiful set in silver, and the village of Rari produces delicate earrings and figures woven from dyed horsehair. In Panama, molas, the layered reverse-appliqué panels made by Guna women, can be framed, sewn onto bags or worn as part of a blouse. Ask who made them and buy as close to the source as you can.

How to Buy Well

Prioritize provenance: ask who made a piece, where and how, and favor cooperatives and makers selling their own work. Handmade objects have small irregularities; perfect uniformity at a low price can signal machine-made copies. Carry small bills for markets, bargain lightly if at all with individual artisans, and keep receipts for customs.

Matching Gifts to People

Think about how the person you are buying for actually dresses. Minimalists will appreciate an alpaca scarf in a natural shade, a fine silver ring or a toquilla hat with a simple band. Color lovers will wear a Wayuu mochila, a rebozo or a capim dourado bracelet. For anyone who cooks, entertains or simply likes beautiful things at home, a framed mola or a hand-woven table runner from a cooperative is a gift with a story.

For smaller budgets, look to light pieces that still feel special: tagua earrings, a pair of Rari horsehair earrings, Havaianas or a woven bracelet. Group several small items into one bundle wrapped in a local textile, which becomes part of the gift. Whatever you choose, note the maker or community on a card, since provenance is what turns a souvenir into something treasured.

Timing helps as well. Buy bulky or fragile gifts toward the end of a trip, when you know how much space is left, and ship larger purchases home if a maker or cooperative offers reliable shipping. That way, your favorite finds arrive intact and your carry-on stays light.

How to Pack Them

Roll textiles and knits to save space and reduce creases, and use soft pieces to cushion anything fragile. Hats travel best in a box or carried on board. Stuff bags so they keep their shape, and wrap jewelry individually. Plant fibers, wood, seeds and animal products may need to be declared, so check your home country’s customs rules before you fly. title: A Designer Capsule Wardrobe for Latin America, City by City
dek: How to dress for Mexico City, Cartagena, Lima, Buenos Aires and Rio, with the local designers and crafts worth adding to your capsule.
body:
Latin America spans highland capitals, Caribbean ports and Southern Hemisphere seasons, so one suitcase has to work hard. The answer is a tight capsule of neutral, natural-fiber basics that you build out city by city with pieces from local designers and makers. Here is how to pack, and what to look for once you land, with more names in our Latin American fashion designers hub.

The Core Capsule

Start with pieces that layer, wash easily and mix without thinking. Keep the palette tight, two neutrals plus one accent, and let local purchases add the color.

  • Tops — two linen or cotton shirts, two fine knit tees, one light sweater
  • Bottoms — tailored trousers, a midi skirt or relaxed linen pants, dark jeans
  • Layers — a light trench or jacket and a large scarf or wrap
  • Dresses — one easy day-to-night dress
  • Shoes — broken-in walking shoes, sandals and one dressier pair
  • Extras — sunglasses, a packable hat and a compact umbrella

Mexico City: Layers and Polish

Mexico City sits at roughly 2,240 meters, so mornings and evenings run cool even when afternoons are warm, and the rainy season brings regular afternoon showers. Dress in layers, keep a light jacket close and favor closed shoes for long walks. The city dresses with a smart, creative edge, especially in Roma, Condesa and Polanco.

Look for pieces from Carla Fernández and Lydia Lavín, both in our hub, and consider a rebozo, the traditional Mexican shawl, which doubles as a scarf, wrap and evening layer.

Cartagena: Linen and Breathing Room

Cartagena is hot and humid year-round, so pack loose linen and cotton, swap jeans for airy trousers or skirts, and expect to change before dinner. Evenings in the walled city are dressy-casual: think a flowing dress or a crisp shirt rather than beachwear.

This is the place to add Colombian color: ruffles and prints from Johanna Ortiz, swimwear from Agua by Agua Bendita, a Wayuu mochila as your everyday bag and, for a playful touch, a sombrero vueltiao.

Lima: Mild, Gray and Chic

Lima rarely gets very hot or very cold, but its winter brings the garúa, a persistent gray mist, while summer is sunny and warm. A light knit and a jacket cover most days. Barranco and Miraflores have a relaxed, arty style that suits clean basics.

Make alpaca your Lima upgrade: a fine sweater or scarf will earn its place for years. Peruvian designers Meche Correa and ESCVDO, both in our hub, offer contemporary takes on Andean craft.

Buenos Aires: Southern Seasons, Late Dinners

Remember that the seasons are reversed: Buenos Aires winters are cool and damp, summers hot and sticky. Porteños dress with polished ease, and dinners start late, so plan one outfit that moves from a long lunch to a late table.

Leather is the local investment: a well-cut jacket or handmade shoes. Browse Palermo Soho for independent labels, and look up MAYDI, featured in our hub.

Rio de Janeiro: Beach Codes

Rio de Janeiro runs on beach culture, and dressing well here means dressing light. Pack swimwear you love, a cover-up and sandals; buy a canga, the Brazilian sarong that locals use in place of a beach towel, and a pair of Havaianas on arrival. For evenings in Ipanema or Leblon, a simple dress or linen shirt is plenty.

Add Brazilian design with PatBO’s embellished resortwear, from our hub, or Osklen’s minimalist, beach-rooted pieces.

Shoes, Bags and Small Details

Cobblestones are the great equalizer. Colonial centers such as Cartagena’s walled city, historic Mexico City and Lima’s old town are best tackled in flat, supportive shoes, with sandals reserved for beach days and a low block heel or polished loafer for dinners. One crossbody bag that closes securely will cover days in every city on this list, and a woven tote or mochila can join it for markets and the beach.

Small details make the capsule feel finished. A silk scarf ties together a simple outfit and doubles as sun protection; a pair of statement earrings, perhaps something bought along the way, turns a day look into an evening one. Keep accessories in one small pouch so nothing gets left behind in a hotel drawer, and resist packing extra just in case: you will want room for the pieces you find on the road.

If your route mixes climates, pack for the coolest stop and the hottest stop, then let everything in between borrow from both. A thin thermal layer weighs almost nothing and makes highland evenings far more comfortable, while a lightweight scarf handles strong air-conditioning on the coast.

Before You Go

Leave about a quarter of your suitcase empty for what you will buy. Check the season for each stop, especially if your route crosses the equator, and pack a small laundry kit for hand-washing linen and knits. When you shop, buy fewer, better pieces that work with your capsule, and ask makers about care. For neighborhood-by-neighborhood tips, see our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Sustainable Latin American Fashion: Slow-Fashion Labels and Craft Collectives
dek: Natural dyes, backstrap looms and artisan cooperatives: the slow-fashion labels and craft collectives shaping sustainable style in Latin America.
body:
In much of Latin America, slow fashion is not a trend so much as a continuation: hand weaving, plant and insect dyes, and garments made to be mended and passed down. The most interesting labels and collectives today build on those traditions while paying the people who keep them alive. Here is where to look, and what to ask, alongside our Latin American fashion designers hub.

What Slow Fashion Means Here

The term covers a lot of ground. In this region, it most often means hand processes such as backstrap or pedal-loom weaving and hand embroidery; natural fibers such as cotton, wool and alpaca; natural dyes; small production runs; and direct, long-term relationships with artisan communities. A label does not need a certification badge to work this way, and a badge alone does not guarantee it. The best signal is transparency: who made it, where, and how.

Mexico: Design Built on Craft

Carla Fernández, featured in our hub, is perhaps the best-known example of a Mexican designer working closely with artisan communities, translating traditional textile techniques into contemporary, geometric garments. Someone Somewhere is a Mexican brand that brings hand-made artisan details, such as embroidery and woven panels, into everyday basics like T-shirts, totes and sweatshirts, making craft easy to wear.

Natural Dyes in Oaxaca

In the Zapotec village of Teotitlán del Valle, near Oaxaca city, weaving families dye wool with materials such as cochineal, the tiny insect that yields reds and pinks, indigo for blues and local plants for yellows and greens. Many workshops will gladly show visitors the process. Rugs are the signature product, but you will also find bags, scarves and smaller woven pieces that travel easily.

Chiapas and Guatemala: Maya Weaving Cooperatives

Maya backstrap weaving is among the region’s most remarkable textile traditions. In San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, Sna Jolobil is a long-standing cooperative of Maya weavers from highland communities, known for preserving traditional designs and techniques. Across the border in Guatemala, Trama Textiles is a women’s weaving cooperative based in Quetzaltenango, selling backstrap-woven scarves, bags and textiles made by its members.

  • Look for — huipiles, scarves, table runners and bags with clear maker information
  • Why we love it — buying from a cooperative keeps more of the price with the weavers

Peru: Andean Weaving Revived

In and around Cusco, the Center for Traditional Textiles of Cusco (Centro de Textiles Tradicionales del Cusco) works with highland weaving communities to sustain traditional techniques, from spinning by hand to natural dyeing and intricate warp-patterned designs. Its demonstrations are a superb introduction to Andean textiles, and its pieces come with genuine provenance. Peruvian alpaca, a naturally warm and durable fiber, is another slow-fashion staple worth investing in.

Uruguay: Cooperative Knitwear

Manos del Uruguay is a well-known cooperative of artisans, many of them women in rural communities, producing hand-dyed yarns and handmade knitwear. It is a lovely example of craft supporting livelihoods outside the capital. Gabriela Hearst, the Uruguayan designer in our hub, is also widely recognized for placing sustainability and craft at the center of her luxury label. Plan your trip with our Uruguay guide.

Brazil and Upcycling

Osklen, from Rio, has long emphasized natural and alternative materials within its relaxed aesthetic. Across the region, you will also find small studios practicing upcycling, reworking deadstock fabric, vintage garments and textile offcuts into new pieces. These are often one-offs, so buy what you love on the spot, and ask what the source materials were.

Caring for Handmade Pieces

Slow fashion only works if the clothes last, and handmade textiles reward a little attention. Wash naturally dyed cotton and wool by hand in cool water with a gentle, pH-neutral soap, and dry flat in the shade, since strong sun can fade plant and insect dyes over time. Alpaca and wool knits rarely need washing after every wear; airing them out is usually enough, and storing them folded keeps their shape.

Embroidery and backstrap-woven pieces are surprisingly durable, but snags happen. Small repairs are part of the tradition rather than a flaw, and many weavers and local seamstresses will mend a piece for a modest fee. Keep any spare thread or yarn that comes with a garment, and consider a simple mending kit for your suitcase: a needle, a few neutral threads and some safety pins go a long way.

Finally, think in terms of cost per wear. A hand-woven scarf or alpaca sweater may cost more upfront than a fast-fashion equivalent, but bought thoughtfully and cared for well, it can stay in your wardrobe for a decade. That longevity, rather than any label, is the most convincing sustainability credential there is.

How to Shop It

Ask direct questions: who made this, how long did it take, what is it dyed with, and how much of the price reaches the maker? Be wary of vague eco language without specifics. Pay fairly and skip hard bargaining with individual artisans. Follow care instructions for natural dyes, which can shift with harsh detergents or strong sun. title: Latin American Handbags, Leather and Accessories Labels to Know
dek: Wayuu mochilas, Argentine leather, Brazilian straw and more: the Latin American bag and accessory labels and crafts worth knowing.
body:
If you only bring home one thing from a trip through Latin America, make it an accessory. Bags, shoes and small leather goods carry the region’s craft traditions in a form you will use every day, and they travel far better than a dress. Here are the labels and crafts to know, with more designers in our Latin American fashion designers hub.

Colombia: Wayuu Mochilas

The Wayuu mochila is one of the most recognizable bags in the region. Crocheted by Wayuu women in La Guajira, on Colombia’s northern Caribbean tip, these bags carry geometric designs that hold cultural meaning, and the finest are worked with a single thread in a dense, tight stitch. A large, intricate mochila represents a serious investment of time and skill.

  • Look for — tight, even stitching, a firm shape and a well-made strap
  • Ask — whether it is single-thread or double-thread, and who made it

A Note on Molas

Molas, the layered reverse-appliqué panels you will see on many bags in Colombian and Panamanian design, are the textile art of the Guna people, whose communities are centered in Panama’s Guna Yala and also reach into northwestern Colombia. Mola-inspired prints are widespread; genuine hand-sewn molas are something else. If a bag claims to use real molas, ask whether they were made by Guna artisans. In Panama, you can often buy them closer to the source.

Colombia: Leather Houses

Colombia has a strong leather culture, and two names stand out. Mario Hernández is one of the country’s best-known leather-goods houses, recognized for structured handbags, briefcases, belts and wallets. Vélez, from Medellín, makes leather bags, shoes, jackets and accessories with a polished, contemporary feel. Both are reliable choices if you want something well-finished and easy to wear. For jewelry, Mercedes Salazar, featured in our hub, is known for whimsical, handcrafted pieces.

Argentina: Leather Done Well

Argentina’s leather reputation is deserved. Prüne, an Argentine label, is known for its leather handbags, shoes and accessories in clean, wearable shapes and a broad color range. Beyond the labels, Buenos Aires is a fine place to commission or buy a leather jacket: ask about the type of hide, check the lining and stitching, and try several sizes, since cuts vary widely.

Brazil: Straw, Raffia and Playful Shoes

Brazil brings color and humor to accessories. Serpui Marie is known for its straw and raffia bags, often embellished with whimsical details, the perfect summer clutch. Schutz makes fashion-forward shoes and bags with a confident, sexy edge. Melissa, famous for its molded plastic shoes, is a cult favorite, and Havaianas remain the definitive Brazilian flip-flop. In São Paulo, the Jardins district is the place to browse.

Ecuador and Peru: Straw, Nut and Silver

Ecuador’s toquilla straw goes far beyond hats. Sensi Studio, in our designer hub, uses it for sculptural bags and accessories, and you will also find tagua, the vegetable ivory nut, carved into jewelry and buttons. In Peru, look for silver filigree from Catacaos near Piura and alpaca accessories such as scarves and gloves, which pair well with any of the bags above.

Mexico: Silk, Silver and Sandals

Mexico’s accessories story runs from Pineda Covalin’s silk scarves, printed with motifs drawn from Mexican cultures and nature, to handmade leather huaraches and silver jewelry from Taxco. Huaraches range from rustic to refined; look for good stitching, a sturdy sole and a woven upper that feels supple rather than stiff.

Caring for Leather and Straw

A good bag deserves a little maintenance. Condition leather occasionally with a product suited to its finish, keep it away from prolonged direct sun and heat, and store it stuffed and in a dust bag rather than hanging by its strap. Light-colored leathers mark easily, so consider a protective treatment before a long trip.

Straw and raffia need different care. Avoid soaking them, brush off sand and dust gently, and let a damp bag dry naturally in the shade rather than near a heater. Crocheted cotton mochilas can usually be spot-cleaned with mild soap and cool water; ask the seller before washing one fully. Treated well, any of these pieces will look better with age, and that is the whole point of buying craft over fast fashion.

Hardware matters too. Wipe metal clasps and zips after beach days, since salt air can dull finishes, and replace a worn strap before it fails rather than after. Many leather workshops across the region will repair stitching, swap hardware or add a new strap for a fair price, extending a bag’s life by years.

How to Shop It

Inspect before you pay: check stitching, hardware, linings and edges, and ask what a bag is made of. Leather should smell like leather and feel consistent across the surface. For handmade pieces, ask who made them and favor cooperatives or makers selling their own work. Stuff bags with tissue or clothing so they keep their shape in your suitcase, and keep straw away from crushing weight. For more on where to shop, see our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Latin American Menswear and Tailoring: Labels and Craft Worth Knowing
dek: Guayaberas, ponchos, ruanas and polished tailoring: the Latin American menswear labels and traditions worth knowing before you shop.
body:
Latin American menswear has a clear point of view: climate-smart fabrics, garments with real heritage and tailoring that takes fit seriously. From the pleated guayabera to the Andean poncho, the region’s classics have outlasted plenty of trends. Here is what to know, and which labels to look for, alongside our wider Latin American fashion designers hub.

The Guayabera

Few garments are as elegant in the heat as the guayabera. Its origins are claimed by both Cuba and Mexico’s Yucatán, and the debate is half the fun; what is not in doubt is the look: vertical pleats or tucks running down the front, often four patch pockets, and a straight hem worn untucked. In linen or fine cotton, it reads polished without a jacket, and in much of the region a long-sleeved guayabera is perfectly acceptable at weddings and formal daytime events.

Mérida is the classic place to buy one, with makers offering everything from crisp white cotton to colored linen and subtle embroidery.

  • Look for — even, sharp pleats, neat buttonholes and a fabric that breathes
  • Fit tip — it should skim the body, not billow; size down if between sizes

Ponchos, Ruanas and Chamantos

Every Andean and Southern Cone country has its own outer layer, and each is worth knowing. Argentina’s poncho salteño, red with black bands, is a proud symbol of the northwestern province of Salta. Colombia’s ruana, an open-front wool wrap, is the uniform of chilly mornings in Boyacá and the high plains around Bogotá. In Chile, the finely woven, reversible chamanto belongs to the huaso, the country’s horseman, while Peru and Bolivia offer alpaca ponchos in natural shades.

Worn over a sweater and jeans, any of these is a far more interesting choice than a technical jacket, and many fold flat enough to carry home easily.

Argentina: Polo-Club Polish

Argentine menswear draws on the country’s love of polo, leather and well-cut classics. La Martina, a polo-rooted brand, is known for its rugby and polo shirts, knitwear and equestrian details. Etiqueta Negra brings a similar heritage sensibility to tailoring, leather jackets and sporty basics, with a distinctly Buenos Aires sense of dash.

In Buenos Aires, leather is the other draw: a well-made jacket or a pair of handmade shoes is one of the city’s most rewarding purchases. Palermo Soho is the place to browse independent labels.

Brazil: Relaxed Modernism

Brazilian men’s style is casual in the best sense: light fabrics, easy shapes and a beach-to-dinner flexibility. Osklen, from Rio, is known for its minimalist, sporty aesthetic, natural materials and a strong connection to beach culture. Reserva, also from Rio, makes approachable casual menswear: well-cut shirts, shorts, polos and knitwear for warm-weather life. And no Brazilian wardrobe is complete without a pair of Havaianas.

Colombia: Accessible Tailoring

Arturo Calle is a household name in Colombia for suits, shirts and dependable everyday tailoring, and its stores are easy to find in major cities. It is a practical stop if you need a well-fitting shirt or a last-minute suit. For a cultural accent, look for the sombrero vueltiao, the Caribbean coast’s woven hat made from caña flecha fiber by Zenú artisans, which has become a national symbol.

Mexico: Ties, Scarves and Craft

Pineda Covalin is known for silk ties and scarves printed with motifs drawn from Mexican cultures, nature and traditions, making them distinctive gifts that still work with a suit. For something more conceptual, Carla Fernández, featured in our designer hub, creates geometric garments rooted in Mexican textile traditions, many of which work across gender lines.

Peru and Uruguay: Fiber and Restraint

Peru’s alpaca knitwear is the region’s great menswear investment. Kuna, a Peruvian label, is known for refined knits in alpaca and other Andean fibers, from crewnecks to scarves. Uruguay-born Gabriela Hearst, also in our hub, brings a similar quiet-luxury restraint to her menswear, with a focus on craft and considered materials.

Sharp Tailoring, Made Locally

Many Latin American cities still have a strong culture of independent tailors, and having a shirt or trousers made can be both affordable and satisfying. Allow time for at least one fitting, bring a garment you love as a reference, and agree on fabric, details and timing up front. If you are traveling, ask whether finished pieces can be shipped.

A few tailoring habits are worth borrowing wherever you shop. Choose linen, seersucker or tropical-weight wool for warm cities, and keep jackets unstructured so they breathe. Have trousers hemmed to a clean break, and ask for shirt sleeves to be shortened rather than rolled. In highland capitals such as Bogotá and Quito, where evenings turn cool, a light merino or alpaca knit under a jacket does more work than any coat, and it packs flat.

How to Shop It

Buy heritage pieces where they come from: guayaberas in the Yucatán, ponchos and ruanas in the highlands, leather in Buenos Aires. Check fiber content labels on knitwear, try ponchos on for length and weight, and ask makers about care before you pay. For more destination-specific shopping, see our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Chilean and Ecuadorian Fashion Designers and Makers to Know
dek: From Santiago’s design barrios and Valparaíso’s hillside studios to Ecuador’s toquilla straw and Otavalo weaving: the makers worth seeking out.
body:
Chile and Ecuador rarely dominate the fashion-week headlines, and that is a large part of their appeal. Between Santiago’s design-minded barrios, Valparaíso’s hillside studios and Ecuador’s long-standing straw and textile traditions, both countries reward the shopper who values craft over logos. Think of this as a companion to our Latin American fashion designers hub, focused on the makers and traditions worth seeking out.

Santiago: Where Chilean Design Lives

In Santiago, independent design gathers in a few walkable neighborhoods. Barrio Italia, with its converted houses and leafy interior patios, is the city’s go-to for small-label clothing, jewelry and homewares, while Lastarria pairs galleries and cafés with design-forward storefronts. Chilean independent fashion leans toward clean lines, natural fibers and a quietly practical attitude, which makes sense for a capital with real winters and the Andes on the horizon.

The best approach is to wander rather than hunt for a single address. Many of the city’s small labels sell directly from their own studios or showrooms, and the people behind the counter are often the people behind the designs, which makes it easy to ask where and how a piece was made.

  • Look for — knitwear in Chilean wool, minimalist tailoring, and jewelry set with lapis lazuli
  • Why we love it — understated pieces that work as well at home as they do on the road

Mapuche Silverwork

Mapuche platería is one of Chile’s most distinctive adornment traditions. Pieces such as the trapelacucha, a pectoral of linked plates and pendants, and large disc-shaped earrings carry cultural and ceremonial meaning, and Mapuche silversmiths continue the craft today in both traditional and contemporary forms.

Buy with respect. Seek out work made by Mapuche artisans themselves, ask who made a piece and where, and be skeptical of mass-produced lookalikes sold without attribution. A smaller, genuine piece will always mean more than a convincing copy.

Chamantos, Chiloé Wool and Rari Horsehair

Chile’s rural crafts produce some of its most wearable souvenirs. The chamanto, a finely woven reversible poncho traditionally worn by huasos, Chile’s horsemen, is closely associated with the town of Doñihue in the O’Higgins Region. Knitwear from the island of Chiloé, from chunky sweaters to socks and hats in natural wool, is exactly what you want for a trip south.

Then there is crin, the delicate horsehair weaving of Rari, a small village in the Maule Region. Artisans there dye and weave horsehair into tiny figures, butterflies and earrings. They are featherlight, beautifully colored and unmistakably Chilean, and they pack into almost nothing.

Lapis Lazuli: Chile’s Blue Stone

Chile is one of the world’s best-known sources of lapis lazuli, and the deep blue stone appears in everything from fine jewelry to simple pendants. Quality varies widely. The most prized lapis is an even, saturated blue with little white calcite, sometimes flecked with gold-toned pyrite. Ask whether a piece is solid stone or reconstituted, and favor jewelers who answer plainly.

Valparaíso’s Hillside Studios

In Valparaíso, the creative energy lives on the cerros. Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepción are the places to wander for artist-run studios, illustrators, printmakers and small jewelry and clothing makers, many of them selling their own work. The port city’s bohemian streak shows up in bold color, hand-printed textiles and one-off pieces rather than polished seasonal collections, so come with an open mind and a little room in your bag.

Ecuador’s Toquilla Straw Hats

The so-called Panama hat is Ecuadorian through and through, woven from the fibers of the toquilla palm. The traditional weaving of the Ecuadorian toquilla straw hat is recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage, and two places define the craft: Montecristi, on the coast, celebrated for its exceptionally fine weaves, and Cuenca, in the southern highlands, a center for finishing, blocking and shaping. Homero Ortega, a family hat house based in Cuenca, is one of the best-known names.

  • Check the weave — finer, tighter and more even generally means more hours of work
  • Ask about care — whether a hat can be rolled or should travel in a box depends on the weave, so ask the maker
  • Mind the price — the finest Montecristi weaves are investment pieces, and should be priced like them

Otavalo, Salasaca and Andean Textiles

North of Quito, the town of Otavalo is home to Kichwa Otavalo weavers and one of the best-known markets in South America. Alongside souvenir stalls you will find wool ponchos, tapestries, embroidered blouses and scarves. In the central highlands near Ambato, the Salasaca community is known for its woven tapestries with distinctive figurative designs.

Ecuador also offers tagua, the dense nut known as vegetable ivory, carved and dyed into buttons and jewelry, and shigras, colorful bags made from agave fiber. Both make light, characterful gifts.

Sensi Studio and Ecuador’s Contemporary Edge

For a modern take on toquilla straw, Sensi Studio, which we feature in our designer hub, turns the material into sculptural hats, bags and accessories. It is a good example of how Ecuadorian craft moves gracefully into contemporary wardrobes, and a reminder that tradition and fashion are not opposites here.

How to Shop It

In both countries, the best purchases come with a story you can verify. Ask who made a piece, where and how; buy from cooperatives or directly from makers when you can; and carry small bills for markets. Hats travel best in a sturdy box or carried by hand. Chile has strict agricultural controls on arrival, so declare plant- or animal-based items when entering, and check your home country’s rules before flying back. For more city-by-city shopping, browse our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Latin American Fashion Weeks and Design Events Worth Planning a Trip Around
dek: From São Paulo Fashion Week to Colombiamoda and Mexico City’s design season, the established events worth building a trip around.
body:
Timing a trip around a fashion week is the fastest way to see a country’s style scene in motion: the designers, the buyers, the street style and the parties all converge on one city for a few days. Latin America has a handful of well-established events that reward the effort, plus design and craft fairs that are just as rewarding for anyone who loves to shop. Dates shift every season, so treat this as a planning list and always check the official calendar before you book.

São Paulo Fashion Week, Brazil

São Paulo Fashion Week is the region’s heavyweight, a long-running showcase for Brazilian design that ranges from established houses to younger labels working with sustainable materials and regional craft. São Paulo itself is the ideal host: a vast, sophisticated city with serious restaurants, contemporary art and the boutique-lined streets of Jardins to fill the hours between shows.

Expect a strong emphasis on Brazilian identity: lightweight fabrics, bold color, beachwear that doubles as evening wear, and a growing number of designers working with Indigenous and regional craft communities.

  • Why go — the scale and range of Brazilian fashion in one place, plus a city that rewards a long stay.
  • Pair it with — a few days in Rio, or a beach escape down the coast.

Colombiamoda, Medellín

Organized by Inexmoda, Colombiamoda is one of the most important fashion trade events in Latin America, combining runway shows with a large business fair that draws buyers and press. It reflects Colombia’s deep textile and manufacturing heritage, and it is where you can see the country’s swimwear, resort and ready-to-wear talent side by side.

Medellín is at its best when it’s buzzing like this; base yourself in El Poblado or Laureles and leave time for the city’s leafy neighborhoods and mountain views.

Bogotá Fashion Week, Colombia

The capital’s own fashion week has become a focus for Colombian designers with a strong point of view, with plenty of attention to craft, sustainability and collaboration with artisan communities. Bogotá is a cool-weather city of museums, bookshops and excellent restaurants, which makes it an easy place to spend a long weekend around the shows.

Fashion Week México, Mexico City

Mexico City’s fashion week — long known as Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week México — is the main platform for the country’s runway designers. The schedule tends to mix polished ready-to-wear with labels that reinterpret Mexican textile traditions, and the off-calendar presentations, pop-ups and showroom events around the city are often as interesting as the main program.

Mexico City’s design season: Zona Maco and Design Week México

If you care about design as much as clothes, Mexico City has two more dates to watch. Zona Maco is the city’s major contemporary art fair, with a design section and a busy program of satellite events and gallery openings. Design Week México brings installations, talks and studio openings across the city. Either one fills the city with collectors and creatives, and with them a wave of exhibitions, dinners and pop-ups.

  • Why go — a concentrated dose of Mexican design, art and craft, and an easy excuse to shop Roma, Condesa and Polanco.

Buenos Aires Fashion Week, Argentina

BAFWeek has been a fixture of the Argentine calendar for years and remains a good window onto the country’s designers, from tailored, minimal ready-to-wear to more experimental work. In Buenos Aires, the best way to extend the experience is on foot: the independent studios and boutiques of Palermo Soho are where much of the city’s design energy actually lives.

Craft and dress: Expoartesanías and the Guelaguetza

Two events are not fashion weeks at all, yet they belong on any style-minded traveler’s list. Expoartesanías in Bogotá is Colombia’s great annual craft fair, bringing together artisans from across the country — Wayuu weavers, caña flecha braiders, jewelers, ceramicists and more — under one roof. It is one of the best opportunities anywhere to buy directly from makers.

In Oaxaca, the Guelaguetza is a celebration of the state’s Indigenous cultures, music and dance, and an unforgettable showcase of regional dress — embroidered huipiles, ribbons, flowers and all. It’s a cultural festival first, so go to watch and learn rather than shop, though Oaxaca’s textile villages and markets are close at hand.

Which event suits you?

Each of these events has its own personality. For pure runway spectacle and the broadest view of a national industry, São Paulo is hard to beat. For a sense of fashion as business — fabrics, manufacturing, swimwear, the buyers who decide what reaches stores — Colombiamoda is the most revealing. Mexico City’s design season suits travelers who want art, architecture, food and fashion in a single trip, while Buenos Aires appeals to anyone drawn to tailoring, leather and an independent studio culture. And if your interest is craft first, Expoartesanías and Oaxaca will show you the traditions that so many of the region’s designers draw from.

Whichever you choose, give yourself a few days on either side. The shows are a starting point; the real discoveries tend to happen in showrooms, markets and neighborhood boutiques once the crowds thin out.

Before you go

Most runway shows are invitation-only, but fashion weeks increasingly include public programming: talks, exhibitions, pop-up markets and designer sales. Follow the event and the designers you love on their official channels, which is where public tickets and side events are usually announced.

  • Check the official calendar — dates and formats change from season to season.
  • Book early — hotels near the venues fill quickly during big events.
  • Plan showroom visits — many designers open their studios by appointment during fashion weeks.
  • Dress the part, comfortably — expect long days and plenty of walking.

For the designers to have on your radar before you arrive, start with our Latin American fashion designers hub, and use our shopping guides to plan your free afternoons.

title: How to Shop Latin American Designers Well: Provenance, Fair Pay and Fakes
dek: Provenance, artisan cooperatives, fair pay, spotting knockoffs and building a travel capsule: how to shop Latin American designers well.
body:
The best Latin American fashion is rooted in place: in a specific craft, a specific community, often a specific pair of hands. Shopping it well means paying attention to where a piece comes from, who made it and whether they were paid fairly. Here’s a practical guide for anyone building a wardrobe from our Latin American fashion designers hub and beyond.

Start with provenance

Provenance is the most useful question in your shopping vocabulary. A good designer or seller should be able to tell you where a piece was made, what it’s made of and which artisans or workshops were involved. Labels that collaborate with craft communities usually say so openly, often naming the region, the technique and sometimes the makers themselves.

  • Ask — Where was this made? Who made it? What is the fiber? How long does a piece like this take?
  • Look for — specifics. “Hand-embroidered in Chiapas” means more than “artisan-inspired”.

Vague language is a signal to dig a little deeper. Words like “ethnic”, “tribal” or “inspired by” often mean a traditional design has been reproduced without involving the community it came from.

Artisan cooperatives and collaborations

Across the region, artisan cooperatives organize makers so they can sell directly, set prices collectively and keep more of what they earn. Buying from a cooperative — at a village workshop, a craft fair or a shop run by the makers themselves — is one of the simplest ways to ensure your money reaches the right people.

Many contemporary designers also work in partnership with artisan communities, commissioning embroidery, weaving or braiding and building it into their collections. The best collaborations credit the artisans, pay them fairly and treat traditional techniques with respect rather than as decoration. Designers such as Carla Fernández in Mexico have made this kind of collaboration central to their work.

Paying fairly

Handmade pieces take time. A finely brocaded huipil, a single-thread Wayuu mochila or a fine toquilla-straw hat can represent weeks or months of work. Haggling may be customary in some markets, but pressing too hard on a handmade piece undervalues the maker’s skill. If a price seems impossibly low for the amount of work involved, ask yourself who is absorbing the difference.

  • Rule of thumb — negotiate lightly, if at all, with individual makers; buy fewer, better pieces.
  • Tip — paying in cash in local currency is often appreciated at small stalls and workshops.

Spotting knockoffs

Popular crafts attract imitations, from machine-made “Wayuu” bags to printed fabric mimicking Otomí embroidery. A few checks help:

  • Look at the back — real embroidery and weaving show the work on the reverse; prints do not.
  • Check for consistency — handmade pieces have subtle irregularities; perfect uniformity often signals machine production.
  • Test the fiber — real alpaca and wool feel different from synthetics, and honest sellers state fiber content.
  • Consider the price — an “heirloom” piece at a souvenir price usually isn’t one.
  • Buy designer pieces direct — from the label’s own store, studio or official site.

Customs and shipping

Rules vary by country and change often, so treat this as general guidance and check current regulations before you travel. Keep receipts for everything you buy, since you may need to declare purchases on arrival home. Items made from certain animal products or plant materials can face restrictions; if a piece includes feathers, shells, exotic leathers or seeds, ask about documentation or skip it.

For larger pieces, many designers and some cooperatives can ship internationally. Ask about tracking and insurance, and be aware that import duties may apply on arrival. Fragile items like straw hats are usually best carried in your hand luggage.

Building a capsule travel wardrobe from Latin American labels

A capsule wardrobe built around Latin American pieces works beautifully for travel: a few statement items anchored by simple basics. Think of it as a collection with a story.

  • One statement top — an embroidered blouse or huipil that pairs with jeans or tailored trousers.
  • A versatile shawl — a rebozo or alpaca wrap for planes, cool evenings and mountain cities.
  • A good hat — a toquilla-straw hat from Ecuador for sun-heavy destinations.
  • A great bag — a Wayuu mochila or a well-made leather piece.
  • One standout dress — something with color, ruffles or craft detailing for dinners and events.
  • Swimwear — Brazil and Colombia are both known for excellent swim and resort design.

Keep the rest neutral — linen, cotton, simple denim — so each piece can shine and everything works together.

Caring for handmade pieces

Buying well also means keeping pieces in good shape. Hand-dyed textiles may bleed, so wash them gently by hand in cold water, separately, and dry them flat in the shade. Store embroidered pieces folded loosely or rolled, away from direct sunlight, and air out wool and alpaca regularly to keep moths away. Straw hats prefer to be stored crown-down or on a hat stand, away from humidity, and should never be folded unless they were made to roll. When in doubt, ask the maker or seller how they would care for it — they know their materials best.

How to shop it

Before your trip, read up on the crafts and designers of the places you’re visiting, and follow designers on their official channels to find studios and pop-ups. Once you arrive, ask questions, pay fairly and choose pieces you’ll wear for years. For city-by-city recommendations on where to shop, see our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Luxury Shopping in Latin America: The Best Neighborhoods, City by City
dek: Polanco, Jardins, Leblon, Palermo and more: the neighborhoods worth the trip for luxury and boutique shopping in Latin America.
body:
Luxury shopping in Latin America is less about logo-heavy malls than about neighborhoods: leafy streets where international maisons sit near local designers’ flagships, concept stores and ateliers that open by appointment. Know where to go and a single afternoon can cover both. This is our city-by-city edit of the districts worth the trip; for deeper dives, our Latin America shopping guides are the place to start.

Mexico City: Polanco, Roma and Condesa

Polanco is Mexico City‘s address for international luxury, with Avenida Presidente Masaryk as its polished main artery and plenty of fine dining between fittings. For a different mood, cross to Roma and Condesa, where tree-lined streets and Art Deco buildings hide independent boutiques, concept stores and studios from Mexican designers who reinterpret craft traditions in contemporary ways.

  • Best for — global labels in Polanco; Mexican designers, homeware and jewelry in Roma and Condesa.

São Paulo: Jardins

São Paulo is Brazil’s fashion capital, and Jardins is its most elegant shopping district. Rua Oscar Freire and the surrounding streets combine international names with Brazilian fashion, jewelry and design houses, and the area’s cafés and restaurants make it easy to linger. Set aside more time than you think; the city rewards slow exploring.

Brazilian luxury has its own accent: fine jewelry set with the country’s colored gemstones, beautifully made sandals and leather goods, and resort wear cut from light, fluid fabrics. Neighboring Pinheiros and Vila Madalena are worth a detour for younger, more independent labels and design stores.

Rio de Janeiro: Ipanema and Leblon

In Rio de Janeiro, shopping comes with a sea breeze. The streets just back from the beach in Ipanema and Leblon are lined with boutiques for swimwear, resort wear, sandals and fine jewelry — the relaxed-but-polished Carioca uniform in retail form. Leblon tends to feel the more exclusive of the two.

Shopping here follows the rhythm of the beach: browse in the late afternoon, then stay for sunset and dinner. Look especially for Brazilian swimwear, which is cut with an expertise few other countries can match, and for linen and cotton pieces made for the heat.

Bogotá and Medellín

Bogotá‘s upscale shopping clusters in the north of the city: the Zona Rosa around the Zona T, the Chicó area and the more village-like Usaquén, which has a pleasant small-town feel. Expect Colombian designers known for ruffles, color and exceptional craftsmanship alongside international brands. The city’s cooler climate also makes it a good place to shop for tailoring, knitwear and outerwear, and Usaquén’s Sunday market is a pleasant way to round out a morning of browsing with local crafts.

In Medellín, El Poblado is the hub, and the streets around Provenza are full of independent boutiques, swimwear labels and cafés. Colombia’s strong textile heritage shows: quality local fashion is easy to find here.

Cartagena: the walled city

Cartagena‘s colonial walled city is one of the most beautiful places in the region to shop. Inside the old walls, colorful colonial houses hold designer boutiques, fine jewelry (Colombian emeralds are a specialty — buy only with certification) and resort wear made for the Caribbean heat. Nearby Getsemaní adds a more bohemian, artsy edge. Shop in the morning or early evening, when the streets are cooler.

Lima: Barranco, Miraflores and San Isidro

In Lima, Barranco is the bohemian choice, with galleries, design stores and concept shops spread through its colorful old mansions. Miraflores and San Isidro are more polished, with upscale fashion and plenty of alpaca and fine-fiber knitwear. Barranco’s walkable streets also make it easy to combine shopping with a drink overlooking the Pacific. Peru’s luxury story is largely about materials: look for baby alpaca and vicuña, and expect to pay accordingly for the real thing.

Buenos Aires: Palermo and Recoleta

Buenos Aires offers two very different shopping experiences. Recoleta, with its grand Belle Époque architecture, is the classic luxury district, centered on elegant Avenida Alvear. Palermo — especially Palermo Soho — is where the city’s independent designers, leather goods and concept stores live, in low-rise buildings along shady, cobbled streets. Argentine leather remains a highlight; look for well-cut jackets, bags and shoes.

Palermo is also where you’ll find the city’s best design and homeware stores, and its weekend markets and plazas add a relaxed, browsing-friendly atmosphere. Plan for long lunches: shopping in Buenos Aires is never in a hurry.

Santiago: Vitacura and Alonso de Córdova

Santiago‘s luxury shopping is concentrated in the eastern neighborhoods, especially Vitacura, where Alonso de Córdova is lined with high-end fashion, design showrooms and galleries. It’s a calm, polished area, best explored with a lunch break in between. Look for Chilean designers working with wool and natural fibers, along with Andean-inspired knitwear and fine jewelry using lapis lazuli, a stone closely associated with Chile.

How to shop it

A few habits make luxury shopping in Latin America smoother. Many designers’ flagships and ateliers welcome appointments, especially for made-to-measure work, so it’s worth contacting them before you arrive. Carry a passport for larger purchases, since some countries offer tax refunds for visitors and stores will need your details — ask in-store about the current rules.

  • Shop local designers — they are the reason to shop here rather than at home; our Latin American fashion designers hub has names to know.
  • Verify high-value items — ask for certificates for emeralds, gold and fine fibers.
  • Go weekdays — boutiques are quieter and staff have more time for you.
  • Keep receipts — useful for refunds and for declaring purchases at customs.

title: Latin American Artisan Textiles and Crafts: A Shopper’s Guide
dek: Huipiles, rebozos, Wayuu mochilas, molas and real Panama hats: how to recognize Latin America’s great crafts and buy them well.
body:
Some of the most covetable pieces in Latin America were never shown on a runway. They come off backstrap looms, out of embroidery hoops and from hands that have braided the same straw for generations, and they are the backbone of the region’s contemporary fashion scene — the reason so many of the names in our Latin American fashion designers hub work alongside artisan communities. Here is what to look for, where each craft comes from, and how to buy it in a way that does right by the people who make it.

Huipiles: Mexico and Guatemala

The huipil is a loose, sleeveless tunic worn by Indigenous women across southern Mexico and Guatemala, and it is less a garment than a language. Motifs, colors and construction can signal a specific town, and the finest are woven on a backstrap loom with brocade patterns built into the cloth rather than added afterward. In Mexico, Oaxaca and Chiapas are the great huipil regions; in Guatemala, the highland Maya communities around Lake Atitlán and beyond keep an extraordinary range of styles alive.

  • Look for — tight, even weaving, motifs that read the same on both faces in brocade work, and a seller who can tell you which community made it.
  • Wear it — over a slip dress or with wide-leg trousers; a good huipil does the heavy lifting in any outfit.

Otomí embroidery from Hidalgo

Those joyful cloths covered in flowers, deer, birds and rabbits — often stitched in a single bright color, sometimes in a full rainbow — are tenangos, the embroidery of the Otomí communities around Tenango de Doria in Hidalgo, Mexico. Designs are drawn freehand onto the fabric and then filled in with dense satin stitch, which is why no two pieces are identical.

The motif has been widely copied in printed fabric and on mass-produced homeware, so the tell is simple: real tenango is embroidered, and you should be able to see and feel every stitch, with a visible back.

Rebozos: Mexico’s essential shawl

The rebozo is a long rectangular shawl worn as a wrap, a sling or a head covering, finished with an elaborately knotted fringe called the rapacejo. The most prized are made with ikat dyeing, where threads are resist-dyed before weaving to create a softly blurred pattern. Santa María del Río in San Luis Potosí and Tenancingo in the State of Mexico are two of the best-known centers.

  • Look for — hand-knotted fringe (the slower and more intricate, the better) and the slight feathering at pattern edges that marks true ikat.

Wayuu mochilas from La Guajira, Colombia

Crocheted by Wayuu women in La Guajira, the desert peninsula on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, the mochila is a sturdy, brilliantly patterned shoulder bag whose geometric designs, called kanaas, draw on Wayuu cosmology and the natural world. A traditional single-thread bag is crocheted with one strand, giving an especially tight, fine fabric that takes considerably longer to make.

You will find mochilas all over Cartagena and beyond, at every quality level. Turn the bag inside out: a well-made one is tight and even on the inside too, with a strap woven separately on a loom.

Sombrero vueltiao and toquilla-straw hats

Colombia’s national symbol, the sombrero vueltiao, is braided from caña flecha, a cane fiber, by Zenú artisans in the savannas of Córdoba and Sucre. Its distinctive black-and-cream bands are braided in rounds — the more rounds, the finer and more flexible the hat.

And the so-called Panama hat? It is Ecuadorian. These hats are hand-woven from toquilla straw, mainly in Manabí province, where Montecristi is famous for its finest weaves, and finished in and around Cuenca. They earned the misleading name by being shipped through Panama. Quality is judged by the density and evenness of the weave; hold one up to the light and look for a fine, regular pattern of tiny rings.

Guna molas from Panama

Molas are panels of layered cloth made by Guna women of Guna Yala, the island-dotted autonomous region on Panama’s Caribbean coast. Using reverse appliqué, the maker cuts through stacked layers of fabric to reveal the colors beneath, then hand-stitches the edges under. Designs range from intricate geometrics to animals and everyday scenes, and molas are traditionally sewn into the front and back of a woman’s blouse.

  • Look for — tiny, nearly invisible stitches, narrow even channels and multiple layers. Sold as panels, they frame beautifully or can be set into a jacket or tote.

Alpaca and Andean weaving

In the Peruvian Andes, weaving traditions go back millennia, and around Cusco and the Sacred Valley you can still see spinning, natural dyeing and backstrap weaving in action. Alpaca, prized for warmth and softness, is the fiber most travelers come home with, with baby alpaca (the fine first fleece, not the age of the animal) at the luxurious end.

Be skeptical of very cheap “alpaca” sold in tourist markets, which is often synthetic or blended. Real alpaca feels cool to the touch at first and has a natural weight; an honest seller will tell you the fiber content.

How to buy well

Wherever you are, the same principles apply. Buy as close to the maker as you can: cooperatives, artisan-run stalls and village workshops keep more of the price with the people doing the work. Ask questions — who made it, where, how long it took — and treat the answers as part of what you are paying for. Pay fairly for handwork rather than bargaining hard over pieces that took weeks.

  • Ask about provenance — a good seller knows the community and the technique.
  • Check the hand — irregularities are a feature; a perfectly uniform print usually is not handmade.
  • Respect meaning — some garments and motifs carry ceremonial significance; ask before cutting up or repurposing.
  • Pack smart — roll textiles rather than folding them, and carry straw hats in your hand luggage.

For where to shop city by city, our Latin America shopping guides pick up where this one leaves off.

title: Latin American Jewelry Designers to Know: Emeralds, Gold and Filigree
dek: Colombian emeralds, Mompox filigree, Brazilian gems and Andean silver: the Latin American jewelers and traditions worth knowing.
body:
Long before anyone talked about Latin American fashion, the region was famous for what it wore at the neck and wrist: gold, silver and some of the world’s most coveted gemstones. Today that heritage lives on in both fine-jewelry houses and family workshops still practicing centuries-old techniques. Here are the jewelers and traditions on our radar, from our guide to Latin American fashion designers.

Mompox Filigree: Colombia’s Living Craft

In Santa Cruz de Mompox, a riverside colonial town in Colombia’s Caribbean interior, goldsmiths and silversmiths practice filigrana momposina — filigree made by twisting impossibly fine threads of metal and shaping them into lace-like earrings, pendants and brooches. The craft is the town’s signature, passed down through family workshops, and watching an artisan coil and solder the wire by hand is an education in patience.

  • Look for — airy earrings and flower motifs in gold or silver
  • Getting there — Mompox is often combined with a trip to Cartagena
  • Tip — buy directly from workshops and ask about the metal content

Filigree pieces are surprisingly light for their size, which makes them comfortable as statement earrings. Designs range from traditional floral and religious motifs to cleaner, modern shapes made by younger artisans.

Colombian Emeralds: Know Before You Buy

Colombia is synonymous with emeralds, and its famous mining areas, including Muzo and Chivor in Boyacá, have produced stones admired for their deep, vivid green. Bogotá is the trading hub, and the city’s jewelers range from heritage houses to contemporary designers. Because emeralds are almost always treated with oils or resins to improve clarity, ask what treatment a stone has had and request a certificate from a recognized gem lab for any significant purchase. Our Bogotá guide covers the rest of your visit.

For a more fashion-forward take on Colombian jewelry, see our profile of Mercedes Salazar, known for whimsical, handcrafted statement pieces.

Paula Mendoza: Sculptural Gold, Colombian Roots

Colombian designer Paula Mendoza makes jewelry that reads like small sculpture — organic, often asymmetrical forms with a strong sense of movement and a nod to pre-Columbian goldwork. Her pieces sit happily between art object and everyday wear: a single cuff or pair of earrings does all the talking an outfit needs.

Her work is a good reminder that pre-Columbian goldsmithing — the kind displayed at Bogotá’s celebrated Museo del Oro — remains a living influence on contemporary Colombian design. Seeing that collection first will change how you look at modern Colombian jewelry.

H.Stern: Brazil’s Gemstone Heritage

Headquartered in Rio de Janeiro, H.Stern is Brazil’s best-known fine jewelry house and a showcase for the country’s extraordinary range of colored gemstones — tourmalines, topazes, citrines, amethysts and more. Its designs range from classic to contemporary, but the constant is a celebration of Brazilian stones. A visit offers an excellent crash course in what Brazil’s mines produce. Plan around it with our Rio de Janeiro guide.

Brazil’s gem diversity is the real story here. Few countries produce such a range of colored stones, and learning to compare tones and cuts in person is the best preparation before buying anywhere in the country.

Antonio Bernardo and Carla Amorim: Brazilian Design-Led Jewelry

Antonio Bernardo, a Rio jeweler, is known for clean, architectural designs and clever mechanics — rings that move, interlock or reveal something unexpected. It is jewelry that appeals to anyone who loves good industrial design. Carla Amorim, based in Brasília, takes a softer route, with organic, nature-inspired forms in gold set with Brazilian gems.

Brazil’s jewelry scene also includes Ara Vartanian, known for daring, modern diamond settings, and Silvia Furmanovich, whose work blends fine jewelry with artisanal techniques — both profiled elsewhere on the site.

Together, they show the two poles of contemporary Brazilian jewelry: one rooted in engineering and precision, the other in nature and color. Both are worth seeing in person, where the craftsmanship and the quality of the stones become obvious.

Peruvian Silver and ILARIA

Peru has a deep silversmithing tradition, and its contemporary jewelers often draw on Andean and pre-Columbian motifs. ILARIA is a Peruvian silver jewelry brand known for pieces that combine sterling silver with Andean-inspired design, sometimes alongside local stones. It’s a good benchmark for quality before exploring smaller workshops in Lima and the highlands.

Andean silver often features motifs like stylized animals, stepped crosses and geometric patterns borrowed from textiles. Ask about the meaning of a design — it’s part of what you’re buying.

More Silver Traditions: Taxco and Chordeleg

Two more names belong on any jewelry lover’s map. Taxco, in Mexico’s state of Guerrero, is a historic silver town whose workshops have been producing silver jewelry and objects for generations. Chordeleg, in Ecuador’s Azuay province near Cuenca, is known for its filigree in gold and silver — a fascinating counterpoint to Colombia’s Mompox. In both places, look for a .925 stamp on sterling silver and buy from workshops that make what they sell.

Prices in both towns are typically by weight plus workmanship, so it pays to compare a few workshops before committing. The best pieces will be clean on the back as well as the front — a quick way to judge care and skill.

How to Buy Jewelry in Latin America

  • Ask for certificates on significant gemstones, and ask how the stone has been treated
  • Check metal stamps — .925 for sterling silver, karat marks for gold
  • Buy from makers — workshops and cooperatives can tell you exactly how a piece was made
  • Get a receipt — useful for customs declarations and insurance back home
  • Pack it in your carry-on — never in checked luggage

title: Latin American Swimwear and Resortwear Labels Worth the Suitcase Space
dek: From Rio’s sculptural one-pieces to Colombia’s print-happy bikinis, the Latin American swim and resort labels we’d pack first.
body:
Latin America doesn’t just have the beaches — it has the swimwear to match. Brazil and Colombia in particular have turned swim and resortwear into a design discipline, with cuts, prints and fabrics that make a strong case for buying your bikini where you’ll actually wear it. Here are the labels on our radar, from our wider guide to Latin American fashion designers.

Lenny Niemeyer: Rio’s Sculptural Swim

Lenny Niemeyer is one of the most respected names in Brazilian swimwear, and her Rio label treats a swimsuit like a piece of design. Expect architectural one-pieces, elegant cutouts, interesting hardware and a palette that runs from earthy neutrals to graphic prints. It is swimwear for people who would rather look chic than merely tan.

  • Look for — sculpted one-pieces and coordinating cover-ups
  • Why we love it — it bridges the beach and the beach club seamlessly

The label also does elegant cover-ups, sarongs and beach accessories, so it’s easy to build an entire vacation wardrobe around one swimsuit. Fabrics and finishes are designed to look as good off the sand as on it.

Adriana Degreas: São Paulo Glamour

From São Paulo, Adriana Degreas brings a dose of old-school glamour to the shoreline. Her designs often feature bold prints, retro-inspired silhouettes, dramatic cutouts and coordinated kaftans and resort pieces that move straight from sand to dinner. If your ideal holiday involves a sun hat and a very good cocktail, this is your label.

The collections tend to feel like a complete holiday wardrobe rather than a rack of separates — swimsuits designed alongside matching wraps, wide-leg trousers and dresses. Buy the set and the packing decisions make themselves.

Salinas: The Classic Brazilian Bikini

For the archetypal Rio bikini — cheerful prints, flattering cuts and that unmistakable Brazilian confidence — Salinas is a reliable starting point. The label leans colorful and playful, with plenty of mix-and-match options. It’s a fun, accessible way to bring a bit of Ipanema home. Our Rio de Janeiro guide covers where to put it to use.

Brazil’s beach culture is also a lesson in confidence: cuts are generally smaller than in the US or Europe, and nobody is self-conscious about it. If you prefer more coverage, most labels offer fuller styles — just ask.

Beyond the Bikini: Farm Rio and Osklen

Resortwear is where Brazil really shines. Farm Rio is beloved for exuberant, tropical prints — think lush botanicals, parrots and fruit in saturated color — across dresses, skirts and swim. Osklen, founded in Rio, offers the opposite mood: relaxed, minimalist beachwear with an emphasis on natural materials and an easy, sun-faded palette. One packs a punch, the other packs light; both work beautifully in places like Trancoso.

We’ve also written about PatBO, whose embellished, party-ready designs carry the same Brazilian love of color into evening.

Both labels are a smart way to dress for warm-weather cities as well as beaches: a Farm Rio dress works on a São Paulo rooftop, and Osklen’s linen-and-cotton basics suit almost any coastal town in the region.

Maaji: Colombia’s Reversible Wonder

Colombia’s swimwear industry is concentrated around Medellín, and Maaji is one of its most recognizable exports. The label is known for reversible pieces with mismatched, whimsical prints on each side — effectively two swimsuits in one, which is a gift to anyone trying to pack light. The overall mood is playful, artful and sporty. Read more in our Medellín guide.

Beyond swim, the label has expanded into activewear and beach accessories with the same mismatched, illustrative spirit. Sizing tends to be generous with options, and the reversible format makes it a particularly smart buy for long trips.

Onda de Mar: Polished Colombian Resort

Onda de Mar offers a more polished take on Colombian swim, with elegant one-pieces, refined prints and matching resortwear that feels made for a long lunch on a boat. It pairs well with the city we most associate with it in spirit: Cartagena, where the dress code is effortless and the light is always golden.

For more from Colombia, see our profiles of Agua by Agua Bendita, known for its handmade, embroidered and appliquéd swim, and Johanna Ortiz, whose romantic ruffles have become shorthand for Latin American resort style.

The look is grown-up but never stiff: think clean necklines, flattering structure and prints that nod to the tropics without shouting. It’s an easy brand to build a capsule around, especially if you prefer one-pieces.

The Finishing Touches: Hats and Bags

No resort wardrobe is complete without the right accessories, and the region’s crafts deliver. The so-called Panama hat is actually woven from toquilla straw in Ecuador; labels like Sensi Studio, which we profile separately, give it a contemporary edge. In Colombia, Wayuu mochilas — colorful crocheted bags made by Wayuu women in La Guajira — make a perfect beach tote. When buying either, look for cooperatives or makers who can tell you who made the piece and where.

A good toquilla hat is tightly and evenly woven, and the finest grades take weeks of skilled work. Wayuu mochilas vary widely in quality too, so look for dense, even stitching and a sturdy strap.

Before You Go

  • Sizing runs small and cheeky — Brazilian cuts in particular tend to offer less coverage; check size charts and ask for fuller-coverage options if you prefer
  • Buy in season — summer in Brazil and the Southern Cone runs roughly December to March, when new collections arrive
  • Rinse after every swim — salt, chlorine and sunscreen shorten the life of even the best lycra
  • Think in sets — many labels make matching cover-ups, so a single purchase can double as a dinner outfit

title: Peruvian Fashion Designers and Andean Luxury: Alpaca, Vicuña and Pima Cotton Explained
dek: A guide to Peru’s luxury fibers — alpaca, vicuña and Pima cotton — plus the designers and weavers turning them into heirlooms.
body:
Few countries can claim three world-class luxury fibers, but Peru can: alpaca, vicuña and Pima cotton. Understanding the difference between them is the key to shopping well, from Lima’s design studios to the weaving communities around Cusco. Here is our primer, plus the names on our radar, as part of our guide to Latin American fashion designers.

Alpaca: The Everyday Luxury

Alpacas are domesticated camelids raised in the high Andes, and their fleece is soft, warm, lightweight and naturally free of the lanolin found in sheep’s wool. There are two breeds. Huacaya, the fluffier and far more common of the two, produces a crimped, springy fiber. Suri grows long, silky locks with a lustrous drape. ‘Baby alpaca’ refers to an especially fine grade of fiber, not to the age of the animal.

  • Feels like — softer than most wool, with a gentle halo
  • Best for — sweaters, wraps, scarves and travel throws
  • Watch for — blends sold as ‘alpaca’; check the label for fiber percentages

Alpaca comes in a remarkable range of natural shades — creams, fawns, browns, grays and near-blacks — which is why many of the most beautiful Peruvian knits are left undyed. That natural palette is also a good sign you’re looking at genuine fiber.

Vicuña: The Rarest of Them All

The vicuña is the wild ancestor of the alpaca and appears on Peru’s coat of arms. Its fiber is among the finest in the world, and because the animals are protected, it can only be gathered through regulated shearing of wild herds — a practice rooted in the traditional Andean round-up known as the chaccu, in which animals are gathered, shorn and released. Each animal yields very little fiber, which is why vicuña is so extraordinarily expensive.

If you encounter vicuña for sale, legitimate pieces should come with documentation of their origin. A suspiciously cheap ‘vicuña’ scarf at a market stall is almost certainly something else.

Pima Cotton: Peru’s Coastal Secret

Peruvian Pima is grown along the country’s northern coast and prized for its extra-long staple — longer fibers that spin into yarn that is smoother, stronger and less prone to pilling. The result is cotton with a subtle sheen and a buttery hand, perfect for T-shirts, knit basics and baby clothes. If alpaca is Peru’s winter luxury, Pima is its summer one.

Look at the fabric closely: good Pima jersey has an even, dense knit and a soft surface that improves with washing. It’s an easy, unglamorous purchase that you’ll reach for more often than almost anything else you bring home.

Arequipa’s Alpaca Houses: Kuna and Sol Alpaca

Arequipa, the White City, sits at the heart of Peru’s alpaca industry, and two of its best-known retail brands are tied to the major fiber groups based there. Kuna offers refined alpaca and vicuña-blend knitwear and accessories with a clean, contemporary look. Sol Alpaca focuses on high-quality alpaca garments and home pieces with a classic, understated palette. Both are reliable places to learn what good alpaca actually feels like before you shop elsewhere. Our Arequipa guide covers the city beyond the knitwear.

Sitka Semsch: Lima Knitwear with a Modern Edge

Lima-based designer Sitka Semsch is known for knitwear that treats Peruvian fibers like a contemporary design material rather than a souvenir. Expect generous, fluid silhouettes, refined textures and a muted palette that feels quietly luxurious. It’s the label to visit if you want alpaca that looks at home in a minimalist city wardrobe.

The appeal here is restraint. Instead of leaning on folkloric motifs, the designs let the fiber’s softness and drape carry the look — proof that Andean materials can feel entirely of the moment.

Ani Álvarez Calderón: Sustainability as Signature

Ani Álvarez Calderón is a Lima designer whose work is closely associated with sustainability and upcycling, reworking materials into bold, often surprising pieces. Her collections show how Peruvian design can look forward while respecting resources. Pair a visit with our other Peruvian profiles — Meche Correa’s embroidery-rich designs, Mozhdeh Matin’s alpaca knitwear and ESCVDO’s artisan-made pieces — and you’ll get a sense of how varied Lima’s scene is. Start planning with our Lima guide.

Cusco: Going to the Source of Andean Weaving

In Cusco, the Center for Traditional Textiles of Cusco works with weaving communities in the surrounding region to keep traditional techniques, natural dyes and community designs alive. Its spaces are a good place to see how textiles are made, learn to read regional patterns and buy pieces where the makers benefit directly. A handwoven textile from a community cooperative is a very different object from a factory-made ‘Andean’ print, and once you’ve seen the difference, you won’t unsee it. See our Cusco guide for planning the rest of your stay.

Weavers in the Sacred Valley and surrounding highland communities often use backstrap looms and plant- and insect-based dyes, including cochineal for reds. Each community has its own patterns and colors, so a single textile can tell you a lot about where it came from.

How to Shop It

  • Touch before you buy — real baby alpaca is soft, not scratchy; synthetic blends often feel slick or squeaky
  • Read the label — fiber percentages tell you more than the word ‘alpaca’ on a sign
  • Expect documentation for vicuña — and be wary of bargains
  • Buy from cooperatives and makers — ask who wove it and where; good sellers will tell you
  • Stock up on Pima basics — light, packable and easy to justify

The Latin American Designer Edit
