title: Argentine and Uruguayan Fashion Designers to Know: Buenos Aires Ateliers, Knitwear and Leather
dek: From Buenos Aires tailoring and textile labs to Uruguay’s hand-knit wool, the Río de la Plata designers worth knowing.
body:
The Río de la Plata has always dressed with intent — a little European polish, a lot of local attitude, and a deep respect for wool and leather. Buenos Aires is the engine, with a design scene that runs from romantic prints to near-architectural tailoring, while Uruguay quietly supplies some of the region’s most beautiful knitwear. Consider this our edit of the names on our radar, part of our wider guide to Latin American fashion designers.

Jazmín Chebar: Buenos Aires Romance, Done Wearably

If you want to understand how porteñas dress on a good day, start with Jazmín Chebar. The label is a Buenos Aires mainstay known for feminine, easy pieces — floaty dresses, soft blouses, well-cut denim and prints that feel considered rather than loud. It is the kind of wardrobe that moves from a long lunch in Palermo to a late dinner without a costume change.

  • Look for — printed dresses, relaxed tailoring and pieces built for layering
  • Why we love it — it captures the city’s effortless, slightly bohemian polish

The appeal is consistency. Collections tend to evolve rather than reinvent, so a piece bought on one trip slots easily alongside another bought years later — exactly what you want from a label you discover while traveling.

Pablo Ramírez: The Discipline of Black

Pablo Ramírez is one of Argentina’s most distinctive designers, celebrated for precise tailoring and a palette that leans heavily — and gloriously — on black. His work draws on a sense of Argentine history and ceremony, then strips it back to strong lines, sharp shoulders and impeccable construction.

This is clothing for people who believe a single perfect jacket outranks a closet of trends. Think of it as the counterpoint to the city’s romantic side: severe, elegant and very hard to forget.

Kostüme: Sculpture You Can Wear

The Buenos Aires duo behind Kostüme approach clothing almost like industrial design. Expect clean geometry, unexpected volumes, considered cutouts and a mostly monochrome palette that lets the shapes do the talking. Pieces often feel genderless and modular, with the kind of structure that photographs beautifully against the city’s grand old façades.

  • Look for — architectural outerwear, graphic separates and minimalist accessories
  • Best for — anyone whose wardrobe is already 80 percent black

What makes Kostüme feel distinctly Buenos Aires is the confidence: these are clothes that assume the wearer has opinions. They also travel well, since strong shapes in solid colors are easy to mix with what you already own.

Tramando: Textile Experiments from Martín Churba

Martín Churba’s Tramando is where Buenos Aires fashion gets experimental with fabric itself. The label is known for surface treatments, layered and manipulated textiles, and an artisanal sensibility that turns a simple top or scarf into something closer to a textile study. If you like clothing with a story stitched into the material, this is your stop.

The pieces often blur the line between fashion and craft, and they reward a close look — the texture, the layering and the finishing are the point. Accessories and scarves are an easy entry if a full garment feels like a commitment.

Leather Worth Packing an Empty Bag For: Cardón and Humawaca

Argentina’s cattle culture has long made leather one of its signature exports, and two labels show its range. Cardón channels the countryside — campo-inspired leather goods, belts, boots and rugged, gaucho-tinged casualwear that ages well. Humawaca takes the opposite route, with contemporary, design-led leather bags in clever shapes and colors that feel more gallery than ranch.

  • Cardón — heritage leather, belts and country-chic staples
  • Humawaca — playful, modern bags and small leather goods
  • Tip — ask about the hide and finish; good leather should smell like leather, not chemicals

For a minimalist contrast, we’ve also written about MAYDI, another Argentine label in our designer hub.

Uruguay: Manos del Uruguay and the Art of Wool

Uruguay is sheep country, and its finest fashion export may be the humble sweater. Manos del Uruguay is a nonprofit organization working with cooperatives of rural artisans, best known for hand-dyed yarns and hand-knit garments with rich, painterly colors. Buying from them means buying directly into a long-running craft network — and the pieces have the kind of slight irregularity that only real hands produce.

Uruguay also gave the fashion world Gabriela Hearst, whose quietly luxurious, ranch-rooted aesthetic we profile elsewhere on the site. Between the two, you get a clear picture of the country’s sensibility: natural fibers, understated color and an emphasis on making things that last. Planning a trip? Start with our Uruguay guide.

Montevideo’s own design scene is small and personal, with independent makers working in wool, leather and natural fibers. The best approach is to slow down, ask questions and favor pieces where you can trace the hands behind them.

Where to Shop in Buenos Aires

Palermo Soho is the obvious starting point, with designer-owned shops tucked along its leafy, low-rise streets — ideal for an afternoon of slow browsing between cafés. Recoleta skews more classic and polished. Many of the labels above also sell through their own websites, which is handy for checking what’s currently in stock before you go. Our Buenos Aires guide covers how to split your time between neighborhoods.

How to Shop It

  • Go seasonal — the Southern Hemisphere calendar runs opposite to the north, so winter coats and knits land when it’s summer back home
  • Prioritize materials — wool, leather and tailoring are where the region truly excels
  • Ask about provenance — especially for knitwear and leather; makers are usually proud to explain
  • Check customs rules — leather goods are easy to carry, but know your home country’s allowances
  • Leave room in your suitcase — a Río de la Plata sweater takes up more space than you think

For more on browsing the region’s best streets and markets, see our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Brazilian Fashion Designers to Know: Fashion, Swim and Resort
dek: Brazilian fashion designers to know, from Rio’s print-loving labels and sculptural swimwear to São Paulo’s sharp tailoring.
body:
Brazilian fashion is often reduced to the bikini, but the country’s designers cover everything from conceptual tailoring to hand-embroidered romance. Here are the Brazilian fashion designers to know across fashion, swim and resort — a natural next step after our guide to Latin American fashion designers, where you will also find our profiles of PatBO, Martha Medeiros, Silvia Furmanovich and Ara Vartanian.

Two cities define the scene. Rio de Janeiro is the spiritual home of swim and resort, where clothes are built for heat, movement and the walk from beach to bar. São Paulo is the business and fashion-week capital, with a more urban, tailored and experimental edge. The best Brazilian wardrobes borrow from both.

Osklen — Rio’s Eco-Minded Essential

Founded by Oskar Metsavaht in Rio de Janeiro, Osklen distills the city’s beach-to-street lifestyle into clean, contemporary clothing. The label is known for its focus on sustainability and Brazilian materials, with relaxed silhouettes, natural fabrics and a pared-back palette that suits warm weather perfectly.

The label also has a strong menswear offering, making it a rare stop where couples can shop together. Its pieces are the kind you will reach for long after the tan has faded.

  • Look for — linen and cotton separates, minimalist swim, easy resort pieces
  • Why we love it — Rio cool, without the clichés

Farm Rio — Joy in Print

If Osklen is Rio’s minimalism, Farm Rio is its exuberance. The label is famous for vibrant, nature-inspired prints — tropical fruit, birds, foliage — on breezy dresses and separates that feel like a holiday. It is unabashedly cheerful and one of the most recognizable Brazilian brands abroad.

The prints are the draw, but the cuts are easy and forgiving, which makes Farm Rio a smart choice for vacation dressing. Pair a printed dress with flat sandals and a straw bag, and you have a full Rio uniform.

  • Look for — printed maxi dresses, colorful co-ords, playful accessories

Lenny Niemeyer — Sculptural Swim

Lenny Niemeyer is a byword for elegant Brazilian swimwear. Her Rio label is known for sculptural cuts, sophisticated color and graphic details that give swimsuits an almost architectural quality. These pieces are designed to be worn from the sand to lunch with a sarong or wide trousers.

The appeal is quiet confidence: swimwear that flatters without relying on tiny cuts, and that looks as good in a city pool as on a beach in Bahia.

  • Look for — architectural one-pieces, refined bikinis, chic cover-ups

Adriana Degreas — São Paulo Resort Glamour

Based in São Paulo, Adriana Degreas brings a glamorous, fashion-forward eye to swim and resort wear. Expect bold prints, statement details and polished silhouettes — swimwear that feels like ready-to-wear, and resort pieces that hold their own at a city dinner.

Her collections are a favorite with travelers who want a single suitcase to work for both a beach weekend and a stylish city stay.

  • Look for — statement swimsuits, printed kaftans, resort separates

Água de Coco — From the Northeast Coast

Born in Fortaleza, on Brazil’s northeastern coast, Água de Coco is a long-standing name in Brazilian beachwear. The label is known for print-rich swim and resort collections with a sunny, tropical spirit — ideal if you want something unmistakably Brazilian for your next beach trip.

It is a reminder that Brazilian beach culture stretches far beyond Rio, and that the northeast has its own vibrant style traditions.

  • Look for — printed bikinis, flowing beach dresses, coordinated sets

Isabela Capeto — Romance and Handwork

Rio designer Isabela Capeto is beloved for romantic, handcrafted clothing. Her work is known for embroidery, appliqué and decorative details layered onto feminine silhouettes, with a vintage-inspired charm that feels personal rather than precious. It is the Brazilian answer to bohemian luxury.

Each piece feels collected rather than bought, and her love of handwork connects naturally to Brazil’s broader traditions of embroidery and lace.

  • Look for — embroidered dresses, embellished blouses, one-of-a-kind details

São Paulo Tailoring: Herchcovitch and Cris Barros

São Paulo is Brazil’s fashion capital, home to São Paulo Fashion Week and a more urban, tailored aesthetic. Alexandre Herchcovitch is one of the city’s most influential designers, known for an edgy, subversive streak and strong graphic sensibility. Cris Barros, by contrast, designs refined, feminine clothing with clean lines and luxurious fabrics — the kind of wardrobe that works from boardroom to dinner.

Between them, they capture São Paulo’s range: one side bold and boundary-pushing, the other refined and grown-up. Both are a welcome counterpoint to the beachwear that dominates Brazil’s image abroad.

  • Alexandre Herchcovitch — graphic, rebellious, sharply cut
  • Cris Barros — polished, elegant, quietly luxurious

How to Shop Brazilian Designers

  • São Paulo — the Jardins district, especially around Rua Oscar Freire, is the classic address for designer shopping
  • Rio de Janeiro — Ipanema and Leblon are where to find swim, resort and Rio labels
  • Fashion week — São Paulo Fashion Week is the country’s flagship event; check the official calendar for dates
  • Sizing — Brazilian swimwear often runs smaller and cuts higher than North American styles, so try before you buy
  • Check ahead — confirm current stockists on each label’s official channels before you travel

A final tip: Brazilian resort wear is designed for real heat and humidity, so favor natural fibers and loose cuts if you are heading north to the beaches of Bahia or the northeast. Your suitcase — and your comfort — will thank you.

From the beaches of Rio to the ateliers of São Paulo, Brazilian fashion is as varied as the country itself. For more on where to shop, see our Latin America shopping guides.

title: Colombian Fashion Designers to Know: From Bogotá to Medellín
dek: Colombian fashion designers to know, from Bogotá’s conceptual ateliers to Medellín’s swim labels and mola-inspired accessories.
body:
Colombia punches far above its weight in fashion, with a design scene that runs from sculptural Bogotá ateliers to the swimwear powerhouses around Medellín. We have already profiled several of the country’s best-known names; here are more Colombian fashion designers worth knowing. For the full regional picture, start with our guide to Latin American fashion designers.

Already on Our Site

If you are new to Colombian fashion, our existing profiles are the perfect primer: Johanna Ortiz and her ruffled, romantic resort wear; Silvia Tcherassi’s polished Caribbean glamour; Pepa Pombo’s vivid knitwear; Kika Vargas’s playful volume; Mercedes Salazar’s whimsical jewelry; and Agua by Agua Bendita’s hand-embellished swimwear. The designers below round out the picture.

Colombian designers share a few traits worth noticing: a confident way with color, a deep respect for handwork, and a genius for clothes that suit warm weather and long celebrations. Whether you are shopping in the capital or on the coast, you will find that sensibility everywhere.

Esteban Cortázar — Colombian Talent, Paris Polish

Born in Colombia and based in Paris, Esteban Cortázar brings Latin warmth to a distinctly European polish. His work is known for fluid, body-conscious dresses, clean lines and an assured use of color — clothes that move beautifully and feel sensual without being fussy.

His pieces have a timeless quality that makes them easy to wear season after season, and they translate well from a Bogotá evening to a European city break.

  • Look for — draped dresses, sleek separates, bold color blocking
  • Why we love it — effortless glamour with Colombian roots

Olga Piedrahita — Bogotá’s Conceptualist

Olga Piedrahita is one of the most respected names in Bogotá, known for an architectural, intellectual approach to clothing. Her pieces play with structure, layering and volume, often in restrained palettes that let the construction speak. It is fashion with a strong artistic sensibility — closer to sculpture than to trend.

Bogotá’s cooler, highland climate suits her layered approach perfectly, and her work is a good reminder that Colombian style is not only about the tropics.

  • Look for — sculptural coats, layered dresses, unexpected proportions
  • Why we love it — proof that Colombian fashion has a serious avant-garde

Amelia Toro — Refined Femininity

Also based in Bogotá, Amelia Toro designs refined, feminine clothing with an emphasis on craftsmanship. Expect elegant silhouettes, careful detailing and a timeless sensibility that makes her pieces work for city life and special occasions alike. Her work often highlights handwork, bringing artisan detail into polished, wearable designs.

It is the kind of label you discover once and return to on every trip, building a wardrobe piece by piece.

  • Look for — elegant dresses, tailored blouses, handcrafted details

Mola Sasa — The Mola, Made Modern

Mola Sasa takes the mola — the intricate reverse-appliqué textile art of the Guna people — and turns it into vivid, collectible accessories. The brand collaborates with Guna artisans, and its clutches, bags and statement pieces put the craft front and center with bold color and graphic shapes.

It is a lovely example of how heritage technique can travel into contemporary fashion when the makers remain part of the story. Pair it with a trip to Cartagena, where a bright clutch looks right at home against colonial walls.

  • Look for — mola clutches, embellished bags, statement accessories
  • Why we love it — artisan craft treated as luxury

Maaji and Onda de Mar — Swim, Colombian Style

Colombia is a swimwear superpower, and much of that energy comes from the Medellín area. Maaji is known for playful, reversible swimwear covered in cheerful prints — two looks in one, which makes it a packing-friendly favorite. Onda de Mar leans more glamorous, with sophisticated swim and resort pieces made for poolside lunches and sunset drinks.

Between the two, you can cover a whole beach holiday — and Colombian cuts tend to be flattering and well constructed, with fabrics that hold their shape after a day in salt water.

  • Maaji — reversible bikinis, mix-and-match prints, playful cover-ups
  • Onda de Mar — polished one-pieces, kaftans, resort dressing

Wayuu Mochilas: Buy Them Right

The colorful mochilas you will see across Colombia are crocheted by Wayuu women from La Guajira, on the country’s northern Caribbean coast. Each design carries meaning, and a well-made bag can take weeks to complete. Look for tight, even stitching and ask about the maker; buying through cooperatives or directly from Wayuu artisans helps ensure the money reaches the women who make them.

Be cautious of very cheap versions, which may be machine-made or produced outside the community. A genuine mochila is an investment in a living tradition, and it will last for years.

How to Shop Colombian Designers

  • Bogotá — the Zona Rosa, Zona G and Usaquén areas are good starting points for design-led shopping
  • Medellín — El Poblado is the hub for fashion and swim labels
  • Cartagena — the walled city is the place for resort wear and accessories
  • Colombiamoda — Medellín’s well-established fashion fair is a great way to see the industry in action; check the official calendar for dates
  • Ask questions — many Colombian labels work with artisan communities, and staff are usually glad to explain how a piece was made

A practical note: Bogotá’s high-altitude weather calls for layers, while Cartagena and the Caribbean coast are hot year-round. Shop accordingly — sculptural coats in the capital, breezy linen and swim on the coast.

Colombian fashion is generous, colorful and deeply crafted. Pack light on the way in — you will want the space on the way home.

title: Mexican Fashion Designers to Know: Where Craft Meets the Runway
dek: Mexican fashion designers who bring indigenous craft, sharp tailoring and silk storytelling to the runway, from Mexico City to Guadalajara and Oaxaca.
body:
Mexico has one of the richest textile cultures on earth, and its best contemporary designers treat that heritage as a living conversation rather than a costume. If you already know Lydia Lavín and Carla Fernández, here is who to add to your list. For the wider region, see our guide to Latin American fashion designers.

What ties these labels together is a refusal to choose between tradition and modernity. Some work hand in hand with artisan communities; others take inspiration from Mexican history, architecture or humor and translate it into thoroughly contemporary clothing. All of them are worth seeking out on your next trip.

Yakampot — Craft, Reimagined

Yakampot, led by designer Francisco Cancino, is one of the clearest examples of Mexican craft meeting runway polish. The label draws on indigenous textile techniques — weaving, embroidery, hand-finishing — and reinterprets them in contemporary silhouettes that feel at home far beyond a folk-art context. The result is luxurious and modern, with heritage embedded in the cloth rather than printed on top of it.

Collections often lean on rich, earthy palettes and strong structure, so pieces read as elegant first and “artisanal” second — exactly the balance many designers aim for and few achieve.

  • Look for — textured dresses, woven details, sculptural outerwear
  • Why we love it — it treats artisan technique as high fashion, not decoration

Julia y Renata — Guadalajara’s Detail Obsessives

Sisters Julia and Renata Franco built their label in Guadalajara, and it shows a real love of intricate surface work. Their clothes are layered with texture — openwork, appliqué, hand-finished details and inventive fabric manipulation — on feminine, often voluminous silhouettes.

These are special-occasion pieces with personality: romantic but never saccharine, and very much rooted in Mexican craftsmanship.

  • Look for — statement dresses, textured blouses, intricate trims

Carmen Rion — Texture as Language

Mexico City designer Carmen Rion works in a quieter register. Her pieces are built around texture and hand processes — knits, weaves and layered fabrics in a restrained, frequently monochrome palette. The shapes are relaxed and wearable, but the materials give everything a tactile, almost sculptural quality.

If you like clothing that feels like wearable art without shouting about it, this is your label.

  • Look for — handmade knits, layered tunics, neutral-toned separates

Sánchez-Kane — Tailoring With a Wink

Barbara Sánchez-Kane is the conceptual counterweight on this list. Her Mexico City label takes classic tailoring — suits, shirting, pinstripes — and pushes it into gender-fluid, surreal territory, with exaggerated proportions and plenty of wit. It is a reminder that “Mexican fashion” does not have to mean embroidery and color; it can also mean ideas.

The clothes are as fun to look at as they are to wear, and the craftsmanship underneath the concept is what keeps them from feeling like a gimmick.

  • Look for — deconstructed suiting, statement shirting, outerwear with a twist

Lorena Saravia — Modern Minimalism

Lorena Saravia offers clean, modern lines for the woman who wants beautiful basics with a Mexican sensibility. Expect fluid silhouettes, natural tones and an emphasis on fabric quality, often with subtle craft details that only reveal themselves up close. It is a smart choice for travel wardrobes: pieces mix easily and work from a gallery morning to a long dinner.

It is the label to reach for when you want something that feels distinctly Mexican in spirit but slips seamlessly into a wardrobe you already own.

  • Look for — easy dresses, wide trousers, elevated neutrals

Pineda Covalin — Culture in Silk

For a gift — or a souvenir with genuine design credentials — Pineda Covalin is a classic. The Mexican house is known for silk scarves, ties and accessories printed with motifs drawn from Mexican culture, nature and pre-Hispanic iconography, rendered in vivid color. It is one of the easiest ways to bring a piece of Mexican design home in your carry-on.

The scarves double as a crash course in Mexican iconography, and they fold small enough to make a thoughtful present for everyone on your list.

  • Look for — silk scarves and pocket squares, printed accessories

Oaxaca: Go to the Source

No conversation about Mexican fashion is complete without Oaxaca, where many of the techniques that inspire runway designers are still practiced by family workshops. The Zapotec weaving village of Teotitlán del Valle is known for wool textiles colored with natural dyes, including the deep reds of cochineal, and the state’s embroidered blouses vary dramatically from community to community.

If you buy here, buy directly from makers or cooperatives wherever you can, ask who made the piece and where, and be wary of machine-made copies sold as handwork. Paying fairly for artisan work is the best way to make sure these traditions continue.

How to Shop Mexican Designers

  • Mexico City — Roma, Condesa and Polanco are the neighborhoods to explore for independent and established labels
  • Check before you go — many designers sell through their own studios or by appointment; confirm on their official channels
  • Fashion week — Mexico City hosts a well-established fashion week; check the official calendar for dates
  • Respect the craft — when a design draws on an indigenous technique, ask how the label works with the community behind it
  • Leave room — textured knits and structured pieces take up space, so pack a foldable tote for the trip home

It also helps to slow down. Many of the most rewarding finds come from conversations — with a designer at a studio, or an artisan at a market stall — rather than from a quick sweep through a shopping street.

Mexican fashion rewards curiosity. Start with these names, then let the cities — and the workshops — lead you to the next ones.

title: Up-and-Coming Latin American Designers to Watch: Our Editor’s Radar
dek: Six up-and-coming Latin American designers on our radar, from Mexico City tailoring to Lima alpaca and Buenos Aires textile experiments.
body:
Every season the conversation about Latin American fashion gets louder, and the most interesting voices are rarely the ones with the biggest ad budgets. These are the up-and-coming Latin American designers on our radar — labels with a clear point of view, a strong relationship to craft, and clothes that look like nobody else’s. Consider this a companion to our full guide to Latin American fashion designers.

A note on the word “emerging”: we use it loosely. Some of these names have loyal followings at home and are only now landing on international radars; others have been quietly building for years. What unites them is that they reward the traveler who goes looking.

Sánchez-Kane — Mexico City

Barbara Sánchez-Kane designs with a sense of humor and a sharp pair of scissors. Her label, based in Mexico City, is known for gender-fluid tailoring that takes the codes of the classic suit — lapels, pinstripes, crisp shirting — and bends them toward the surreal. Expect exaggerated proportions, unexpected cutouts and pieces that sit somewhere between fashion and performance art.

It is not quiet clothing, but it is beautifully made, and the tailoring holds up even when the concept is at its most playful.

  • Look for — deconstructed suiting, shirting with a twist, statement outerwear
  • Why we love it — it proves Mexican fashion can be conceptual without leaning on folkloric shorthand

Juana de Arco — Buenos Aires

Founded by designer Mariana Cortés, Juana de Arco is one of the most distinctive labels in Buenos Aires. The house works with a handmade, collage-like approach: patchwork, bold color, hand-finished details and a strong commitment to reusing and reworking textiles. Pieces feel personal, slightly bohemian and very much of the city’s creative scene.

This is clothing for people who like their wardrobe to have a story. Nothing is overly polished, and that is entirely the point.

  • Look for — patchwork dresses, colorful knits, playful swim and intimates
  • Why we love it — a label where sustainability is part of the aesthetic, not a marketing line

Tramando — Buenos Aires

Martín Churba’s Tramando is a textile lab as much as a fashion label. The focus is on surface: layered, printed, heat-treated and manipulated fabrics that turn a simple shape into something sculptural. Silhouettes tend to be relaxed and architectural, letting the textile do the talking.

If you care about how a fabric is made as much as how a garment is cut, Tramando is a natural stop on any Buenos Aires shopping day — Palermo Soho is the obvious neighborhood to pair it with.

  • Look for — textured tops, layered dresses, experimental scarves
  • Why we love it — Argentine fashion at its most inventive

Sitka Semsch — Lima

Peru’s fiber heritage is extraordinary, and Sitka Semsch is one of the designers giving it a quietly modern voice. Based in Lima, she works largely in alpaca and other Peruvian fibers, building soft, enveloping knitwear with a minimalist, almost architectural line. The palette leans neutral — oatmeal, charcoal, cream — so the texture and drape carry the design.

These are the pieces you buy once and wear for a decade, and they make a far better souvenir than anything at the airport.

  • Look for — oversized knits, long cardigans, layered tunics
  • Why we love it — Andean fiber with a contemporary, gallery-calm aesthetic

Andrés Otálora — Colombia

Colombian designer Andrés Otálora has a gift for drama. His work is romantic and maximal, with voluminous ruffles, saturated color and silhouettes made for an entrance. There is a strong sense of Colombian festivity in the clothes, filtered through couture-level construction.

Think wedding guest, think resort evening, think anywhere you want to be the most memorable person in the room.

  • Look for — ruffled gowns, statement sleeves, bold tropical color
  • Why we love it — unapologetic glamour with real dressmaking behind it

Handred — Rio de Janeiro

Handred offers a softer, more pared-back vision of Brazilian style. The Rio label is known for relaxed tailoring in linen and other natural fabrics, with an easy, often genderless cut that suits a tropical climate perfectly. It is the opposite of the loud-print stereotype: neutral tones, fluid shapes and an emphasis on comfort.

If your idea of luxury is a perfectly cut linen shirt and wide trousers for a long lunch by the beach, start here.

  • Look for — linen shirting, wide-leg trousers, unstructured jackets
  • Why we love it — Brazilian ease without the clichés

How to Shop Emerging Designers on the Road

Smaller labels rarely have sprawling store networks, so a little planning goes a long way. Check each designer’s own website or social channels before you travel to confirm where their pieces are currently sold — many work by appointment, through their own studio, or in concept stores that rotate stock frequently.

  • Follow the fashion weeks — events such as Mexico City’s fashion week, Colombiamoda in Medellín and São Paulo Fashion Week are good places to spot new names; check the official calendar for dates
  • Ask about materials — designers working with natural fibers or artisan techniques are usually happy to explain provenance
  • Pack light — leave space in your luggage, because one good piece tends to become three
  • Go deeper — our destination guides cover the best shopping neighborhoods city by city

Keep an open mind about sizing and fit, too. Independent labels often cut differently from global brands, and many offer alterations or made-to-order options if you ask.

Buying directly from independent designers is one of the most rewarding ways to experience a city’s culture. You come home with something singular, and the money goes straight to the people making it.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in December
dek: New Year’s Eve in Rio, Brazilian summer and the start of the Caribbean dry season: where to go in Latin America in December.
body:
December is high season across much of Latin America. Summer arrives in the Southern Hemisphere, the Caribbean and Central America shift into their dry season, and holiday celebrations light up cities from Cartagena to Rio.

It’s a wonderful month to travel, but also one of the busiest — so plan early, especially around Christmas and New Year’s.

Rio de Janeiro

Réveillon on Copacabana Beach is one of the world’s great New Year’s Eve parties, with fireworks over the ocean and huge crowds dressed in white, a tradition associated with good luck and peace. Some revelers toss flowers into the sea as offerings to Iemanjá.

Beyond the beaches, the Christmas season brings lights and decorations, and a visit to Christ the Redeemer or Sugarloaf Mountain is best timed for early morning, before summer clouds and crowds build.

The rest of December is pure Rio summer: hot days at Ipanema and Leblon, sunsets at Arpoador, and cocktails in Santa Teresa. Expect heat, humidity and the occasional downpour.

Book early for New Year’s. See our Rio de Janeiro guide.

Trancoso

Trancoso is a popular holiday destination during Brazilian summer, especially around New Year, when the Quadrado glows with lanterns and the beaches fill with visitors from across Brazil and beyond.

Beyond the Quadrado, the area’s beaches — backed by cliffs, palms and reefs — are ideal for long walks and swims. Nearby villages like Arraial d’Ajuda and Caraíva offer different moods, from lively to rustic, and are easy to combine with a stay in Trancoso. Expect warm, humid weather and occasional summer showers.

Before Christmas, the pace is typically calmer. Read our Trancoso guide.

Cartagena

Cartagena’s dry season usually begins in December, bringing sunshine, breezes and holiday lights to the walled city. Christmas and New Year’s are festive, and demand is high.

Beyond the walled city, the colorful neighborhood of Getsemaní comes alive at night, with street art and music. It’s also a good time for day trips to the mud volcano at Totumo or the Rosario Islands, when seas are generally calmer as the dry season settles in.

Consider a day at the Rosario Islands or on the beaches of Barú. Our Cartagena guide has more.

Lima

Lima’s summer sun returns around December, perfect for the Costa Verde, paragliding off the Miraflores cliffs and long lunches of ceviche. It’s a good gateway for the rest of Peru, too, although the Andes are in their rainy season now.

Lima’s food scene is a destination in itself, from cevicherías to markets and Nikkei cooking, a fusion of Japanese and Peruvian flavors. Barranco’s street art, galleries and bars make it one of the city’s most atmospheric neighborhoods for an evening.

See our Lima guide.

Costa Rica

Costa Rica’s Pacific-side dry season usually begins in December, with green landscapes still lush from the rains. It’s a great time for beaches, national parks like Manuel Antonio and wildlife watching.

On the Caribbean side, the weather can be more mixed in December, so the Pacific coast is the stronger bet for beach time. Inland, Arenal Volcano and the Monteverde cloud forest make great additions, with hanging bridges, hot springs and wildlife.

Holiday weeks are busy, so book early. Read our Costa Rica guide.

Patagonia

Summer arrives in Patagonia in December, with long days and trails in full swing. It’s an excellent time for trekking, boat trips and glacier visits before the January peak.

The Perito Moreno Glacier, Torres del Paine and the trails around El Chaltén are all at their best with summer’s long days, though the wind is legendary. Expect changeable weather and bring layers, waterproofs and sunscreen — the sun is strong at these latitudes.

Our Patagonia guide covers the essentials.

Plan it

December tips:

  • Book early — holiday weeks fill fast across the region.
  • Pack for summer in the south, dry-season heat in the Caribbean.
  • Check official information for entry rules and park permits.

Pairing ideas: Rio and Trancoso combine naturally for a Brazilian summer trip, while Cartagena works well with a few days in Medellín or Bogotá. Lima is an easy gateway to the rest of Peru, and Costa Rica rewards a mix of beach, volcano and cloud forest.

Whether you’re chasing fireworks in Rio or glaciers in Patagonia, December is a month to celebrate — just plan early.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in November
dek: Patagonia opens, Puerto Vallarta dries out and spring blooms in the Southern Cone: where to go in Latin America in November.
body:
November is a month of beginnings. Patagonia’s main trekking season gets going, Mexico’s Pacific coast shakes off the rains, and the Southern Cone warms into late spring. In central Mexico, the dry season settles in just as Día de Muertos wraps up.

Best of all, it comes before the December rush — so you get strong weather odds with a little more breathing room.

Patagonia

November marks the start of Patagonia’s main season, with lengthening days and fewer crowds than midsummer. Trails around Torres del Paine and El Chaltén open up, wildflowers begin to appear and the landscapes feel fresh after winter.

On the Argentine side, El Calafate is the gateway to the Perito Moreno Glacier, and El Chaltén to the trails around Fitz Roy. On the Chilean side, Puerto Natales is the usual base for Torres del Paine. Early-season visits often reward travelers with quieter trails and dramatic light.

The weather is famously unpredictable — especially early in the season — so be ready for wind, rain, sun and even snow in a single day. Some services may still be ramping up, which is worth checking when you plan.

Our Patagonia guide covers the essentials.

Puerto Vallarta

The rains usually end by November, leaving the Sierra Madre hills green and the beaches of Banderas Bay sunny and warm. It’s an easy time for strolling the Malecón, taking a boat to the southern coves and exploring the old town’s cobbled streets.

Beyond the beaches, the town’s old center, with its cathedral, cobbled streets and Malecón sculptures, is easy to explore on foot. Nearby, the villages of Sayulita and San Pancho, to the north, offer surf and a laid-back vibe, while the jungle-backed coves to the south can be reached by boat.

Día de Muertos celebrations take place in early November, and by the end of the month, the dry season is fully underway. Humpback whales usually begin arriving around December.

See our Puerto Vallarta guide.

Uruguay

Late spring is mild in Uruguay, perfect for strolling the cobblestoned streets of Colonia del Sacramento, walking Montevideo’s long waterfront Rambla and visiting wineries known for Tannat, the country’s signature red grape. Coastal towns are quiet before the summer season.

November is also a good time to drive the Atlantic coast before the summer crowds arrive, from Punta del Este’s peninsula to the fishing village of José Ignacio and the rustic, off-grid village of Cabo Polonio, reached by special off-road vehicles across the dunes.

Whales may still be seen along the Atlantic coast early in the month. Read our Uruguay guide.

Mendoza

Late spring brings warm days and green vineyards to Mendoza, while the high peaks keep their snow. It’s an ideal time for wine tasting, long lunches among the vines and outdoor adventures from rafting on the Mendoza River to horseback riding in the foothills.

Late spring is also a good time to visit the Uco Valley, where vineyards sit at higher altitudes against the Andes, and to drive toward Aconcagua via the mountain road to Chile. Evenings are cool, so bring a layer for dinners outdoors.

See our Mendoza guide.

Mexico City

November marks the start of Mexico City’s dry season, bringing clearer skies and cooler evenings. The first days of the month overlap with Día de Muertos, on November 1 and 2, when altars and marigolds fill public spaces.

November is also a great month for day trips, including the pyramids of Teotihuacan, the colonial city of Puebla and the silver town of Taxco. With clear skies and cooler temperatures, the city’s parks, from Chapultepec to the Alameda, are at their most inviting.

After the holiday, it’s a great time for museums, markets and day trips to Teotihuacan. Our Mexico City guide has more.

Plan it

November rewards travelers who like to get ahead of the crowds. A few tips:

  • Patagonia weather — layers and waterproofs are essential.
  • Book early for Día de Muertos in Mexico City.
  • Hurricane season officially ends November 30 in the Caribbean.

Pairing ideas: combine Mendoza with Santiago or Buenos Aires, or pair Mexico City with Puerto Vallarta for a mix of city culture and beach time. Uruguay is a short ferry ride from Buenos Aires, making it easy to add on.

Check current official information before you travel.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in October
dek: Día de Muertos, jacaranda season and dry days in western Mexico: where to go in Latin America in October, from Oaxaca to Paraty.
body:
October is Mexico’s season of marigolds and memory — the moment when markets and plazas start filling with orange blooms as the country prepares for Día de Muertos. Farther south, spring blossoms return to Buenos Aires, and Brazil’s coast warms up ahead of summer. It’s a month of color everywhere you look.

It’s also a transition month in much of Mexico, as the rains taper off and drier days settle in — very good news for anyone planning to be outdoors.

Oaxaca

Oaxaca is one of Mexico’s most evocative places to experience Día de Muertos, observed from October 31 through November 2. In the days before, markets overflow with marigolds, sugar skulls, candles and pan de muerto, and families build elaborate altars to welcome back the spirits of loved ones.

Visits to cemeteries, where families gather with candles, flowers and music, are deeply moving. Late October is also a lovely time to explore the city’s mezcal culture and textile villages.

Treat it as a family and religious tradition — be respectful and ask before photographing. Book early and read our Oaxaca guide.

Mexico City

Mexico City’s Día de Muertos celebrations include public altars, marigold displays and, in recent years, a large parade — check the current schedule. The rainy season usually winds down during October, bringing clearer skies.

October is also a great time to explore the city’s museums, from the National Museum of Anthropology to the Frida Kahlo Museum in Coyoacán, and to eat your way through the markets, where seasonal pan de muerto starts appearing in bakeries.

See the altars around the Zócalo, stroll the plazas of Coyoacán and consider a trip to the canals of Xochimilco. Our Mexico City guide covers the neighborhoods.

Buenos Aires

Spring brings jacaranda trees into purple bloom across Buenos Aires, typically from late October into November. Warm days make it perfect for exploring parks and plazas, from the Bosques de Palermo and their rose garden to Recoleta’s leafy squares.

Spring also brings the city’s outdoor life back into full swing, with Sunday fairs in San Telmo, afternoons along the waterfront in Puerto Madero and evenings on the terraces of Palermo. It’s a good time for a day trip to the Tigre Delta, where rivers and islands stretch north of the city.

It’s also a lovely season for outdoor dining and weekend fairs. See our Buenos Aires guide.

Guadalajara

October generally marks the end of Guadalajara’s rainy season and the arrival of pleasant, drier weather. The city’s month-long Fiestas de Octubre fair is a longstanding tradition — check the current program — and Día de Muertos preparations begin as the month goes on.

The city’s historic center, with its cathedral and Hospicio Cabañas and its famous Orozco murals, is best explored on foot in the drier weather. Lake Chapala, Mexico’s largest lake, is an easy day trip, with lakeside towns known for their mild climate.

It’s a great time for Tlaquepaque’s galleries, mariachi music in the city where it’s deeply rooted, and a day trip to the agave landscapes around Tequila. Read our Guadalajara guide.

Paraty

Spring on Brazil’s Costa Verde brings warming weather before the summer crowds and the heavier rains of high summer. Paraty’s historic center and bay islands are ideal for relaxed exploring, and hiking trails wind through the Atlantic Forest to beaches and waterfalls.

October is also a good time for schooner trips around the bay, when the water is warming up and the islands are quiet. Paraty is known for its cachaça, and a visit to one of the historic distilleries in the surrounding hills makes a relaxed afternoon.

Add Ilha Grande or Rio to round out your trip. Our Paraty guide has more.

Plan it

October is a month to plan around the calendar. A few essentials:

  • Book Día de Muertos early — Oaxaca and Mexico City fill up fast.
  • Respect traditions — cemeteries and altars are family spaces.
  • Hurricane season continues in the Caribbean through November.

If you’re heading to Mexico, consider spending the lead-up in Mexico City or Guadalajara and the main days in Oaxaca — or vice versa. Buenos Aires and Paraty are strong picks if you’d rather trade festival crowds for spring sunshine.

Check current official information before you travel.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in September
dek: Independence celebrations, spring whales and Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast: where to go in Latin America in September.
body:
September is a patriotic month in Latin America, with independence festivities in Mexico and Chile. Spring arrives in the Southern Cone, bringing whales, blossoms and warmer days, while Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast enjoys one of its drier stretches.

Many destinations are in shoulder season, so crowds are lighter and the pace is easier — a quietly great month for travelers with flexible schedules.

Costa Rica’s Caribbean Coast

While the Pacific side is in its rainy season, the Caribbean coast is often drier around September and October. That makes it a good time for Puerto Viejo’s laid-back beaches, the reef and rainforest of Cahuita National Park, and the Afro-Caribbean cooking the region is known for — think rice and beans cooked in coconut milk.

If you do visit the Pacific side, the rainy season typically brings sunny mornings and afternoon storms, along with fewer visitors and lush landscapes. Many travelers combine the Caribbean coast with Arenal Volcano’s hot springs for a well-rounded trip.

Green sea turtles nest at Tortuguero roughly from July to October, and nighttime nesting tours must be done with authorized guides. The canals there, reached by boat, are also excellent for spotting monkeys, birds and caimans.

Our Costa Rica guide has the regional breakdown.

Mexico City

Mexico’s independence celebrations peak on the night of September 15, when the Grito rings out from the National Palace over the Zócalo, followed by a military parade on September 16. The whole month is filled with patriotic decorations, and it’s the season for chiles en nogada, the dish whose green, white and red echo the flag.

Beyond the fiestas, September is a good moment to explore the city’s food markets, where seasonal produce is abundant, and neighborhoods like Roma and Condesa, whose tree-lined streets look lush after the rains.

It’s rainy season, typically with afternoon showers, so plan museums like the National Museum of Anthropology for later in the day and outdoor sights for the morning. Read our Mexico City guide.

Santiago

Chile’s Fiestas Patrias center on September 18 and 19, with fondas (festive fairs), empanadas, cueca dancing and plenty of wine. Spring is arriving, and the Andes still wear their snow.

Spring in the capital also means blossoming parks and the start of outdoor dining season. It’s a great time for day trips to the coast — Valparaíso and Viña del Mar — or the vineyards of the Casablanca and Maipo valleys, where early spring green is starting to show.

Around the holidays, many locals head out of town and businesses close, so plan ahead. Otherwise, September is a lovely time for the city’s hills, parks and markets, with vineyards waking up for spring.

See our Santiago guide.

Uruguay

Southern right whales visit Uruguay’s Atlantic coast roughly from July to November, and spring is a good time to spot them — sometimes from shore — around Punta del Este and the Rocha coast. The beach towns are quiet and uncrowded before summer.

Spring is a lovely time for Uruguay’s quieter pleasures: a long lunch in a coastal village, wine tasting among Tannat vines, and cycling or walking the waterfront Rambla in Montevideo. September also brings more hours of daylight, and Colonia’s cobblestones look their best in the soft light.

Pair whale watching with Montevideo’s Ciudad Vieja and Rambla, and the historic quarter of Colonia del Sacramento. Our Uruguay guide covers the route.

Mendoza

Spring comes to Mendoza as vines begin to bud and snow still caps the Andes, making for dramatic vineyard views. Days warm up while visitor numbers stay moderate.

For a change of scene, the road toward the Chilean border climbs past Puente del Inca and viewpoints for Aconcagua, the highest peak in the Americas. The pass can close in bad weather, so check conditions before setting out.

It’s a great season for cycling between wineries in Maipú, long lunches in the Uco Valley and tasting the region’s Malbec. Read our Mendoza guide.

Plan it

September planning notes:

  • Check holiday closures around September 16 in Mexico and September 18–19 in Chile.
  • Pack for spring in Uruguay and Mendoza — warm days, cool nights.
  • Hurricane season continues in the Caribbean; stay flexible.

Pairing ideas: Santiago and Mendoza are linked by a spectacular Andes crossing, weather permitting, while Uruguay combines easily with Buenos Aires by ferry.

Confirm current entry rules and park regulations with official sources before you travel.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in August
dek: Medellín’s flower festival, tango season in Buenos Aires and humpback whales in Panama: where to go in Latin America in August.
body:
August is festival and wildlife season in Latin America. Flower parades take over Medellín, tango warms up a wintry Buenos Aires, and humpback whales cruise the Pacific off Panama. The Andes stay dry and sunny, making this one of the best months of the year for highland trips.

It’s a popular month for vacations, too, so the earlier you plan, the more choice you’ll have.

Medellín

The Feria de las Flores usually runs in early August and is the city’s signature celebration. Its highlight is the Desfile de Silleteros, in which flower growers from the nearby hills of Santa Elena carry elaborate floral arrangements on their backs through the streets.

The city’s neighborhoods are worth time too: El Poblado and Laureles are leafy and walkable, with plenty of cafés serving excellent Colombian coffee.

Around the parade, expect concerts, horse processions, classic car shows and a citywide party mood. Medellín’s famously spring-like climate makes all of it pleasant to enjoy outdoors.

Beyond the feria, ride the Metrocable for views over the valley, visit the murals of Comuna 13, and consider a day trip to the colorful town of Guatapé. Check official festival dates, then see our Medellín guide.

Buenos Aires

Winter in Buenos Aires is mild by northern standards — cool, sometimes damp, rarely freezing — and the city’s tango festival has traditionally taken place in August, with performances, classes and a world championship. Scheduling can shift, so check current dates.

August also brings a cultural calendar in full swing, from theater on Avenida Corrientes to concerts and exhibitions. It’s a good moment to try classic winter comforts like locro stew and hot chocolate with churros in a historic café.

It’s also prime season for cozy cafés, browsing along Avenida Corrientes, and long dinners of steak and red wine. Theaters and concert halls are busy, including the Teatro Colón.

Our Buenos Aires guide covers where to base yourself.

Panama

Humpback whales migrate from the Southern Hemisphere to Panama’s Pacific waters roughly between July and October, and the Pearl Islands and the Gulf of Chiriquí are popular areas for sightings. It’s rainy season, but mornings are often bright, with showers building later.

Rainy-season Panama has its perks, too: rainforests are at their greenest, and the Pacific islands and highland towns like Boquete are lush and quiet. Mornings are generally the best window for boat trips, before afternoon showers roll in.

Choose responsible operators that follow whale-watching guidelines, and pair a boat day with time in Casco Viejo and at the Panama Canal. Read our Panama guide.

Cusco

August is deep dry season in the Peruvian Andes: sunny days, cold nights and exceptionally clear skies over the Sacred Valley. It’s a superb month for trekking, and August is also traditionally a time of offerings to Pachamama, Mother Earth, in Andean communities.

Popular dry-season treks include the Inca Trail (permits required, booked through licensed operators), the longer Salkantay route and the colorful slopes of Rainbow Mountain. Whatever you choose, give yourself a couple of days in Cusco first to adjust to the altitude — the city sits at roughly 3,400 meters.

This is peak season, so book Machu Picchu entry and trains well ahead and check current official ticketing. Our Cusco guide has the details.

Quito

Quito’s dry season continues through August, often with breezy afternoons and clear views of the surrounding volcanoes. It’s a great base for Cotopaxi National Park, the Otavalo market and the cloud forest around Mindo, famous for its birdlife.

The city itself rewards a few days: the gilded interior of La Compañía church, the views from El Panecillo and the lively streets of La Ronda. At roughly 2,800 meters, Quito is also a gentle introduction to Andean altitude.

Combine it with a Galápagos trip for a classic Ecuador itinerary. See our Quito guide.

Plan it

For August:

  • Book ahead for Medellín’s feria and peak-season Cusco.
  • Layers — Andean nights and Buenos Aires winters are genuinely cold.
  • Rain gear for Panama’s wet season.

A smart combination: Quito and Cusco for Andean culture, or Medellín with Panama City, which are a short flight apart. Buenos Aires works well on its own — give it at least four or five days to settle into its late-night rhythm.

Check official sources for current festival dates, entry rules and park regulations.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in July
dek: Galápagos wildlife, whale sharks, the Guelaguetza and Andean ski slopes: where to go in Latin America in July.
body:
July is peak vacation season for travelers from the north, and Latin America has plenty of midyear magic to match. Think cool-season wildlife in the Galápagos, national holidays in Peru, whale sharks off the Yucatán, fresh powder above Santiago and a very big party in Oaxaca.

The trade-off is that the Caribbean is now in hurricane season and parts of Mexico and Central America are in their rainy season — usually meaning afternoon showers rather than washouts, but worth planning around.

Galápagos

The cool, or garúa, season generally runs from about June to November. The Humboldt Current brings nutrient-rich water that draws abundant marine life, and many seabirds are busy with courtship and nesting. The trade-off: cooler water, misty skies and choppier seas.

For many wildlife lovers, that’s a fair deal. Snorkeling alongside sea lions, spotting penguins around the western islands and watching blue-footed boobies do their famous high-stepping display are the kinds of moments people plan whole trips around.

Bring or rent a wetsuit for snorkeling and pack seasickness remedies for crossings. Our Galápagos guide breaks down cruise and land-based options.

Lima

Lima’s winter skies are famously gray, but the city’s food scene doesn’t take a season off. Late July brings Fiestas Patrias, Peru’s independence holidays on July 28 and 29, with red-and-white flags on balconies, parades and plenty of celebration.

Winter is also a good season for a side trip south along the desert coast to Paracas, where boat trips visit the seabird- and sea-lion-rich Ballestas Islands, or inland to the vineyards and dunes around Ica.

It’s a great moment for long ceviche lunches, market visits, and exploring the bohemian lanes of Barranco and the clifftop parks of Miraflores. The pre-Inca adobe pyramid of Huaca Pucllana, right in Miraflores, is a striking reminder of how deep the city’s history runs.

Travel demand spikes around the holiday, so book flights and buses early. Read our Lima guide.

Riviera Maya

Whale shark season in the waters off Isla Holbox and Isla Mujeres runs roughly from June to September, and July is a popular time to swim alongside these enormous, gentle filter feeders. On land it’s hot and humid, with passing showers that cool things off.

Away from the water, July is a good month for exploring cenotes, which stay cool and refreshing whatever the weather, and for early-morning visits to Tulum’s clifftop ruins. Holbox itself is a car-free island of sandy streets and hammocks — a slower, simpler counterpoint to the busier resort strip.

This is hurricane season, so watch forecasts, consider travel insurance and check sargassum conditions before you commit to a beach. Choose whale shark tours that follow the official guidelines. Our Riviera Maya guide has more.

Santiago

Midwinter usually brings some of the season’s best ski conditions to the Andes above Santiago, with slopes within roughly a couple of hours of the city. It’s easy to combine ski days with city time, wine tasting in the nearby valleys and a trip to Valparaíso.

If you have extra time, the desert of San Pedro de Atacama in the far north is a popular winter escape, with clear skies, salt flats and spectacular stargazing — just a flight away.

Even without skis, winter has its charms: clear days after rain showcase the snowy peaks, and the city’s museums, markets and wine bars feel wonderfully unhurried.

Mountain roads can require chains and conditions vary, so check before you go. Our Santiago guide covers the logistics.

Oaxaca

The Guelaguetza is Oaxaca’s great festival of regional dance, music and dress, usually held on the last two Mondays of July, with concerts, parades and food fairs filling the city throughout the month. Delegations from across the state bring their traditions to the Cerro del Fortín, and the atmosphere is colorful, proud and joyous.

July is also rainy season, which usually means afternoon showers and a lush, green valley — beautiful for drives out to the villages and ruins.

Check official festival dates and ticketing, and book lodging early. See our Oaxaca guide.

Plan it

July is busy, so plan smart:

  • Reserve festival tickets for the Guelaguetza early.
  • Pack a warm layer for Lima’s damp chill and the Galápagos water.
  • Hurricane season — for the Caribbean, stay flexible and insured.

Confirm current entry rules, park fees and tour regulations with official sources before you travel.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in June
dek: Inti Raymi, Festa Junina and Andean blue skies: where to go in Latin America in June, from Cusco and Quito to Bogotá and Santiago.
body:
June belongs to the Andes. The dry season is in full swing from Peru to Ecuador, solstice festivals fill plazas, and the Southern Hemisphere slips into winter. Meanwhile, the Caribbean enters hurricane season on June 1 — so this is a month to head for the mountains.

Bring a warm jacket, a sense of occasion and a little patience with altitude. The rewards are clear skies, dramatic landscapes and some of the most vivid celebrations of the year.

Cusco

Inti Raymi, the Festival of the Sun, is held on June 24 in Cusco, with its main ceremony staged at the Sacsayhuamán ruins above the city. The days leading up to it bring parades, music and dancing to the Plaza de Armas, and the dry-season skies are usually brilliantly clear.

Outside the festival itself, June is ideal for trekking. Rainbow Mountain, Lake Humantay and the Inca Trail are all popular dry-season routes, although the Inca Trail requires permits booked through licensed operators. Nights are cold at altitude, so pack accordingly.

This is one of the busiest weeks of the year, so book lodging and Machu Picchu entry well in advance and check current official ticketing. Our Cusco guide covers the essentials.

Quito

Quito’s drier season typically runs from about June to September, making it prime time for the colonial Old Town, the TelefériQo up the slopes of Pichincha, and day trips to Cotopaxi National Park or the cloud forests around Mindo.

June’s generally clearer skies also improve the odds of seeing the snow-capped volcanoes that ring the city. Quito’s historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is packed with ornate churches, and the equator monument at Mitad del Mundo is an easy half-day trip.

Northern Ecuador also marks the solstice with its own Inti Raymi celebrations, especially around Otavalo. Read our Quito guide.

Bogotá

Bogotá has two drier spells a year, and midyear is one of them. The weather at roughly 2,600 meters is always cool and changeable, but June tends to offer more sunny breaks for exploring La Candelaria, the Gold Museum and the ride up Monserrate.

Beyond the historic center, north Bogotá’s Usaquén neighborhood hosts a popular Sunday market, and the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá, roughly an hour or so north of the city, makes a memorable day trip.

Pack a jacket and an umbrella regardless — it’s that kind of city. See our Bogotá guide.

São Paulo

June is Festa Junina season across Brazil, with countryside-themed parties, bonfires, plaid shirts, square dancing (quadrilha) and seasonal treats like pé-de-moleque and quentão. São Paulo hosts plenty of these gatherings, and the cooler, drier winter weather suits a city best explored on foot.

Winter is also a good season for the city’s museums and cultural centers, many housed in striking modernist buildings. Neighborhoods like Pinheiros and Vila Madalena are full of bars and street art, and the Mercado Municipal is a classic stop for its famous mortadella sandwich. Evenings can be surprisingly chilly, so pack a sweater.

Pair festival nights with museum days. Our São Paulo guide has neighborhood picks.

Santiago

Winter means snow in the Andes, and ski areas lie within roughly a couple of hours of Santiago. Openings depend on snowfall, often in mid to late June, so check conditions before planning around them.

If skiing isn’t your thing, winter is still a rewarding time to visit. Museums and markets are less crowded, the wine bars are cozy, and the Central Valley vineyards are quiet after the harvest. Valparaíso’s colorful hillsides make a good day trip, too, and the coast is often milder than the capital.

On clear days after rain, the snow-capped peaks behind the city are spectacular. Our Santiago guide covers day trips and neighborhoods.

Plan it

June tips:

  • Book Inti Raymi early — Cusco fills up quickly around June 24.
  • Respect the altitude in Cusco, Quito and Bogotá — take it slowly for the first day or two.
  • Caribbean trips — if you do head to the coast, travel insurance and flexible bookings are wise during hurricane season.

A classic June route pairs Cusco with Quito for a double dose of Andean culture — or combine Quito with a Galápagos trip in the cool season. Bogotá and São Paulo make easy city breaks, while Santiago lets you mix wine, mountains and snow in one trip.

Verify current entry requirements and ticketing with official sources.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in May
dek: Andean dry season, Galápagos transitions and crisp city autumns: where to go in Latin America in May, from Cusco to São Paulo.
body:
May is a sleeper month. Crowds thin after Easter, the Andes shift into their dry season, and the Southern Cone’s cities settle into crisp autumn. It’s a great time for travelers who want strong weather odds without the intensity of peak season — and a few more tables available at dinner.

Cusco and the Sacred Valley

The Andean dry season roughly spans May to September, and May is a lovely opening act: skies clear, the hills are still green from the rains, and the big midyear crowds haven’t fully arrived. It’s an ideal time for the Sacred Valley, the terraced ruins of Pisac and Ollantaytambo, and, of course, Machu Picchu.

In Cusco itself, the San Blas neighborhood’s steep lanes and artisan workshops, the Qorikancha temple and the San Pedro Market are all rewarding. Evenings get cold quickly after sunset, so pack a warm layer for dinner.

Machu Picchu tickets and Inca Trail permits are limited and the systems change, so check official information and book well ahead. Read our Cusco guide, and give yourself time to acclimatize to the altitude before any big hikes.

Galápagos

May sits at the edge of the warm season, often combining still-pleasant water temperatures with the first cooler, nutrient-rich currents. That shift can make for rewarding wildlife watching and snorkeling while seas remain relatively manageable.

On land, the islands are still relatively green from the warm-season rains, and giant tortoises can be seen in the highlands of Santa Cruz. Many travelers combine a cruise or island-hopping trip with a few days in Quito or Guayaquil.

Cruises and land-based trips both work well now. Our Galápagos guide explains how the seasons shape itineraries.

São Paulo

Autumn brings São Paulo milder temperatures and generally drier weather, perfect for a food-and-culture city break. Walk Avenida Paulista and visit the MASP museum, spend an afternoon in Ibirapuera Park, and eat your way through Liberdade, Pinheiros and Vila Madalena.

The city is also a gateway for weekend trips: the historic coastal town of Paraty is roughly five hours away by road, and the beaches of the northern São Paulo coast are closer. May’s milder weather makes either detour pleasant.

This is a city you experience through its tables, galleries and bars rather than its beaches. Start with our São Paulo guide.

Riviera Maya

May is shoulder season on Mexico’s Caribbean coast: hot, mostly dry and quieter after spring break, and still ahead of the official start of hurricane season. Cenotes are especially welcome in the heat, and early-morning visits to Tulum or Cobá beat both the sun and the tour buses.

The heat makes water-based adventures especially appealing — snorkeling off Akumal, swimming in the cenotes around Tulum and exploring the lagoon at Bacalar, farther south, all offer a break from the sun. Farther inland, the colonial city of Valladolid and the ruins of Chichén Itzá are within reach for a long day trip — go early, as midday heat in May is serious.

Sargassum can increase as summer approaches, so check current beach conditions before you commit. See our Riviera Maya guide.

Buenos Aires

Late autumn in Buenos Aires means cool, crisp days and plane trees turning along the avenues. It’s steak-and-Malbec weather — and a great time to catch a tango show or a neighborhood milonga.

Autumn is also a good time for a day trip to the Tigre Delta, where a network of rivers and islands lies just north of the city, or a ferry to Colonia del Sacramento in Uruguay.

May 25 is a national holiday marking the May Revolution, often celebrated with hearty traditional dishes like locro. Our Buenos Aires guide has more.

Plan it

May planning notes:

  • Altitude first — build a slow day or two into any Cusco trip.
  • Layers — Andean mornings and Buenos Aires evenings are cool.
  • Check official sources for Machu Picchu tickets and Galápagos rules, which are updated periodically.

Short on time? Cusco pairs naturally with Lima for a Peru-focused trip, while the Galápagos combine easily with Quito. São Paulo and Buenos Aires are a quick flight apart and make a satisfying two-city autumn escape — just bring a warmer layer than you think you’ll need.

Whatever you choose, May’s lighter crowds give you more flexibility, so it’s a good month to travel a little slower and linger where you like.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in April
dek: Autumn light in the Southern Cone, last dry weeks in Costa Rica and sunny Caribbean beaches: where to go in Latin America in April.
body:
April is a quietly excellent month for Latin America. In the south, autumn brings mild days and golden vineyards. Farther north, it’s the tail end of the dry season, with warm weather before the rains arrive. Just keep an eye on Semana Santa, which falls in March or April depending on the year and fills beaches, buses and hotels across the region.

Costa Rica

April is typically the last full month of the Pacific-side dry season, so Guanacaste and the Nicoya Peninsula are still sunny, hot and beach-ready. Surf towns hum, sunsets are reliably fiery, and wildlife watching can be rewarding as animals gather near rivers and water sources.

Heat builds as the month goes on, so plan beach time for mornings and late afternoons, and save the midday hours for shade, siestas and fresh fruit. By late April or May, the first rains usually begin to turn the landscape green again.

Inland, the volcanic landscapes around Arenal make a good contrast to beach days. Semana Santa is a major domestic travel week, so book early if your dates overlap. Our Costa Rica guide covers the regions.

Santiago

Early autumn is harvest time in Chile’s Central Valley, and the vineyards of the Maipo, Casablanca and Colchagua valleys are all within day-trip or overnight range of the capital. Days are warm, evenings cool, and the Andes look sharp against clear skies.

Autumn also clears the air a little compared with summer, and the city’s parks and hills — Cerro San Cristóbal and Cerro Santa Lucía among them — make good vantage points. The neighborhoods of Lastarria and Bellavista are ideal for evening strolls, with plenty of cafés and wine bars to choose from.

Add a trip to the colorful, funicular-laced hills of Valparaíso — about an hour and a half away — for a well-rounded visit. Read our Santiago guide.

Buenos Aires

Autumn is one of Buenos Aires’ most comfortable seasons. Mild temperatures make it easy to walk the city from Recoleta’s grand avenues to La Boca’s painted facades, linger in historic cafés, and keep local hours — dinner rarely starts early here.

It’s also a great season for day trips to the countryside, where estancias offer a taste of gaucho culture, asado and horseback riding under wide skies.

Theaters, galleries and bookshops are in full swing, too, making it a great month for a culture-heavy trip. Our Buenos Aires guide has neighborhood picks.

Guadalajara

Guadalajara’s dry season generally lasts until the rains arrive around June, so April is warm and sunny. It’s a great time for exploring the historic center’s cathedral and plazas, the artisan streets of Tlaquepaque, and a day trip to the blue agave fields around the town of Tequila.

Semana Santa is observed with processions and religious services in many of Jalisco’s towns, which can be moving to witness respectfully. The city’s murals by José Clemente Orozco, particularly at the Hospicio Cabañas, are worth a slow visit on a hot afternoon.

Afternoons can run hot, so plan outdoor sightseeing for mornings and evenings. See our Guadalajara guide.

Punta Cana

April remains in the Dominican Republic’s drier stretch, well ahead of hurricane season, with warm water and long beach days. After the northern winter rush, the pace can feel a touch calmer — outside Semana Santa, when domestic travelers head to the coast in force.

Beyond the resort strip, consider a day in the colonial zone of Santo Domingo, home to some of the oldest colonial buildings in the Americas, or a boat trip to Isla Saona. Both are long days, but they offer a different view of the country.

It’s a good month for snorkeling and catamaran days on calm seas. The Punta Cana guide covers beaches and easy excursions.

Plan it

A few April essentials:

  • Look up Semana Santa — it can shift prices and closures across the region.
  • Bring a light layer for Santiago and Buenos Aires evenings.
  • Sun protection is non-negotiable in Guanacaste and Punta Cana.

If you’re choosing just one trip, think about the mood you want: vineyards and city culture in Santiago and Buenos Aires, or sun and sea in Costa Rica and Punta Cana. Guadalajara splits the difference, with food, crafts and agave country all within easy reach.

Confirm current entry requirements and any park rules with official sources before you travel.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in March
dek: Harvest festivals, calm Galápagos seas and jacaranda season: where to go in Latin America in March, from Mendoza to Mexico City.
body:
March is a month of graceful transitions. The Southern Hemisphere slides from summer into early autumn, the grape harvest gets underway in Argentina’s wine country, and Mexico and the Caribbean are still enjoying their dry season. It’s a smart shoulder-ish month with plenty to celebrate — and a few fewer elbows than February.

Mendoza

Harvest season in Mendoza generally runs from about February into April, and the Fiesta Nacional de la Vendimia — the region’s grape harvest festival — usually peaks in early March with parades, the crowning of a harvest queen and a grand theatrical finale in an open-air amphitheater. Exact dates vary, so check the current program.

Harvest time is also good for outdoor adventures: rafting on the Mendoza River, horseback rides in the foothills, and the drive toward Aconcagua, the highest peak in the Americas, on the road to Chile.

Beyond the festivities, it’s a beautiful time for vineyard visits in Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley, with the Andes as a backdrop and vines heavy with fruit. Our Mendoza guide has the wine-region breakdown.

Buenos Aires

By March, the worst of the summer heat has usually eased and porteños are back from their beach holidays, which means cafés, milongas and parrillas are buzzing again. It’s lovely weather for walking Palermo’s leafy streets, browsing San Telmo’s antiques and staying out for a very late dinner.

Late summer is also a fine moment for day trips — the Tigre Delta, just north of the city, is at its leafiest, and the ferry across the Río de la Plata to Colonia del Sacramento in Uruguay makes an easy excursion.

Pair it with Mendoza for a classic wine-and-city trip — they’re about a two-hour flight apart. Read our Buenos Aires guide.

Riviera Maya

March is still dry season on Mexico’s Caribbean coast, with warm water and sunny days before the heavier heat of late spring. It’s a great time for cenote swimming, exploring the ruins at Tulum and Cobá, and slow beach days from Playa del Carmen south toward Tulum.

Spring break and Semana Santa (March or April, depending on the year) can bring crowds, and seaweed (sargassum) varies from year to year — check current conditions. See our Riviera Maya guide.

Galápagos

The islands’ warm season runs roughly from December to May, bringing calmer seas, warmer water for snorkeling and greener landscapes after occasional showers. March is a comfortable time to be on the water, especially if you’re prone to seasickness, and marine iguanas and sea lions are reliably good company year-round.

Warm-season sunshine also makes for inviting beaches, such as Tortuga Bay on Santa Cruz, and the highlands where giant tortoises roam are lush and green.

Visitor rules and fees are set by the national park, so confirm current requirements. Our Galápagos guide explains cruise versus land-based trips.

Paraty

As Brazilian summer winds down, Paraty’s colonial center — roughly halfway between Rio and São Paulo — starts to feel more relaxed. The water is still warm for schooner days among the bay’s islands and beaches, and the forested hills of the Costa Verde stay lush and dramatic.

The car-free historic center, with its whitewashed buildings and big uneven paving stones, is made for slow, sensible-shoes wandering. Inland, the hills hide waterfalls and cachaça distilleries worth an afternoon.

Late-summer showers are possible, so keep your plans flexible. The Paraty guide covers beaches, waterfalls and day trips.

Mexico City

Late winter into spring is jacaranda season in Mexico City, when purple blossoms line avenues and parks; timing varies a little each year but often peaks around March. It’s also the dry season, with warm, clear afternoons ideal for museums, markets and neighborhood wandering in Roma, Condesa and Coyoacán.

Spring is also an ideal time for a day trip to the pyramids of Teotihuacan, about an hour northeast of the city, before summer rains set in. Go early to beat the heat and the crowds.

Mornings can be hazy, so save rooftop views for later in the day. Start with our Mexico City guide.

Plan it

March is a flexible month, but a few things help:

  • Check Vendimia and Semana Santa dates — both move around and affect availability.
  • Pack for two seasons if you’re combining Argentina with Mexico or the Caribbean.
  • Verify park rules for the Galápagos and other protected areas before booking.
