title: Where to Go in Latin America in February
dek: Carnaval season, whale watching and Patagonia’s summer peak: where to go in Latin America in February, from Rio to Panama.
body:
February is Latin America in full voice. Carnaval season usually lands in February or early March, the Southern Hemisphere is still basking in summer, and much of Mexico and Central America is enjoying its dry season. Whether you want glitter and drums or whales and glaciers, this is a month with very few bad options — just a few crowded ones.

Rio de Janeiro

Carnaval falls on dates that shift each year — usually February, sometimes early March — and Rio is its most famous stage. The samba school parades at the Sambadrome are the headline act, a dazzling all-night spectacle of floats, costumes and percussion. But the free street parties known as blocos, which take over neighborhoods from Santa Teresa to Ipanema, are where the city really lets loose.

Between parties, the city’s classics are at their summery best: the cable car up Sugarloaf Mountain, the train or road to Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado, and a lazy afternoon on the sand at Leblon. Go early for views — clouds often build later in the day.

Even outside Carnaval week, February is peak beach season: hot, humid and gloriously busy, with sunsets at Arpoador drawing applause. Confirm this year’s dates first, then read our Rio de Janeiro guide.

Trancoso

Bahia’s southern coast is in high summer, and Trancoso’s grassy Quadrado — lined with brightly painted houses and anchored by a small white church — is at its most atmospheric after dark, when lanterns glow and dinner runs late. Days belong to long beaches backed by cliffs and palms, with warm water and a barefoot dress code.

Nearby villages such as Arraial d’Ajuda and Caraíva offer different moods — the latter reached by a short canoe crossing and known for its sandy, car-free lanes. Both are summer favorites.

Carnaval brings a second wave of visitors to the area, so plan and book accordingly. The Trancoso guide covers the beaches and nearby villages worth a detour.

Puerto Vallarta

Humpback whales winter in Banderas Bay roughly from December to March, and February is a sweet spot for sightings — breaching, tail slaps and, if you’re lucky, a mother and calf. Add dry-season sunshine, warm water and the cobblestoned charm of the Zona Romántica, and it’s an easy sell.

Beyond the bay, dry-season days are ideal for boat trips to the southern coves, snorkeling around the Marietas Islands (access to some areas is restricted, so check current rules) and sunset strolls along the Malecón, dotted with sculptures.

Whale-watching boats are regulated, so choose operators that follow local rules on distance and approach. Start with our Puerto Vallarta guide.

Panama

Panama’s dry season runs roughly from mid-December to April, making February ideal for exploring Casco Viejo’s restored plazas on foot, watching enormous ships inch through the Panama Canal locks, and sailing out to the palm-dotted islands of Guna Yala (San Blas), where the Guna people govern their own territory.

The dry season also means clearer trails in the rainforest of Soberanía National Park, a short drive from the capital, and smoother crossings to the islands. Afternoons in the city are hot, so plan walking for mornings and evenings.

Panama celebrates Carnaval with real gusto too, especially in the town of Las Tablas. Our Panama guide lays out how to combine the city with island time.

Patagonia

Summer is still in full swing, and February keeps the long days while the trails can feel a touch less frantic than in early January. It’s a strong month for the classic treks around Torres del Paine and the Fitz Roy massif near El Chaltén, and for boat trips among the icebergs of Lago Argentino.

On the Argentine side, El Calafate is the jumping-off point for the Perito Moreno Glacier, where walkways face a wall of ice that periodically sheds chunks into the lake with a thunderous crack. Over in Chile, Puerto Natales is the usual base for Torres del Paine.

Weather here changes by the hour, so build buffer days into any itinerary. See our Patagonia guide for routes and logistics.

Plan it

February is festival-heavy, which means planning is everything:

  • Confirm Carnaval dates — they move every year and can reshape your whole itinerary, for better or worse.
  • Expect peak demand in Rio, Trancoso and Patagonia; booking several months ahead is sensible.
  • Hydrate and pace yourself — Brazilian summer heat plus a week of blocos is a marathon, not a sprint.

As always, check current official entry and park information before you travel.

title: Where to Go in Latin America in January
dek: Southern summer, Caribbean dry season and crisp highland sunshine: January’s best Latin America trips, from Patagonia to Punta Cana.
body:
January might be the easiest month of the year to plan a Latin America trip. The southern half of the continent is deep in summer, the Caribbean and much of Central America are in their dry season, and the Mexican highlands trade rain for bright, cool days. The catch? Everyone else knows it too — so book early, pick your pace, and let the weather do the heavy lifting.

Patagonia

January sits at the heart of the Patagonian summer, which is exactly when you want to be at the bottom of the world. Days are long — daylight can stretch well into the late evening — and the trails around Torres del Paine and El Chaltén are at their most accessible. The Perito Moreno Glacier near El Calafate is a spectacle in any season, but summer makes the whole circuit far easier to string together.

Pack for wind, not just cold; it is famously relentless this time of year, and sunshine can turn to sleet within the hour. It’s also the busiest stretch of the season, so reserve lodging and refugios well ahead. Our Patagonia guide covers how to split your time between the Chilean and Argentine sides.

Uruguay

This is Uruguay’s high season, when Punta del Este fills with sun-seekers from across the region and the quieter coast around José Ignacio and Cabo Polonio hums with beach-town energy. The Atlantic stays on the brisk side, but long evenings, grills fired up at sunset and an unhurried rhythm make up for it.

Inland, the wineries around Montevideo and the Carmelo area are pleasant summer detours, and Colonia del Sacramento’s cobblestoned historic quarter is lovely in the long evening light.

Montevideo’s Carnaval, often described as one of the longest-running in the world, usually gets going in late January with candombe drumming and murga theater — check the current calendar. The Uruguay guide has the full coastal breakdown.

Cartagena

Colombia’s Caribbean coast is in its dry season from roughly December through April, and January delivers steady sunshine plus trade-wind breezes that take the edge off the heat. It’s prime time for wandering the walled city at golden hour, boating out to the Rosario Islands, and lingering over ceviche and fresh juice in Getsemaní.

Beyond the old town, January is also a good month for the mud volcano at Totumo or a boat day to the beaches of Barú, when seas are generally calm and skies bright.

It’s also peak season, with crowds and demand at their highest in the first week of the month. Start with our Cartagena guide to choose a neighborhood.

Costa Rica’s Pacific Coast

On the Pacific side — Guanacaste and the Nicoya Peninsula in particular — the dry season runs roughly December to April, and January is reliably sunny, with golden, dusty landscapes and glassy morning surf. It’s excellent beach weather, and inland the cloud forests of Monteverde feel refreshingly cool by comparison.

The Caribbean coast plays by different rules and can be wetter now, so plan your route accordingly. See the Costa Rica guide for the regional split.

Oaxaca

Oaxaca’s dry season means clear blue skies, warm afternoons and genuinely chilly nights — ideal weather for walking the Centro’s colorful streets, climbing through the ruins of Monte Albán and heading out to the mineral pools of Hierve el Agua or the mezcal villages of the surrounding valleys.

January also tends to feel a little calmer once the holiday rush has passed. Our Oaxaca guide maps out the neighborhoods, markets and day trips.

Punta Cana

For a pure warm-weather escape, the Dominican Republic’s east coast is in its drier, breezier season and comfortably outside hurricane season, which runs June 1 to November 30. Expect sunny days, turquoise water and plenty of company from colder climates.

Humpback whales gather in Samaná Bay roughly from January to March — a long day trip, but a memorable one. Details are in the Punta Cana guide.

Plan it

January rewards early planners. A few quick pointers before you book:

  • Book ahead — Patagonia lodging, Cartagena and Uruguay’s beach towns can fill up months in advance.
  • Pack for range — Oaxaca nights and Patagonian winds both call for a real jacket, even if the rest of your trip is swimsuits.
  • Check the rules — park permits, fees and entry requirements change, so confirm current official information before you go.

title: Punta del Este: A Guide to Uruguay’s Beach Capital
dek: Calm Playa Mansa, surfy Playa Brava, sea lions and Casapueblo sunsets — a guide to Punta del Este and its coastline.
body:
Punta del Este is where Uruguay goes glamorous. This slim peninsula, where the Río de la Plata meets the Atlantic, draws a well-heeled summer crowd from across the region — yet it’s also a place of wide beaches, sea lions and some spectacular sunsets. Here’s how to get your bearings.

Getting Oriented

Punta del Este sits on the coast of Maldonado department, roughly two hours east of Montevideo by car or bus. The town occupies a narrow peninsula with high-rise apartments along the shore, a grid of streets at its tip, and beaches running along both sides. The peninsula’s two coasts have very different personalities — and that’s the first thing to understand.

The wider area, often simply called “Punta” by visitors, stretches well beyond the peninsula itself, taking in residential districts, pine-shaded neighborhoods and a string of beach communities along the coast. Having a car, or budgeting for taxis, makes it much easier to explore beyond the center.

Playa Mansa vs Playa Brava

The names say it all. Playa Mansa (“tame beach”) runs along the western, bay-facing side, where the water is generally calmer and the evenings are made for sunset watching. Playa Brava (“wild beach”) faces the open Atlantic on the eastern side, with stronger waves, more wind and a surfier crowd.

  • Pick Playa Mansa — for swimming with kids, calm water and sunsets over the bay.
  • Pick Playa Brava — for surf, bracing waves and long beach walks.

Lifeguard flags matter on the Brava side; the Atlantic currents deserve respect.

La Mano and the Peninsula

On Playa Brava, giant concrete fingers rise out of the sand: La Mano (also called Los Dedos), a sculpture by Chilean artist Mario Irarrázabal from the early 1980s. It has become the city’s unofficial symbol, and yes, everyone takes the photo.

From there, walk or cycle toward the tip of the peninsula, past the lighthouse and the rocky point where the two waters meet. The old town grid has shops, cafés and a relaxed feel outside peak season.

The Port, the Marina and the Sea Lions

Punta del Este’s port is a lively mix of yachts, fishing boats and seafood spots. Sea lions often lounge near the docks, hoping for scraps from the fishermen cleaning their catch — an entertaining, if slightly chaotic, sight. Keep a respectful distance; they’re wild animals.

For a closer look at a real colony, boat trips head out to Isla de Lobos, a small rocky island a short distance offshore that’s home to one of the region’s largest sea lion colonies and a tall lighthouse. Landings are generally not permitted, so visits are made by boat. Departures depend on season and sea conditions — check current options locally. Closer in, Isla Gorriti, across the bay, is another popular boat outing.

La Barra

East of town, across the rolling bridge over the Arroyo Maldonado, La Barra is Punta’s bohemian-chic neighbor. It has a laid-back, surfy personality, with boutiques, galleries and beach bars that come alive in summer. Continue further along the coast and you’ll reach the quieter, more exclusive beaches that lead toward José Ignacio.

Casapueblo at Punta Ballena

West of Punta del Este, on the headland of Punta Ballena, sits Casapueblo, the whitewashed, Mediterranean-meets-sandcastle creation of Uruguayan artist Carlos Páez Vilaró. Built over many years, it cascades down the cliff toward the sea and houses a museum, gallery and hotel. Sunset here is a local ritual. Check current visiting information before you go, as access and ticketing can change.

Practical Tips

Peak season runs from late December through January, when the town is packed, prices climb and the nightlife runs late. For a calmer visit, consider December or February–March. Outside summer, many businesses reduce hours or close, and the town takes on a quiet, off-season charm.

Punta del Este works well as a stop on a wider trip. See our Uruguay guide for more on the coast, and the four-day Uruguay itinerary for how to combine it with Montevideo and Colonia.

title: Best Time to Visit Rio de Janeiro: Weather, Seasons and Carnival
dek: Hot summers, a moving Carnival date and mild, drier winters: how to pick the right season for your Rio de Janeiro trip.
body:
There’s no truly bad time to visit Rio — it’s a tropical city with warm weather most of the year. But the season you choose shapes everything from beach days to crowds to how much you’ll sweat climbing to a viewpoint. Here’s how the year breaks down.

Rio’s Seasons at a Glance

Rio is in the Southern Hemisphere, so its seasons run opposite to North America and Europe. Summer spans roughly December through March, and winter runs from about June through August.

  • Summer (December–March) — hot, humid and lively, with frequent afternoon downpours.
  • Autumn (April–May) — still warm, gradually less humid, and calmer after the summer rush.
  • Winter (June–August) — mild and generally drier, with cooler evenings.
  • Spring (September–November) — warming up again, with the city easing back into beach mode.

Summer: Peak Heat and Peak Energy

Summer is when Rio feels most like Rio: packed beaches, outdoor parties, late nights and a festive mood that runs from the holidays through Carnival. It’s also genuinely hot and humid, and some days are sweltering, especially away from the ocean breeze.

Summer is typically the rainiest stretch of the year, though rain often comes as heavy, short-lived afternoon storms rather than all-day drizzle. Plan sightseeing — especially Christ the Redeemer and Sugarloaf — for mornings, when views are more likely to be clear and the heat is gentler.

Carnival and New Year’s Eve

Rio’s two biggest celebrations fall in summer, and both transform the city.

  • New Year’s Eve (Réveillon) — huge crowds gather on Copacabana Beach, many dressed in white, for fireworks over the water.
  • Carnival — held in the days before Lent, so the date moves each year and usually lands in February or early March. Expect the samba school parades at the Sambadrome and street parties, called blocos, all over the city.

Both are unforgettable, and both come with the year’s highest demand. Accommodation fills up well in advance and often requires minimum stays, so book early and check the exact Carnival dates for your year before planning anything else.

Winter: Mild, Drier and Relaxed

Winter is a strong option if you prefer comfortable temperatures for walking and hiking. Days are typically warm and pleasant, skies are often clearer, and humidity drops. Evenings can feel cool enough for a light jacket, and the ocean is noticeably chillier.

Beach days still happen, particularly on sunny afternoons, but they’re less of a guaranteed daily event. In exchange, you get easier sightseeing, better conditions for trails in Tijuca National Park, and fewer crowds outside of Brazilian school holidays in July.

The Shoulder Seasons

For many travelers, the sweet spot is autumn (April–May) or spring (September–November). Temperatures are warm enough for the beach, the most intense summer heat has passed or not yet arrived, and prices tend to be more reasonable than during Carnival and the holidays.

Weather can be changeable in these months, so build some flexibility into your plans for viewpoints and boat trips.

Crowds, Holidays and Sea Conditions

Weather is only half the equation. Brazilian school holidays — the long summer break around December and January, plus a shorter stretch in July — bring domestic travelers to the beaches and popular sights. Long holiday weekends do the same, so it’s worth checking the Brazilian calendar before you lock in dates.

The Atlantic also changes with the seasons. Water is warmest in late summer, while winter swells can make some beaches rougher and better suited to surfers than swimmers. Wherever you go, pay attention to lifeguard flags and local advice — currents along Rio’s open beaches can be strong in any month.

So When Should You Go?

  • For festivals and energy — late December through Carnival, if you book early and don’t mind heat.
  • For hiking and sightseeing — June through August, when conditions are milder and drier.
  • For balance — April–May or September–November, for warm weather with fewer crowds.
  • Whenever you go — pack sunscreen, a light rain layer and something slightly warmer for evenings.

Once you’ve chosen your dates, map out your days with our 3-day Rio itinerary and dig into neighborhoods and logistics in our Rio de Janeiro guide.

title: Where to Stay in Quito: A Neighborhood Guide
dek: From colonial Centro Histórico to leafy La Floresta and the valleys below, here is how to pick the right Quito neighborhood for your trip.
body:
Quito stretches long and narrow along a high Andean valley, which means where you sleep shapes your whole trip — how far you walk, what you eat, how you spend your evenings. The good news: each neighborhood has a distinct personality, and none of them are hard to love. Here is how to choose, with our full Quito guide for everything else.

Centro Histórico: For Architecture and Atmosphere

Quito’s colonial core was one of the first places ever named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it shows. Whitewashed plazas, gilded church interiors, carved balconies and steep lanes make this the most photogenic place to base yourself. Staying here puts you within walking distance of Plaza Grande, the Basílica del Voto Nacional and La Compañía church — the headline sights on most first visits.

The trade-off is that the center quiets down considerably after dark, especially on side streets. Stick to well-lit, busier areas at night, and consider a taxi for evening outings. Calle La Ronda, with its restored facades and lively weekend energy, is a good exception.

La Floresta: For Cafés and Creative Energy

If you want to feel like you actually live in Quito, La Floresta is a strong pick. This residential, tree-lined neighborhood has an artsy, slightly bohemian streak — think independent cafés, street murals, small galleries and an art-house cinema scene. It is calm, walkable and well placed between the old town and the modern north.

It suits travelers who prefer neighborhood rhythm over big-ticket sightseeing on the doorstep. You will likely take short taxi rides to the historic center, but the evenings here are easygoing and pleasant.

La Mariscal: Central and Social, With Some Caveats

La Mariscal, anchored by Plaza Foch, has long been Quito’s traveler hub — dense with guesthouses, bars, restaurants and tour offices. It is convenient, lively and easy for first-timers to navigate by day.

At night, the picture is more mixed. Petty theft is a known concern here, so if you stay, keep valuables out of sight, use app-based or official taxis after dark rather than walking long stretches, and favor the busier blocks around the plaza. Plenty of visitors stay happily in La Mariscal; it simply rewards a little street sense.

González Suárez: For Views and Polish

Perched along the eastern edge of the city, the González Suárez area is known for its upscale high-rises and sweeping views over the Guápulo valley. It feels quieter and more residential, with a polished, established air.

This is a good choice if you value a calm, comfortable base and do not mind taking taxis to most sights. The views at sunrise alone can make an early alarm feel worthwhile.

Guápulo: A Village Below the City

Tucked down a steep hillside beneath González Suárez, Guápulo feels like a small colonial village that the city forgot to swallow. Its centerpiece is a whitewashed sanctuary church, surrounded by winding lanes and a handful of cafés with valley views.

It is atmospheric and peaceful, but the hills are serious — expect steep climbs back up to the main road, especially at altitude. Best for travelers who want charm over convenience.

Tumbaco and Cumbayá: The Valley Option

East of the city and lower in elevation, the valleys of Cumbayá and Tumbaco are noticeably warmer and sunnier. Cumbayá in particular has a relaxed, suburban feel with a pleasant central park and plenty of places to eat, while Tumbaco leans more residential and green.

These areas appeal to longer stays, families and anyone wanting milder weather and a bit more space. The catch is distance: getting into the historic center means a drive of roughly half an hour or more depending on traffic. They also make a handy base if you plan to head out on day trips toward the east.

How to Choose

  • First visit, short stay — Centro Histórico or La Floresta
  • Nightlife and convenience — La Mariscal, with sensible precautions
  • Quiet comfort and views — González Suárez
  • Romance and character — Guápulo
  • Warmer weather, longer stays — Cumbayá or Tumbaco

Whichever you pick, remember that Quito sits at roughly 2,850 meters (about 9,350 feet), so give yourself an easy first day, drink plenty of water and go light on alcohol while you adjust. Taxis and ride-hailing apps are widely used and make it simple to hop between neighborhoods. Once you have your base sorted, map out your days with our three-day Quito itinerary.

title: Art and Design in São Paulo: Museums, Architecture and Street Art
dek: MASP, Pinacoteca, Niemeyer’s Ibirapuera and Beco do Batman: a guide to São Paulo’s art, architecture and design scene.
body:
São Paulo doesn’t wear its beauty on the surface — this is a city of concrete, towers and traffic. But look closer and you’ll find one of the strongest art and design scenes in Latin America, from modernist landmarks to world-class museums and ever-changing street murals.

MASP on Avenida Paulista

The São Paulo Museum of Art, or MASP, is the city’s signature cultural landmark. Designed by architect Lina Bo Bardi, its main volume appears to float above the street, suspended between four bright red pillars, leaving an open public space beneath.

Inside, the collection spans European masters to Brazilian artists. MASP is known for displaying many paintings on transparent glass easels — a bold modernist idea that makes the gallery feel open and unexpected. It’s the natural starting point for an art-focused day on Avenida Paulista.

If Bo Bardi’s work hooks you, seek out SESC Pompeia, her celebrated conversion of an old factory into a community and cultural center, with raw concrete towers linked by aerial walkways.

Pinacoteca: A Brazilian Art Deep Dive

Near Luz Park, the Pinacoteca de São Paulo is one of the city’s oldest art museums and a key place to understand Brazilian art history. The building itself is a highlight: a historic brick structure thoughtfully renovated with open courtyards, skylights and walkways.

Its collection concentrates on Brazilian art from the 19th century onward. Pair it with a walk around Luz Park and a visit to the historic center — by daylight.

Ibirapuera Park and Oscar Niemeyer

Ibirapuera is São Paulo’s great green space and an open-air showcase of modernist architecture. Oscar Niemeyer designed several of its buildings, linked by a long, curving covered walkway known as the marquise.

  • The Bienal Pavilion — home to the São Paulo Bienal, one of the world’s major contemporary art exhibitions, held every two years.
  • The Oca — a white, dome-shaped exhibition hall that looks almost otherworldly.
  • Auditório Ibirapuera — a sharply angled concert hall with a striking red entrance canopy.
  • Museums — the park is also home to the Museum of Modern Art (MAM) and Museu Afro Brasil.

Give yourself at least half a day to explore the buildings, galleries and grounds.

Beco do Batman and Street Art

São Paulo is one of the world’s great street art cities, and the best-known spot is Beco do Batman in Vila Madalena — a small network of alleys where almost every surface is covered in murals. The artwork changes regularly, so no two visits are the same.

Go in daylight, wander the surrounding streets for more murals and galleries, and end with a drink at one of the neighborhood’s bars.

Instituto Tomie Ohtake and Design Shopping

In Pinheiros, the Instituto Tomie Ohtake is a cultural center honoring the Japanese-born Brazilian artist Tomie Ohtake. Housed in a boldly colored building designed by her son, architect Ruy Ohtake, it hosts rotating exhibitions of contemporary art and design.

The surrounding neighborhoods are also ideal for design shopping. Jardins leans toward polished furniture showrooms and high-end boutiques, while Pinheiros has independent design stores, galleries and ceramics studios. Keep an eye out for Brazilian modernist furniture and pieces by contemporary local designers.

A Far Trip Worth Knowing: Inhotim

Serious art lovers often add Inhotim to their Brazil plans — but know that it isn’t a day trip from São Paulo. Located in Brumadinho, in the state of Minas Gerais, it’s usually reached by flying to Belo Horizonte and then driving roughly an hour and a half.

Inhotim combines contemporary art pavilions and large-scale outdoor installations with vast botanical gardens. It deserves at least a full day, ideally two. Check current opening days and ticket information before planning your trip.

Planning Your Art Days

  • Check schedules — museums often close one day a week, and some offer free or reduced-price days; confirm current details before visiting.
  • Group by area — pair MASP with Paulista, the Pinacoteca with Centro, and Beco do Batman with Pinheiros.
  • Use the metro — it’s the fastest way to hop between cultural hubs.

title: What to Eat in São Paulo: Dishes Every Visitor Should Try
dek: Mortadella sandwiches, pastel, virado à paulista and a pizza obsession: a guide to eating your way through São Paulo.
body:
Ask a paulistano what the city does best and there’s a good chance the answer is food. Generations of immigrants — Italian, Japanese, Lebanese, Portuguese and many more — have shaped one of the most diverse dining cities in the Americas. Come hungry and plan accordingly.

The Mortadella Sandwich at the Mercadão

The Mercado Municipal, known to locals as the Mercadão, is a grand market hall in the historic center, famous for its stained-glass windows and abundant fruit stalls. It’s also home to the city’s most iconic sandwich: the sanduíche de mortadela, a bread roll stacked absurdly high with thin-sliced mortadella, often with melted cheese.

It’s more of a spectacle than a light lunch — consider sharing. While you’re there, browse the produce stands, where vendors may offer tastes of tropical fruits. Just ask about the price before you accept a pile of samples.

Pastel, Coxinha and the Snack Counter

São Paulo runs on salgados, the savory snacks sold at bakeries, bars and lanchonetes across the city.

  • Pastel — a thin, crisp, deep-fried pastry filled with cheese, ground beef, heart of palm and more. It’s classic at street markets (feiras), traditionally paired with fresh sugarcane juice, caldo de cana.
  • Coxinha — shredded chicken, often with creamy cheese, wrapped in dough shaped like a teardrop, then breaded and fried.
  • Esfiha and kibe — Middle Eastern pastries and fritters, reflecting the city’s large Lebanese and Syrian communities.
  • Pão de queijo — the chewy cheese bread you’ll find at nearly every café.

Virado à Paulista: The City on a Plate

For a taste of traditional São Paulo home cooking, order virado à paulista. This hearty plate typically includes:

  • Tutu de feijão, beans thickened with manioc flour
  • A pork chop and linguiça sausage
  • Sautéed couve (collard greens) and a fried egg
  • Fried banana, torresmo (crackling) and white rice

It’s a lunchtime classic, traditionally served on Mondays at many old-school restaurants, and it’s designed to fuel a full day of work. Plan an unhurried afternoon afterward.

Pizza: A Paulistano Obsession

Thanks to its large Italian-descended population, São Paulo is famously devoted to pizza, and locals will happily tell you it rivals anywhere in the world. Sunday night pizza is a widely loved tradition among families and friends.

Expect a few local twists: generous toppings, thin crusts and flavors you won’t find in Naples, such as catupiry (a soft, creamy cheese) and calabresa, a spicy Brazilian sausage. Pizzerias are everywhere, from beloved old-school spots to modern wood-fired places.

Japanese Food in Liberdade

São Paulo is home to one of the largest communities of Japanese descent outside Japan, and its heart is Liberdade, a neighborhood just south of the historic center marked by red torii-style gateways and lantern-shaped streetlights.

Come for ramen, sushi, gyoza, Japanese sweets and grocery stores stocked with imported goods. Weekends bring a street market with food stalls and crafts. Japanese influence extends citywide, too — sushi is a staple in São Paulo dining.

The Fine Dining Scene

Beyond comfort food, São Paulo is Brazil’s fine-dining capital. Leading chefs here often focus on Brazilian ingredients — Amazonian fish, native fruits, manioc in countless forms — reinterpreted with contemporary technique. Many of these restaurants are clustered in Jardins, Pinheiros and Itaim Bibi.

Top tables can book up well ahead, so reserve early if a special meal is part of your plans.

Don’t overlook coffee, either. Much of São Paulo’s early wealth was built on the coffee trade, and today the city has a thriving specialty coffee scene alongside the classic cafezinho — a small, strong, often sweetened cup served at counters everywhere. It’s the perfect pause between museums and meals.

Eating Tips for São Paulo

  • Lunch deals — look for the prato feito or prato do dia, a set plate that’s filling and good value.
  • Late dinners — locals tend to eat later in the evening, especially on weekends.
  • Service charge — it’s commonly added to the bill, so check before tipping extra.

title: Cajón del Maipo: A Day Trip from Santiago into the Andes
dek: Canyon views, a turquoise reservoir and mountain hot springs — how to plan a day trip to Cajón del Maipo from Santiago.
body:
Few capitals put the high Andes this close to the city limits. Southeast of Santiago, the Maipo River carves a dramatic canyon into the mountains, and within a couple of hours you can trade traffic for glacier-fed rivers, bare peaks and startlingly blue water. Cajón del Maipo is one of the most rewarding day trips from the city — here’s how to make the most of it.

What Is Cajón del Maipo?

Cajón del Maipo is the canyon of the Maipo River as it runs down from the Andes toward Santiago. The road follows the river upstream through small villages, vineyards at the lower end, and steadily wilder scenery as you climb. Summer brings hikers, cyclists and rafters; winter can bring snow to the higher reaches.

It’s a place for fresh air rather than checklists — the pleasure is in the views, a good lunch and a slow afternoon in the mountains.

San José de Maipo

The main town in the valley, San José de Maipo, is roughly an hour or so from central Santiago depending on traffic. It has a small historic core with a colonial-era church, a few shops and places to eat, and it’s a natural stop for supplies before heading higher. Along the road nearby you’ll find simple roadside spots selling empanadas and homemade treats — a very Chilean way to fuel up.

Embalse El Yeso

The headline sight for many visitors is Embalse El Yeso, a high-altitude reservoir tucked among bare, sculpted peaks. On a clear day the water glows turquoise against the mountains, and the scale of the landscape is hard to capture in photos.

The road up is unpaved in parts and can be rough, so a higher-clearance vehicle or an organized tour is a smart choice. Because the reservoir supplies water to the city, access rules have changed at times — check current conditions before you go rather than assuming you can drive right up to the shore.

Hot Springs and Higher Valleys

Beyond the reservoir turnoff, the road continues toward the area around Baños Morales, a small mountain village known for its mineral springs and as a gateway to Monumento Natural El Morado, where trails lead toward views of a hanging glacier. Farther up the valley, natural hot springs sit high in the mountains, with pools overlooking the peaks.

Soaking in warm water surrounded by the Andes is a memorable way to end the day, but facilities and access can be seasonal. Confirm what’s open before planning your route around a soak.

Getting There: Tours, Driving and Buses

  • Guided tours — the easiest option, especially for El Yeso, since the driver handles the rough road and conditions.
  • Driving yourself — offers flexibility, but check your rental agreement for unpaved roads and bring cash, water and a full tank.
  • Public transit — buses connect Santiago with San José de Maipo and some villages beyond, workable for a lower-valley visit.

Winter Access and Road Conditions

From roughly June to September, snow and ice can affect the upper parts of the canyon. Roads to El Yeso and the higher valleys may be closed at short notice, and authorities can require snow chains. Conditions change quickly, so check the latest official road information on the day, and consider a tour with an operator used to winter driving.

In any season, the altitude means strong sun and cool evenings. Pack layers, sunscreen and sunglasses, even if Santiago feels warm.

Planning Your Day

Start early to beat traffic out of the city and to catch the clearest mountain light. Allow a full day if you’re heading to El Yeso or the hot springs; a half day is enough for San José de Maipo and the lower valley. Mobile signal can be patchy, so download offline maps before you leave.

Cajón del Maipo pairs well with a city-focused itinerary. See how it fits with our Santiago guide and the three-day Santiago itinerary.

title: Where to Stay in São Paulo: A Neighborhood Guide
dek: Jardins, Pinheiros, Vila Madalena and beyond: how to choose the right São Paulo neighborhood for your style and budget.
body:
São Paulo is enormous — a sprawling megacity where the neighborhood you choose can make or break your trip. Traffic is notorious, so staying close to what you want to do matters more here than almost anywhere in South America. These are the areas most visitors should consider.

Jardins: Polished and Central

If it’s your first visit, Jardins is the easy, elegant choice. This leafy, upscale district sits just below Avenida Paulista, putting you within walking distance of MASP, the city’s main cultural corridor and good metro connections.

Streets like Rua Oscar Freire are lined with designer boutiques, and the area is packed with cafés, restaurants and bars. It feels polished and relatively calm, which is exactly why it suits travelers who want comfort and convenience without much guesswork.

Staying on or just off Avenida Paulista itself is a closely related option. The avenue is lined with hotels, cultural centers and metro stations, and on Sundays it has traditionally been closed to cars, turning into a huge promenade for walkers, cyclists and street performers — check current arrangements before you go.

  • Best for — first-timers, shoppers and anyone who wants a central base.
  • Keep in mind — it’s one of the pricier areas, and it quiets down earlier than the nightlife districts.

Pinheiros: Creative and Food-Focused

West of Jardins, Pinheiros has become one of São Paulo’s most exciting neighborhoods, especially for food. It mixes design studios, independent shops, galleries, lively bars and an ever-changing restaurant scene. It’s also well connected by metro, including the yellow line toward Paulista.

The vibe is younger and more creative than Jardins, but still comfortable and walkable. For travelers who plan their days around meals, it’s hard to beat.

Vila Madalena: Bohemian and Lively

Next door to Pinheiros, Vila Madalena is São Paulo’s bohemian quarter. Its hilly streets are known for street art — including the famous alleyway Beco do Batman — small galleries, bars that spill onto the sidewalks and live music, especially samba.

It’s fun, social and full of character, but it can be noisy on weekend nights. If sleep is a priority, choose a room on a quieter side street or look toward the edges of the neighborhood.

Itaim Bibi and Vila Olímpia: Modern and Business-Minded

These neighboring districts form part of São Paulo’s modern business hub, near Avenida Brigadeiro Faria Lima and its gleaming office towers. They are popular with business travelers and anyone who wants contemporary hotels and a strong dining scene.

  • Itaim Bibi — known for upscale restaurants and cocktail bars, with a polished, grown-up feel.
  • Vila Olímpia — more corporate by day, with a busy bar and club scene after dark.

Both are convenient for Ibirapuera Park, though you’ll likely rely on rideshares more than in Jardins or Pinheiros.

Centro: Historic, but Use Caution

São Paulo’s historic center holds some of its most interesting architecture — the Theatro Municipal, the Sé Cathedral, the Mercado Municipal and grand early-20th-century buildings. It’s well worth exploring by day.

As a base, though, Centro isn’t the right fit for most visitors. Some areas feel deserted after business hours, and street crime is more of a concern than in the neighborhoods above. If you do stay here, choose carefully, use rideshares at night and follow current local advice.

Tips for Choosing Your Base

  • Stay near the metro — access to a station can save hours compared with sitting in traffic.
  • Mind the airport — most international flights use Guarulhos, well outside the city; Congonhas, used for domestic flights, is much closer to the center.
  • Think about your evenings — Vila Madalena and Vila Olímpia are lively; Jardins is calmer.
  • Use rideshares after dark — they’re widely used and generally the easiest way to get around at night.

The Bottom Line

For most travelers, Jardins or Pinheiros strikes the ideal balance of location, safety and things to do, with Vila Madalena a great pick for night owls. Once you’ve chosen your base, plan your days with our 3-day São Paulo itinerary and find more in our São Paulo guide.

title: What to Eat and Drink in Santiago: A Chilean Food Guide
dek: Empanadas de pino, pastel de choclo, Mercado Central seafood and Carménère — the dishes and drinks to seek out in Santiago.
body:
Chilean food doesn’t shout for attention the way some Latin American cuisines do — it wins you over quietly, one flaky empanada and one glass of red at a time. Santiago is the best place to sample it all, from market-hall seafood to hearty home cooking and a wine culture that punches well above its weight. Here’s what to order.

Empanadas de Pino

Start here. The classic Chilean empanada is baked, not fried, and filled with pino: minced or chopped beef slow-cooked with plenty of onion, then tucked in with a black olive, a slice of hard-boiled egg and often a raisin or two. The sweet–savory mix surprises some visitors, and converts most of them.

You’ll also find fried versions, often filled with cheese or seafood. Empanadas are a fixture of the September national holidays, but they’re easy to find year-round.

Pastel de Choclo and Home-Style Classics

Pastel de choclo is Chilean comfort food at its finest: a base of pino, chicken, olives and egg, topped with a thick layer of ground sweet corn and baked until golden — traditionally in a clay dish. It’s a summer favorite, when fresh corn is in season, and it’s often finished with a sprinkle of sugar on top.

Keep an eye out for cazuela, a brothy stew with meat, potato, squash and corn, and porotos granados, a summery bean dish with corn and basil.

Street Food: Completos and Sopaipillas

Chile takes its hot dogs seriously. The completo is a generously loaded version, and the most famous style — the italiano — is named for its colors: tomato, mashed avocado and mayonnaise piled high on the bun. Expect a knife-and-fork level of toppings.

Sopaipillas are round, fried rounds of dough, often made with pumpkin. Street vendors serve them topped with pebre, a fresh salsa of tomato, onion, cilantro and chili. On cold, rainy days, look for sopaipillas pasadas, soaked in a warm syrup made from chancaca, an unrefined cane sugar.

Seafood at the Mercado Central

With a long Pacific coastline, Chile has seafood that deserves its reputation. Santiago’s Mercado Central, an ornate iron-framed market hall near the historic center, is the classic place to try it, with fish stalls and simple eateries crowded together under one roof.

  • Caldillo de congrio — a comforting conger eel soup, famously celebrated by Pablo Neruda
  • Paila marina — a rich seafood stew served bubbling in a clay bowl
  • Machas a la parmesana — razor clams baked with Parmesan
  • Ceviche — often with local fish and a bright citrus bite

Touts can be persistent at the entrance restaurants, so feel free to wander before you sit down.

Mote con Huesillo

On a hot afternoon, nothing is more Santiago than mote con huesillo. It’s a sweet, chilled drink of caramel-colored nectar with cooked husked wheat (mote) at the bottom and a whole rehydrated dried peach (huesillo) floating on top. You drink it and eat it at the same time. Look for it at street stands, especially near parks and hills like Cerro San Cristóbal.

Wine, Pisco Sours and Piscolas

Chile is one of the world’s major wine producers, and Santiago sits within easy reach of well-known valleys like Maipo, with Casablanca and Colchagua a bit farther out. The grape to know is Carménère, a variety from Bordeaux that was long mistaken for Merlot in Chilean vineyards before being identified in the 1990s. Today it’s something of a national signature — soft, spicy and deeply colored.

Then there’s pisco, the grape brandy both Chile and Peru claim. The Chilean pisco sour is typically made with lemon juice and sugar, often without the egg white common in the Peruvian version. For something more casual, order a piscola — pisco and cola — which is practically a national pastime.

Eating Well in Santiago: Practical Notes

Chileans tend to eat lunch as the main meal, and many restaurants offer a good-value set lunch on weekdays. Dinner starts later than in the US. Tap water in Santiago is generally considered safe, though many visitors prefer bottled. Tipping around 10 percent is customary at sit-down restaurants, and it’s often suggested on the bill.

title: Where to Stay in Santiago: A Neighborhood Guide
dek: From bohemian Lastarria to leafy Vitacura, here’s how to pick the Santiago neighborhood that fits your trip.
body:
Santiago is a sprawling city, and where you sleep shapes everything — how far you walk, what you eat, and whether the Andes feel like a backdrop or a daily companion. The good news: the neighborhoods most travelers consider sit roughly along one easy east–west line, stitched together by the Metro. Here’s how they compare, so you can match the base to the trip.

Lastarria: Pretty, Walkable and Central

If you want Santiago’s charm in concentrated form, Lastarria is a strong first pick. This compact barrio sits beside Cerro Santa Lucía, with cobbled lanes, European-style facades, independent cinemas and a cultural pulse anchored by nearby museums and performance spaces. Cafés spill onto the sidewalks, and weekend street stalls add a bit of bustle.

You’re within walking distance of the historic center, the Plaza de Armas and Parque Forestal, which makes it ideal for a short first visit. The trade-off is a livelier, more urban feel — and the downtown streets around it quiet down noticeably at night.

Bellavista: Nightlife at the Foot of the Hill

Across the Mapocho River, Bellavista is Santiago’s colorful, after-dark neighborhood. Murals cover the walls, bars and restaurants line the streets, and Pablo Neruda’s house La Chascona tucks into the slope of Cerro San Cristóbal. It’s also the natural jumping-off point for the funicular up the hill.

Stay here if you want to walk home from dinner and drinks. Light sleepers should choose carefully — weekends can run loud and late, and some blocks feel grittier than others.

Providencia: The Balanced Choice

Providencia is where many visitors end up happiest. It’s leafy, residential in parts, well connected on Metro Line 1, and packed with cafés, bakeries, wine bars and everyday conveniences. You’re a short ride from both downtown sights and the business districts to the east.

It lacks the storybook streets of Lastarria, but it makes up for it with comfort and ease. For families, longer stays or anyone who likes to live like a local for a week, it’s a sensible default.

Las Condes and Vitacura: Polished and Upscale

Farther east, the city climbs toward the mountains and the mood turns glossy. Las Condes is home to the skyscraper cluster locals nickname “Sanhattan,” along with large international hotels, malls and a business-travel crowd. It’s orderly, safe-feeling and close to the Andes views that make Santiago so photogenic.

Vitacura, just north, is quieter and more exclusive: tree-lined avenues, art galleries, design boutiques and some of the city’s more refined dining. Both are comfortable bases, though you’ll spend more time on the Metro or in taxis to reach the historic core.

  • Choose Las Condes — if you want big-hotel amenities and easy business access.
  • Choose Vitacura — if you prefer galleries, boutiques and a calmer residential feel.

Barrio Italia: Creative and Low-Key

Straddling Providencia and Ñuñoa, Barrio Italia is a favorite with design lovers. Old houses have been turned into courtyards full of furniture studios, vintage shops, small galleries and cafés. It feels creative and unhurried, with more neighborhood character than tourist traffic.

Accommodation options are more limited here, leaning toward apartments and boutique stays, and Metro access is a little less direct. If you don’t mind a short ride to the main sights, it’s a lovely place to wake up.

Quick Picks by Travel Style

  • First-time visitors — Lastarria or Providencia
  • Nightlife — Bellavista
  • Luxury and business — Las Condes or Vitacura
  • Design and slow travel — Barrio Italia
  • Families — Providencia

Practical Tips Before You Book

Look at a Metro map before you commit — being a few blocks from a Line 1 station makes getting around dramatically easier. Santiago’s summer (December to February) is hot and dry, so air conditioning is worth checking; in winter, heating matters more than you’d expect. As in any big city, keep an eye on your belongings in crowded areas.

Once you’ve chosen a base, use our Santiago guide to plan what’s nearby, or follow the three-day Santiago itinerary to see how each neighborhood fits into a short trip.

title: What to Eat and Drink in Rio de Janeiro: A Local Food Guide
dek: From Saturday feijoada to beachside biscoito Globo and ice-cold chope, here is what to eat and drink in Rio de Janeiro.
body:
Rio eats the way it lives — outdoors, unhurried and with a cold drink within arm’s reach. The city’s food isn’t about tasting menus so much as rituals: the long Saturday lunch, the post-beach snack, the round of draft beer that somehow becomes dinner. Here is what to order, and where the moment calls for it.

Feijoada: The Saturday Institution

If you only plan one big Brazilian meal, make it feijoada. This slow-cooked stew of black beans and assorted cuts of pork and sausage is traditionally served on Saturdays, and in Rio it’s a whole-afternoon affair rather than a quick lunch.

It arrives with a supporting cast that matters as much as the pot itself:

  • White rice — for soaking up the dark, rich broth.
  • Farofa — toasted cassava flour that adds crunch.
  • Couve — finely shredded collard greens sautéed with garlic.
  • Orange slices — a bright, fresh counterpoint to all that richness.

Pace yourself, pair it with a caipirinha, and don’t schedule anything ambitious afterward. A nap is part of the tradition, officially or not.

Churrasco and the Rodízio Experience

Brazilian barbecue is a serious business, and the classic way to eat it is rodízio style: servers circulate with skewers of grilled meat and carve slices directly onto your plate until you signal that you’re done. Picanha — the prized cap of the rump — is the cut most people wait for, usually seasoned with little more than coarse salt.

Most churrascarias also have a generous buffet of salads, sides and hot dishes. A tip from the seasoned: go easy there, because the skewers keep coming.

Beach Snacks and Street Bites

On Rio’s beaches, lunch comes to you. Vendors walk the sand with coolers and trays, and a few items are practically part of the landscape:

  • Biscoito Globo — airy, lightly salty rings of manioc-starch biscuit, sold in their instantly recognizable paper bags. A true carioca beach icon.
  • Mate gelado — iced, sweetened mate tea, often mixed with lemonade, poured from metal tanks.
  • Queijo coalho — squeaky grilled cheese on a stick, cooked over a tiny portable brazier.
  • Coconut water — straight from a chilled green coconut at the kiosks along the promenade.

Away from the sand, look for pão de queijo, the chewy cheese bread originally from Minas Gerais that’s now a staple at bakeries and cafés across Rio. Salgados like coxinha (shredded chicken in a teardrop of dough) and pastel (a crisp, fried pastry pocket) round out the snack menu.

Açaí and the Juice Bar Habit

In Rio, açaí is typically served as a thick, frozen purée in a bowl or cup, often topped with granola and sliced banana. It’s cold, filling and exactly what you’ll crave after a morning in the sun.

Just as essential are the city’s juice bars — open-fronted counters on seemingly every other corner, with long lists of fresh fruit juices. Beyond orange and pineapple, try tropical flavors you might not find at home: acerola, maracujá (passion fruit), caju (cashew fruit) and cupuaçu. Many also serve sandwiches and quick snacks, making them a useful stop at any hour.

Botecos, Chope and Caipirinhas

The boteco is Rio’s great social equalizer: a casual neighborhood bar, often with plastic tables spilling onto the sidewalk, where friends gather over small plates and cold drinks. The menu leans on petiscos — bar snacks like bolinhos de bacalhau (salt-cod fritters), fried cassava, pastéis and grilled sausage.

The drink of choice is chope, Brazilian draft beer, poured light and very cold with a creamy collar of foam. Waiters tend to keep refills coming until you say otherwise, so keep an eye on the tab.

Then there’s the caipirinha, Brazil’s national cocktail: cachaça (sugarcane spirit), lime and sugar, muddled over ice. Variations swap in other fruits, and a caipiroska uses vodka instead of cachaça. Sip slowly — they are stronger than they taste.

Practical Tips for Eating in Rio

  • Lunch is the main event — many Brazilians eat their largest meal midday, and dinner often starts late.
  • Try a por quilo restaurant — pay-by-weight buffets are an easy, affordable way to sample lots of Brazilian dishes.
  • Portions are often built for sharing — ask before ordering one dish per person.
  • Check the bill — a service charge is commonly added, so look before tipping extra.
  • Stay hydrated — heat plus caipirinhas is a combination that sneaks up on you.

For neighborhood picks and how to fit these meals into your days, see our Rio de Janeiro guide and our 3-day Rio itinerary.

title: Day Trips from Rio de Janeiro: Mountains, Beaches and Islands
dek: Imperial Petrópolis, chic Búzios, car-free Ilha Grande and more: the best-loved escapes from Rio, plus when to stay the night.
body:
Rio could keep you busy for weeks, but the state around it is just as compelling — cool mountain towns, turquoise bays and islands with no cars at all. Some of these escapes work as long day trips; others really reward an overnight. Here’s how to choose.

Petrópolis: Rio’s Imperial Mountain Retreat

About an hour and a half north of the city, depending on traffic, Petrópolis sits in the forested hills of the Serra dos Órgãos region. It was the summer retreat of Brazil’s 19th-century emperors, and the town still carries that stately, slightly European air.

  • Museu Imperial — the emperor’s former summer palace, now a museum of imperial-era Brazil.
  • The Cathedral of São Pedro de Alcântara — a Gothic Revival landmark where members of the imperial family are entombed.
  • Palácio Quitandinha — a grand former hotel-casino with striking interiors.

The cooler mountain air is part of the appeal, especially in Rio’s sticky summer. Bring a light layer. Petrópolis is also a gateway to the wider mountain region, where hiking trails, waterfalls and the dramatic peaks of Serra dos Órgãos National Park reward anyone willing to stay a little longer.

Búzios: Polished Beach Town

Roughly two and a half to three hours east of Rio, Armação dos Búzios sits on a peninsula scalloped with more than a dozen beaches. It rose to international fame in the 1960s after a visit by Brigitte Bardot, whose statue now sits on the waterfront promenade.

Days are for beach-hopping — by water taxi, schooner or on foot — and evenings are for the boutiques and restaurants along Rua das Pedras. It’s doable as a very long day trip, but Búzios is more enjoyable with at least one night.

Arraial do Cabo: Brazil’s Caribbean-Colored Water

Also about two and a half to three hours from Rio, Arraial do Cabo is known for water so clear and blue that it’s often compared to the Caribbean. The cold ocean current here keeps the sea brisk but remarkably transparent, which makes it a favorite for snorkeling and diving.

Boat trips around the cape visit beaches and coves that are hard or impossible to reach by land. Popular spots can get crowded in high season, so an early start pays off. Some areas are protected, so follow current rules on access and boat tours.

Ilha Grande: Car-Free Island Escape

Ilha Grande is a large, mountainous island covered in Atlantic Forest, with no cars and a network of hiking trails linking its beaches. Getting there means driving roughly two and a half to three hours to the mainland ports around Angra dos Reis, then taking a boat across to Vila do Abraão, the island’s main village.

Because of that journey, Ilha Grande is far better as an overnight or multi-day trip. Highlights include:

  • Lopes Mendes — a long, powdery beach frequently ranked among Brazil’s most beautiful.
  • Lagoa Azul — a sheltered spot for snorkeling, usually visited by boat.
  • Jungle trails — routes range from easy walks to strenuous hikes; go prepared with water and good shoes.

Paraty: Worth the Overnight

About four hours down the Costa Verde, colonial Paraty is too far for a comfortable day trip but ideal for two or three nights. Its cobblestone historic center, whitewashed churches and island-dotted bay make it one of Brazil’s most atmospheric small towns.

Many travelers pair Paraty with Ilha Grande, since both sit along the same stretch of coast. Plan your stay with our Paraty guide.

How to Plan Your Trips

  • Transport — options include organized tours, intercity buses and private transfers. Tours are simplest for Petrópolis and Arraial do Cabo; for islands and beach towns, independent travel gives more flexibility.
  • Timing — leave early, especially on weekends, when traffic out of the city can be heavy.
  • Weather — summer storms can affect boat trips; keep a buffer day if an island is non-negotiable.
  • Check current info — boat schedules, park rules and entry requirements change, so confirm before you go.

To slot a day trip around the city’s big sights, start with our 3-day Rio itinerary, and find neighborhood and planning advice in our Rio de Janeiro guide.

title: What to Eat in Quito: Traditional Ecuadorian Dishes to Try
dek: Hearty potato soups, puffed cheese empanadas, slow-roasted pork and world-class chocolate: a delicious guide to eating your way through Quito.
body:
Andean cooking was built for cool mountain evenings, and Quito’s food is exactly that — warming, generous and deeply rooted in potatoes, corn and cheese. Add a serious chocolate and coffee culture, and you have a city that is a pleasure to eat through. Here is what to order, with more trip planning in our Quito guide.

Locro de Papa: The Soup That Defines the City

If Quito had an official comfort food, locro de papa might be it. This thick, golden potato soup is enriched with cheese and often finished with slices of avocado on top. It is creamy without being heavy, and on a chilly highland afternoon it is exactly what you want.

You will find it on set-lunch menus all over the city, usually as the starter before a main course — an easy, affordable way to try it the way locals do.

Empanadas de Viento: Big, Puffy and Sugar-Dusted

The name translates roughly as “wind empanadas,” and one look explains why: these are enormous, airy, deep-fried pastries that puff up dramatically. Filled with cheese and often sprinkled with sugar, they land somewhere pleasantly between savory and sweet.

They are a classic afternoon snack, commonly paired with a hot drink. Tear one open while it is still warm and let the steam escape.

Llapingachos and Hornado: Highland Heavyweights

Llapingachos are griddled potato patties stuffed with cheese, typically served with a peanut sauce and accompaniments like fried egg, avocado, sausage or salad. Crisp outside, soft within, they are a highland staple.

Hornado is whole roasted pork, slow-cooked until the skin crackles. Plates usually come with mote (hominy), llapingachos or potatoes, and a tangy onion-and-tomato salad. Look for it in markets, where the roasted pig on display is part of the appeal.

Fanesca: A Seasonal Easter Tradition

Fanesca is Ecuador’s great seasonal dish, prepared during Holy Week before Easter. It is a rich soup made with salt cod and a long list of grains and legumes — beans, corn, lentils and more — simmered in milk and traditionally garnished with things like hard-boiled egg, fried dough and herbs.

Making it is famously labor-intensive, and families take their recipes seriously. If your trip overlaps with the Easter period, make a point of trying it; the rest of the year, it is generally hard to find.

Humitas and Other Corn Classics

Humitas are steamed parcels of fresh ground corn, usually mixed with cheese and wrapped in corn husks. Soft, lightly sweet and very comforting, they are a breakfast and afternoon favorite, often paired with coffee.

While you are at it, look out for tamales, quimbolitos (sweet steamed cakes wrapped in leaves) and roasted corn with cheese from street vendors.

Chocolate, Coffee and Canelazo

Ecuador is renowned for its fine-flavor cacao, and Quito is a wonderful place to taste it. Look for single-origin chocolate bars, tasting experiences and shops showcasing different growing regions. It also makes an excellent edible souvenir.

Ecuadorian coffee has been stepping into the specialty spotlight too, and the city’s café scene reflects that — expect carefully sourced beans from regions like Loja and Pichincha.

When the evening chill sets in, order a canelazo: a hot drink made with cinnamon, fruit juice (often naranjilla) and sugar, traditionally spiked with a sugarcane spirit. It is especially popular around the December holidays and on atmospheric streets like La Ronda. Non-alcoholic versions are easy to find, too.

Practical Tips for Eating in Quito

  • Try an almuerzo — set lunches (soup, main, juice) are the local way to eat well at midday.
  • Visit a market — central markets are great for hornado, fresh juices and fruit you may never have seen before.
  • Ease into altitude — go gently on heavy food and alcohol during your first day or two.
  • Ask about ají — the table hot sauce varies everywhere and is part of the fun.

Build a few of these dishes into your plans with our three-day Quito itinerary, and leave room for at least one empanada de viento. You will not regret it.

title: Day Trips from Quito: Markets, Cloud Forest and Volcanoes
dek: Otavalo’s market, Mindo’s cloud forest, Cotopaxi’s volcano and the equator line: the day trips from Quito worth building into your trip.
body:
Quito is a superb city, but part of its magic is what surrounds it. Within a few hours you can be haggling in an Andean market, walking through misty cloud forest or standing beneath one of the world’s highest active volcanoes. These are the excursions we would prioritize — see our Quito guide for the city itself.

Otavalo Market

About two hours north of Quito, the town of Otavalo is home to one of South America’s best-known Indigenous markets. The Plaza de los Ponchos overflows with textiles, woven blankets, alpaca-blend sweaters, embroidered blouses, jewelry and crafts. Saturday is traditionally the biggest market day, when stalls spill into the surrounding streets.

Friendly bargaining is expected. Many trips pair the market with stops at nearby craft villages, the scenic lakes of the region or the Peguche waterfall, making it an easy, full day out.

Mindo Cloud Forest

Heading northwest, the road drops from the highlands into lush, humid cloud forest. Mindo, roughly two hours from Quito, is a small town surrounded by some of the richest birdlife in the country. Hummingbirds are everywhere, and serious birders come for toucans, tanagers and much more.

  • Birdwatching — early mornings are best; guided walks help you spot more.
  • Waterfalls — trails lead to several cascades in the surrounding forest.
  • Butterflies and chocolate — butterfly gardens and cacao tours are local favorites.
  • Adventure — ziplines and tubing are popular with the more adrenaline-minded.

Pack a rain layer; the name “cloud forest” is not decorative.

Cotopaxi National Park

South of Quito, Cotopaxi’s near-perfect snow-capped cone rises from high, windswept páramo grassland. It is one of the highest active volcanoes in the world, and on a clear day the view is unforgettable. Most visits include a stop at Limpiopungo Lagoon, and many continue up toward the parking area below the refuge for a steep, breathless walk at serious altitude.

Cotopaxi’s volcanic activity has at times led to access restrictions, so check current park conditions and official guidance before you go. Dress in warm layers, bring sun protection and do not rush your climb — you will be well above Quito’s already lofty elevation. Mornings often offer the clearest views.

Mitad del Mundo

Just north of the city, Mitad del Mundo celebrates Ecuador’s position on the equator with a large monument and a painted line where visitors happily straddle two hemispheres. Nearby, a smaller museum offers playful demonstrations and cultural exhibits.

It is an easy half-day trip, and it pairs well with a visit to the Pululahua crater viewpoint, where a small farming community sits inside the caldera of an extinct volcano. Arrive early, as mist often fills the crater later in the day.

Quilotoa: A Long Day or an Overnight

Quilotoa is a volcanic crater filled with a vivid turquoise-green lake, and it is one of the most striking landscapes in the Ecuadorian Andes. It is also a significant journey — several hours each way — which makes a day trip long and tiring.

If you have the time, consider staying overnight in the area. That lets you hike down to the water (and back up, at altitude), walk part of the rim or explore sections of the Quilotoa Loop, a multi-day trekking route through highland villages. Weather can shift quickly, so bring layers.

Planning Your Day Trips

  • Go guided or self-drive — organized tours simplify logistics; buses and private drivers offer more flexibility.
  • Start early — clouds often build over the Andes as the day goes on.
  • Respect altitude — acclimatize in Quito before tackling Cotopaxi or Quilotoa.
  • Layer up — temperatures vary widely between highland, páramo and cloud forest.
  • Check conditions — park access and road status can change, so confirm before you go.

With a few extra days, it is worth slotting one or two of these around our three-day Quito itinerary — the contrast between the city and the landscapes around it is a big part of what makes Ecuador special.

title: Day Trips from Oaxaca: Ruins, Petrified Waterfalls and Artisan Villages
dek: Monte Albán, Hierve el Agua, Mitla, weaving and black-clay villages, the Tule tree and Tlacolula’s Sunday market — the best day trips from Oaxaca.
body:
Oaxaca City sits at the meeting point of three fertile valleys dotted with Zapotec ruins, artisan villages and mezcal fields. Most highlights are within an hour or two, which means you can base yourself in town and head out each morning. Here’s how to plan your excursions, alongside our Oaxaca guide.

Monte Albán: The Mountaintop Capital

Just a short drive west of the city — often around 20 to 30 minutes — Monte Albán was the great capital of the Zapotec people, built on a leveled mountaintop with sweeping views over the valleys. Wander the Gran Plaza, climb the platforms and look for the carved stone figures known as Los Danzantes.

The site museum is small but helpful for understanding what you’re looking at. Go early for cooler temperatures and softer light. There’s little shade, so bring a hat and water. Shuttles and taxis run from town, and a guide adds a lot of context.

The Eastern Valley Route: Tule, Teotitlán, Tlacolula and Mitla

The road east toward Mitla strings together several classic stops, so many travelers combine two or three in one day.

  • El Árbol del Tule — in Santa María del Tule, about 20 to 30 minutes from the city, this ancient Montezuma cypress has one of the widest trunks of any tree on Earth. A quick but memorable stop.
  • Teotitlán del Valle — a Zapotec village famous for handwoven wool rugs. Many family workshops demonstrate carding, spinning and dyeing with natural sources such as cochineal, indigo and marigold.
  • Tlacolula Sunday market — a vast, lively weekly market with deep roots, where people from surrounding villages come to buy and sell produce, barbacoa, bread, textiles and household goods. Go on Sunday morning.
  • Mitla — roughly an hour from the city, this Zapotec site is known for its intricate geometric stone mosaics, unlike anything else in Mesoamerica, with a colonial church built atop part of the complex.

The valley is also mezcal country, and it’s easy to add a palenque visit around Santiago Matatlán along the same road.

Hierve el Agua: The Petrified Waterfalls

About an hour and a half to two hours east, Hierve el Agua is Oaxaca’s most photographed natural wonder. Mineral-rich springs have built up cascades of white rock over thousands of years, so the cliffs look like frozen waterfalls. At the top, natural infinity pools overlook the mountains — bring a swimsuit.

Access has been interrupted at times by local disputes or maintenance closures, so check current conditions before you go. Pairing it with Mitla makes a full, rewarding day. The paths down to the formations can be steep and slippery, so wear shoes with good grip, and avoid visiting right after heavy rain when the trails get muddy.

San Bartolo Coyotepec: Black Clay

Around 30 minutes south of the city, San Bartolo Coyotepec is known for barro negro, the glossy black pottery made from local clay. Artisans polish pieces with stones before firing, which gives them their distinctive metallic sheen. Many workshops welcome visitors for demonstrations — and the pieces make beautiful, if fragile, souvenirs.

Combine it with other craft villages on the southern side of the valley, where you’ll find wood carvings and embroidered textiles.

How to Plan Your Day Trips

  • Group by direction — east for Tule, Teotitlán, Tlacolula, Mitla and Hierve el Agua; west for Monte Albán; south for San Bartolo Coyotepec.
  • Tour, driver or colectivo — organized tours are easiest, private drivers are the most flexible, and shared colectivos are budget-friendly but slower.
  • Check entry details — archaeological sites and community-run attractions set their own fees and hours, which can change.
  • Buy directly — purchasing from the artisans who make the work keeps more money in the villages.

Final Tips

Travel times above are approximate and depend on traffic and stops. Aim for one excursion per day, leave evenings free for the city, and slot them into our three-day Oaxaca itinerary so you can balance ruins, crafts and markets without rushing.

title: Where to Stay in Oaxaca: A Neighborhood Guide
dek: Centro, Jalatlaco, Xochimilco or Reforma? How to choose the right Oaxaca neighborhood — plus when to stay in a village or on the coast.
body:
Oaxaca City is compact, colorful and made for walking — which makes choosing where to stay mostly a question of mood. Do you want to step out into festival bands and church bells, or wake up to roosters and cobblestones? Here’s how the main neighborhoods compare, to pair with our Oaxaca guide.

Centro: In the Thick of It

The historic center is where most visitors stay, and for good reason. Its grid of pastel facades and green-stone buildings is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and nearly everything is within walking distance: the Zócalo, the Templo de Santo Domingo, the pedestrian Andador Turístico (Calle Macedonio Alcalá), galleries, mezcal bars and the main markets.

Staying north of the Zócalo, around Santo Domingo, tends to feel more polished and a little quieter. Closer to the markets, south of the square, it’s busier and more workaday. Either way, Centro is ideal for a first visit or a short trip. Many guesthouses here are set in restored colonial homes arranged around leafy courtyards, which keep things surprisingly peaceful once the door closes behind you.

  • Best for — first-timers, short stays, food lovers and night owls
  • Keep in mind — parades, fireworks and brass bands are part of the soundtrack, especially during festivals

Jalatlaco: Cobblestones and Murals

Just east of Centro, Barrio de Jalatlaco is one of the city’s oldest neighborhoods and one of its most photogenic. Think cobbled lanes, low colorful houses, street art and a pretty church, with a growing roster of cafés and small guesthouses.

It’s a short walk to the center yet feels calmer, which makes it a favorite for couples and longer stays. The flip side: its charm is well known, so expect fellow travelers with cameras in hand. Evenings are low-key — a coffee, a stroll past the murals, then dinner a few blocks away in Centro.

Xochimilco: Oaxaca’s Quiet Barrio

Not to be confused with the canals of Mexico City, Oaxaca’s Barrio de Xochimilco sits just north of Centro. It’s known for the old stone arches of the colonial aqueduct, narrow alleys, a neighborhood church and a relaxed residential feel.

You’re about a ten- to twenty-minute walk from Santo Domingo, depending on where you stay, with more local life and fewer crowds. It suits travelers who want peace in the evenings and don’t mind a gentle stroll into town.

Reforma: Modern and Residential

Farther north, Colonia Reforma is a more modern, middle-class residential area with wider streets, supermarkets, cafés and some well-regarded contemporary restaurants. It has less colonial atmosphere, but it’s practical for longer stays, remote workers and anyone who likes a more everyday Oaxacan routine.

You’ll likely take taxis into Centro, particularly at night, so factor that into your plans.

Beyond the City: Villages and the Coast

If you have extra days, consider a night or two outside the city. Villages in the Central Valleys, such as the weaving town of Teotitlán del Valle, offer community-run guesthouses and a slower rhythm. The hills around San Agustín Etla, north of the city, are another peaceful option, with an arts center set in a former textile mill.

Oaxaca’s Pacific coast — Puerto Escondido, Mazunte, Zipolite and Huatulco — is a different trip entirely. Mountain roads make the drive several hours long, so many travelers fly between the city and the coast. Treat it as its own leg rather than a side trip.

Tips for Booking

  • Book early for big events — the Guelaguetza festival in July and Día de Muertos around the start of November fill the city fast.
  • Ask about noise — rooftops and courtyards are lovely, but street-facing rooms in Centro can be lively.
  • Mind the altitude — the city sits at roughly 1,550 meters, so evenings can be cool in winter. Pack a layer.
  • Check for hot water and heating — smaller guesthouses vary, so read recent reviews.

The Bottom Line

For most visitors, Centro or Jalatlaco is the sweet spot: walkable, atmospheric and close to the food. Choose Xochimilco for quiet, Reforma for everyday living, and add a village or coastal stay if time allows. Then plan your days with our three-day Oaxaca itinerary.

title: What to Eat in Oaxaca: Moles, Tlayudas, Mezcal and More
dek: Seven moles, crispy tlayudas, chapulines, tejate and mezcal — your guide to eating and drinking your way through Oaxaca.
body:
Oaxaca is often called Mexico’s culinary heart, and a few days here make the case convincingly. The cooking is rooted in Indigenous traditions, ancient corn varieties and a patient love of chiles and smoke. Come hungry, and use this guide alongside our Oaxaca guide.

The Seven Moles (and Then Some)

Oaxaca is known as the land of seven moles, though in reality there are many more, and every family has its own version. The classic seven are usually listed as:

  • Mole negro — the famous one: dark, complex and slightly sweet, with chiles, spices, chocolate and charred ingredients.
  • Mole rojo — rich and brick-red, often served at celebrations.
  • Coloradito — a sweeter, lighter red mole.
  • Amarillo — thinner and earthy, often used in empanadas.
  • Verde — bright with fresh herbs such as hoja santa and epazote.
  • Chichilo — smoky, rare and dark, made with distinctive chiles.
  • Manchamanteles — the “tablecloth stainer,” fruity and sweet with plantain and pineapple.

Try mole over chicken, in enmoladas, or with a tamal wrapped in banana leaf.

Tlayudas, Memelas and Masa Magic

A tlayuda is a large, thin tortilla toasted until crisp, smeared with asiento (unrefined pork lard) and black beans, then topped with cabbage, quesillo and meat such as tasajo, cecina or chorizo. Some are folded and grilled over coals; all are best eaten in the evening, the traditional tlayuda hour.

Memelas are thick, hand-pressed masa rounds with pinched edges, topped with asiento, beans, salsa and crumbled cheese — a perfect breakfast. Look for empanadas de amarillo and anything made with quesillo, the stringy local cheese sold in wound balls.

Chapulines and Other Adventures

Toasted grasshoppers, or chapulines, are a Oaxacan classic — crunchy, salty and sharp with lime and chile. Market vendors sell them by the scoop, and you’ll also find them sprinkled on guacamole or tucked into tacos. They’re a snack first, a dare second.

Chocolate, Tejate and Sweet Things

Oaxacan chocolate is ground with sugar and often cinnamon and almonds, then whisked into hot water or milk until frothy. Dunk a slice of pan de yema, an egg-rich bread. You can watch cacao being ground in shops near the markets, and the aroma alone is worth a stop.

Tejate is a pre-Hispanic drink made from maize, cacao, mamey seeds and a flower called rosita de cacao, served cool with a pale foam on top. Look for it in markets, ladled from large painted bowls. Afterward, grab a scoop of nieve, the city’s traditional sorbet, in flavors like tuna (prickly pear) or leche quemada.

Mezcal Country

Most of Mexico’s mezcal comes from Oaxaca. Start with espadín, the most widely cultivated agave, then compare wild varieties such as tobalá or tepextate, which can take many years to mature. Sip slowly, often with orange slices and sal de gusano.

Many travelers visit palenques (small distilleries) in the valleys east of the city, especially around Santiago Matatlán. Tours make it easy to see agave hearts roasted in earthen pits and crushed by stone wheels — just don’t drive afterward.

The Markets: 20 de Noviembre and Benito Juárez

Two side-by-side markets just south of the Zócalo anchor Oaxaca’s food scene. Mercado 20 de Noviembre is famous for its smoke-filled grilling aisle: pick raw meat from a butcher, hand it to a grill cook, then add tortillas, salsas and vegetables from nearby vendors to build your own feast.

Across the street, Mercado Benito Juárez is a maze of produce, chiles, cheese, chocolate, mezcal, flowers and handcrafts. Wander with an open mind and small bills. Both markets are at their busiest around midday, when the comedores are packed with locals on their lunch break.

Eating Well in Oaxaca

  • Carry cash for markets and street stalls.
  • Ask before photographing vendors.
  • Pace your mezcal — the altitude makes it hit a little harder.
  • Take a cooking class if you want to understand mole beyond the plate.

Ready to plan the meals around the sights? Our three-day Oaxaca itinerary builds in market stops and a mezcal tasting.
