title: Best Neighborhoods in Mexico City: Where to Base and Explore
dek: From leafy Condesa to colonial Coyoacán, a neighborhood-by-neighborhood guide to choosing your base in Mexico City.
body:
Mexico City is less a single city than a patchwork of very different villages stitched together by traffic. Where you sleep shapes everything — how far you walk, what you eat for breakfast, how late the night runs. This guide pairs with our Mexico City guide to help you choose a base that fits your trip.

Roma Norte: The All-Rounder

If you want one answer, it’s probably Roma. Tree-lined streets, early-20th-century mansions, independent galleries and a café on nearly every corner make Roma Norte the neighborhood many first-timers fall for. It’s walkable, lively without being frantic, and packed with some of the city’s most talked-about kitchens, from taquerías to tasting menus.

Roma Sur is quieter and a touch more local, with neighborhood markets and fewer visitors. Either way, you’re well placed for Condesa next door and a short ride from the historic center. Plaza Río de Janeiro, with its replica of Michelangelo’s David, is a lovely spot to get your bearings on a first afternoon.

Condesa: Parks, Art Deco and Dog Walkers

Condesa is Roma’s greener, slightly more polished sibling. Its heart is Parque México, ringed by Art Deco apartment buildings, and the oval of Avenida Ámsterdam — once a horse track — makes a lovely loop for a morning walk. Weekends bring joggers, dog walkers and long brunches spilling onto the sidewalks.

It suits travelers who want calm days and a buzzy evening scene within a few blocks. Nights around the busier bar corners can run late, so ask for a room away from the street if you’re a light sleeper.

Polanco: Polished and Upscale

Polanco is Mexico City in a tailored jacket: luxury boutiques along Avenida Presidente Masaryk, embassies, high-end dining and quiet residential blocks. It sits beside Bosque de Chapultepec, which puts the Museo Nacional de Antropología and Chapultepec Castle within easy reach.

It’s a smart pick for business travelers, families or anyone who values polish and a sense of calm. The trade-off is a slightly less bohemian feel and a longer ride to the Centro.

Centro Histórico: History at Your Doorstep

Stay in the historic center and you wake up steps from the Zócalo, the Metropolitan Cathedral, the ruins of the Templo Mayor and the Diego Rivera murals in the Palacio Nacional. Pedestrian Calle Madero links the main square to the Palacio de Bellas Artes and the Alameda Central.

Days are electric; some streets empty out after dark, so it’s worth choosing a well-located, well-reviewed base and taking rideshares at night. It’s ideal for short, sightseeing-heavy trips and architecture lovers. Rooftop terraces overlooking the cathedral are one of the neighborhood’s quiet pleasures — sunset over the Zócalo is hard to beat.

Coyoacán: Colonial Charm in the South

Coyoacán feels like a small town that the city grew around — cobblestones, bougainvillea, cozy plazas and the famous Casa Azul, where Frida Kahlo was born and later lived. Weekends bring families to Jardín Centenario for churros, ice cream and street performers, and the local market is great for a casual lunch.

It’s a gentle, romantic base for slower trips or return visits, though it’s farther from Roma, Condesa and the center. Build in travel time if you’re planning a packed schedule.

Juárez: Central and Up-and-Coming

Juárez sits between Roma and Paseo de la Reforma, which makes it one of the most convenient bases in the city. It mixes grand older buildings with newer cafés, cocktail bars and design shops, and it’s a short walk to the Ángel de la Independencia and the broad, sculpture-lined Paseo de la Reforma, which closes to cars for cyclists on Sunday mornings. The Zona Rosa section is busier and a hub of LGBTQ+ nightlife.

Choose Juárez if you want a central location with a creative edge and easy access to both the Centro and Chapultepec.

How to Choose

  • First visit, want it all — Roma Norte or Condesa
  • Luxury and museums — Polanco
  • Short trip, big sights — Centro Histórico
  • Slow and charming — Coyoacán
  • Central with a creative streak — Juárez

Mexico City is huge and traffic is real, so a well-placed base saves you hours. Once you’ve picked your neighborhood, map out your days with our three-day Mexico City itinerary — and plan to wander, because every colonia rewards it.

title: Day Trips from Mexico City: Pyramids, Colonial Towns and Canals
dek: Teotihuacán, Puebla and Cholula, Xochimilco, Taxco and Valle de Bravo — the most rewarding day trips from Mexico City.
body:
Mexico City could keep you busy for weeks, but some of its best experiences sit just beyond the sprawl. Ancient pyramids, tiled colonial cities, flower-decked canals and hill towns are all within reach for a day. Once you’ve covered the basics in our Mexico City guide, pick one or two of these escapes.

Teotihuacán: The City of the Gods

About an hour northeast of the city, depending on traffic, Teotihuacán is one of the most impressive archaeological sites in the Americas. Walk the Avenue of the Dead between the vast Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon, and imagine the metropolis that thrived here long before the Aztecs arrived and gave it its name.

  • Go early — the site is exposed and the midday sun is fierce. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
  • Float above it — hot-air balloon flights at sunrise are a popular splurge.
  • Check before you go — rules on climbing the pyramids have changed over the years, so confirm current access and entry details with official sources.

Puebla and Cholula: Talavera, Mole and a Hidden Pyramid

Roughly two hours east by road, Puebla is a handsome colonial city known for its Talavera tiles, grand cathedral and baroque churches. It’s also a serious food destination: this is the home of mole poblano, and in late summer, the patriotic chiles en nogada.

Next door, Cholula hides one of the largest pyramids in the world by volume beneath a grassy hill crowned by a golden church. On a clear day, the view of the Popocatépetl volcano behind it is unforgettable. Puebla and Cholula make a full, rewarding day — or a relaxed overnight.

Xochimilco: Canals and Trajineras

Technically still within Mexico City but a trip in its own right, Xochimilco is a network of ancient canals and chinampas — the floating-garden farms of pre-Hispanic times — recognized by UNESCO. Hop aboard a brightly painted trajinera, float past mariachi boats and snack vendors, and let the afternoon drift by.

Want a quieter experience? Some trips focus on the working chinampas and ecological side of the canals, with a gentler pace and a look at how local farmers still grow flowers and vegetables here.

Weekends are festive and loud; weekdays are calmer. Allow roughly an hour or more to get there from central neighborhoods, and agree on boat pricing before you set off.

Taxco: Silver on the Hillside

About two and a half to three hours south, in the state of Guerrero, Taxco tumbles down a mountainside in a jumble of whitewashed houses and red-tile roofs. The town grew rich on silver mining and remains famous for its silverwork. The pink-stone Santa Prisca church, a baroque masterpiece, anchors the main square.

It’s a long day, so leave early — or stay the night to see the town glow after dark. Streets are steep and narrow; comfortable shoes are non-negotiable. Shop for silver with a little care — reputable pieces are typically stamped .925.

Valle de Bravo: Lakeside Weekend Energy

Roughly two and a half to three hours west, Valle de Bravo is a pretty lakeside town beloved by chilangos escaping for the weekend. Expect cobbled lanes, a lively plaza, sailing and boat rides on the lake, and paragliding off the surrounding hills.

In winter, roughly November to March, monarch butterflies gather in forest sanctuaries in the wider region — confirm current seasons and access locally if that’s on your list. Given the drive, Valle works best as an overnight.

Planning Your Day Trips

  • Start early — traffic leaving and re-entering the city can add a lot of time.
  • Choose your transport — first-class buses, private drivers and organized tours all work; guided trips simplify longer routes.
  • Avoid overloading — Taxco and Valle de Bravo shine brighter with an overnight.

Travel times here are approximate and vary with traffic and route. Fit a day trip around the city highlights in our three-day Mexico City itinerary, and give yourself at least one day to simply rest your feet.

title: Best Time to Visit Mendoza: A Season-by-Season Guide
dek: Harvest parties, spring blossoms, snowy Andes or sizzling summer vineyards? Here is how each season shapes a trip to Mendoza.
body:
Mendoza sits in the rain shadow of the Andes, which means sunshine is almost a given — the real question is what kind of sunshine you want. Grape harvest, autumn gold, snow-capped peaks or long, hot summer evenings each make a different trip. Here is how the seasons play out, so you can match the calendar to your plans.

Harvest Season: Late Summer to Autumn

For many wine lovers, this is the sweet spot. The grape harvest generally runs from around February into April, depending on the variety and the altitude of the vineyard. Wineries are busy and buzzing, the air smells faintly of fermenting fruit, and the vines are heavy with grapes.

By April and into May, temperatures soften and the vineyards turn shades of amber and rust against the mountains. It is arguably the most photogenic time of year, with warm days and crisp evenings perfect for a glass of Malbec by a fire.

Fiesta de la Vendimia

Mendoza’s grape harvest festival, the Fiesta Nacional de la Vendimia, is the city’s biggest celebration. The main events usually take place in early March, with parades of decorated floats through the city center, folk music, and a grand theatrical show in an amphitheater set against the foothills, capped by the crowning of a harvest queen.

It is a joyful time to visit, but it is also peak season. Book accommodation, restaurant tables and winery visits well ahead — the city fills up with visitors from across Argentina — and check the official program for exact dates, which vary from year to year.

Spring: Blossoms and Budbreak

Spring in the Southern Hemisphere runs roughly September to November, and it is a lovely, underrated time to come. Fruit and almond trees blossom, the vines begin to leaf out, and snow still dusts the high Andes behind the vineyards.

Days are pleasantly warm, crowds are lighter than during harvest, and wineries are often more relaxed. One thing to watch for is the zonda, a hot, dry wind that can blow down from the mountains in late winter and spring, bringing dust and a sudden spike in temperature.

Winter: Cold Nights and Ski Season

From roughly June to August, Mendoza gets chilly, especially at night, though days are often clear and bright. The vines are bare and pruned, so the landscape is starker — but the mountain views are at their most dramatic, with the Andes heavily blanketed in snow.

Winter is ski season in the high Andes, and several ski areas are reachable from the province, making it possible to pair a few days on the slopes with long, cozy winery lunches. Be aware that heavy snow can close the mountain road toward Chile, so build flexibility into any plans that head up into the cordillera.

Summer: Hot, Lively and Long Days

December through February brings the heat. Afternoons in the city often feel very hot, and the sun is intense at this altitude. The upside is long daylight, lively evenings and green, leafy streets thanks to the city’s famous irrigation channels and shade trees.

  • Plan winery visits and outdoor activities for the morning.
  • Retreat to a shaded lunch or a pool in the heat of the afternoon.
  • Consider higher-altitude wine areas like the Uco Valley, where it is often a little cooler.
  • Pack a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water.

Summer is also a good time for mountain adventures such as rafting or hiking in the foothills, when the high roads are reliably open.

So, When Should You Go?

If wine is the main event, aim for March to May, when you get harvest energy, the Vendimia and gorgeous autumn color. For quieter wineries and mild weather, spring is a strong choice. Winter suits travelers who want to combine skiing and wine, while summer works if you do not mind the heat and plan your days around it.

Whenever you go, our 3-day Mendoza itinerary will help you shape the days, and the full Mendoza guide covers where to stay, eat and explore.

title: Day Trips from Medellín: Guatapé, Jardín, Coffee Farms and More
dek: Climb El Peñol, wander colonial Santa Fe de Antioquia, sip coffee on a farm and breathe mountain air at Parque Arví.
body:
Leave Medellín’s valley in almost any direction and you’ll find lakes, coffee-covered hills and colonial towns painted every color imaginable. Antioquia is one of Colombia’s most scenic regions, and many of its highlights are within an easy day’s reach. Once you’ve explored the city with our Medellín guide, these are the trips to add.

Guatapé and El Peñol

This is Medellín’s classic day trip, and it lives up to the hype. About two hours east of the city, a vast reservoir spreads across the landscape in a maze of green islands and inlets. Rising above it is El Peñol, a colossal granite monolith with a zigzagging staircase of roughly 700 steps running up its side. The view from the top is spectacular.

Nearby, the town of Guatapé is famous for its zócalos — colorful relief panels decorating the lower walls of houses, depicting everything from animals to scenes of local life. Add a boat ride on the reservoir, and you’ve got a full, very satisfying day.

  • Climb early to beat the heat and the weekend crowds.
  • Wear comfortable shoes and bring water for the stairs.
  • Consider staying the night if you want to enjoy the lakes at a slower pace.

Santa Fe de Antioquia

Northwest of Medellín, roughly an hour and a half to two hours away, Santa Fe de Antioquia was once the capital of the region and has preserved its colonial character beautifully: whitewashed houses, cobblestone streets, wooden balconies and handsome churches. It sits at a lower altitude than Medellín, so expect real heat — plan a leisurely lunch and a long, shady break.

Just outside town, the Puente de Occidente is a 19th-century suspension bridge spanning the Cauca River, an engineering landmark that’s worth the short detour.

Jardín: Worth an Overnight

Jardín, in southwestern Antioquia, is one of Colombia’s loveliest towns, with a lively main plaza anchored by a striking stone basilica, rows of brightly painted houses and coffee-draped mountains all around. You can hike to waterfalls, ride small cable cars up to viewpoints, and look for the vivid Andean cock-of-the-rock, a bird that gathers at sites near town.

At about three to four hours each way, it’s a long day trip. We strongly recommend spending at least one night — the plaza is at its most charming in the evening, when locals gather over coffee and conversation.

Coffee Farm Visits

You don’t have to travel all the way to Colombia’s famous Coffee Axis to learn how your morning cup is made. Several farms in the hills around Medellín offer tours that walk you from plant to roast: picking, processing, drying, and, of course, tasting. Availability and formats vary, so book ahead and check what’s included, including transportation from the city.

Parque Arví: Nature on the Edge of the City

For a lighter outing, Parque Arví is a large nature reserve in the mountains above Medellín, with forest trails, picnic areas and remnants of ancient paths. Getting there is part of the adventure: take the metro to the Metrocable, then continue on a separately ticketed cable-car line that soars over the pine-covered ridge. It’s cooler up there, so pack a layer.

The surrounding Santa Elena area is known for its flower-growing tradition, celebrated each year during the city’s famous flower festival.

Tour, Bus or Driver?

Medellín’s intercity bus terminals connect to all of these towns, and buses are an inexpensive, straightforward option if you’re comfortable with a little independent navigation. Organized tours bundle transport, a guide and often a meal, which is handy for Guatapé or coffee farms. For groups or families, hiring a private driver for the day offers the most flexibility — stop at viewpoints, linger over lunch and set your own pace on winding mountain roads.

Planning Tips

  • Start early, especially for Guatapé, to beat traffic and crowds.
  • Go midweek when possible; weekends and holidays draw big local crowds.
  • Check official information for cable-car operations, park access and transport schedules, which can change.
  • Pack for two climates — sun protection for hot lowland towns and a layer for the mountains.

Fit your favorites around the city highlights in our 3-day Medellín itinerary.

title: What to Eat in Mexico City: Dishes and Food Experiences Not to Miss
dek: Tacos al pastor, chilaquiles, tlacoyos, mezcal and the markets that tie them together — a delicious guide to eating in Mexico City.
body:
Mexico City is one of the world’s great eating cities, and much of the best food costs very little and comes on a paper plate. Pace yourself: breakfast, a mid-morning snack, a long late lunch and tacos at night is a perfectly reasonable schedule here. Use this list alongside our Mexico City guide to eat your way across the capital.

Tacos, Tacos, Tacos

Tacos al pastor are the city’s signature. Pork is marinated in chiles and achiote, stacked on a vertical spit called a trompo and shaved onto small corn tortillas with a sliver of pineapple — a technique that traces back to shawarma brought by Lebanese immigrants. Add onion, cilantro and salsa, and order more than you think you need.

Don’t stop there. Look for suadero (tender beef confited in fat), tacos de canasta (soft, steamed “basket tacos” sold from bicycles in the morning) and weekend barbacoa, slow-cooked lamb served with a cup of rich consommé.

Breakfast Like a Local

  • Chilaquiles — fried tortilla pieces simmered in salsa verde or roja, topped with cream, cheese and onion, often with egg or chicken. The ultimate morning comfort food.
  • Tamales and the guajolota — tamales sold from street carts at dawn, sometimes tucked into a bolillo roll to become a “guajolota,” a carb-on-carb classic.
  • Café de olla and pan dulce — cinnamon-spiced coffee and a sweet roll such as a concha.

Masa Snacks: Tlacoyos, Quesadillas and More

Much of the city’s street food begins with masa. Tlacoyos are oval corn cakes stuffed with beans, fava or requesón, griddled and topped with nopales, salsa and crumbled cheese — often made from blue corn. Sopes, huaraches and gorditas are close relatives.

A local quirk: in the capital, a quesadilla doesn’t automatically include cheese. Fillings like squash blossom, huitlacoche or mushrooms are common, so ask “con queso” if you want it.

Market Culture

Markets are where the city’s appetite is on full display. Neighborhood mercados are ideal for a cheap, hearty lunch at a counter — think pozole, quesadillas or a comida corrida set meal. Bigger markets reward a wander:

  • Mercado de la Merced — sprawling and intense, with produce, chiles and snacks in every direction.
  • Mercado de San Juan — known for specialty and unusual ingredients, from imported cheeses to exotic meats.
  • Mercado de Coyoacán — a popular stop for tostadas after visiting the southern neighborhood.
  • Mercado de Jamaica — primarily a flower market, but worth it for the color alone.

Sweet Things and Late-Night Treats

Churros dunked in thick hot chocolate are a classic any time of day. Street carts sell esquites (corn kernels in a cup with mayo, lime and chile) and elote on the cob, while ice-cream vendors scoop fruit flavors like mango, guanábana and tamarind.

What to Drink: Mezcal, Pulque and Beyond

Mezcal is sipped slowly, often with orange slices and sal de gusano. Ask for an espadín if you’re new, or explore wild agaves once you’ve got your bearings. Unlike tequila, which must come from specific regions and blue agave, mezcal can be made from many agave species, and its smoky flavor comes from roasting the hearts in earthen pits. Pulque, the milky fermented sap of the maguey, predates the Spanish and is served in traditional pulquerías — sometimes curado, blended with fruit or oats.

For something lighter, try an agua fresca like horchata or jamaica, or a michelada — beer with lime, salt and spicy seasonings.

Practical Tips for Eating Well

  • Choose busy stalls with high turnover — locals are the best quality control.
  • Eat your main meal in the afternoon, as many locals do; comida is the day’s big event.
  • Carry small bills and coins; many street vendors only take cash.
  • Go easy on salsas until you’ve tested their heat.
  • Stick to bottled or purified water, and start gently with street food if your stomach is sensitive.

Hungry for a plan? Our three-day Mexico City itinerary leaves plenty of room for tacos between the museums.

title: The Andes from Mendoza: A Day Trip to Aconcagua and Puente del Inca
dek: Follow the mountain road west from Mendoza past Potrerillos and Uspallata to Puente del Inca and the Aconcagua viewpoint on this epic Andes day trip.
body:
Mendoza’s vineyards are lovely, but the real showstopper is the wall of mountains on the horizon. A day trip west along the high road toward Chile takes you from turquoise reservoirs to ancient Inca trails and the foot of Aconcagua, the highest mountain in the Americas. Here is what to expect along the way.

The Route: Heading West Toward Chile

The journey follows the main mountain highway that links Mendoza with Chile, climbing steadily through the Andes. It is a full-day outing, with several hours of driving each way and plenty of stops along the route. You can join an organized tour, hire a private driver or drive yourself if you are comfortable with mountain roads.

The scenery changes constantly — from desert foothills to red and ochre canyon walls and, eventually, snowcapped peaks. Pack snacks and water, since services can be spread out once you leave the valleys.

Potrerillos Reservoir

About an hour from the city, the road reaches the Potrerillos reservoir, a striking turquoise lake framed by mountains. It is a popular spot for a first photo stop, and the surrounding area is known for outdoor activities such as rafting on the Mendoza River, kayaking and horseback riding in the warmer months.

Uspallata

Continuing west, the road opens onto the high valley of Uspallata, a small town surrounded by poplar trees and multicolored hills. The landscapes here are so dramatic that they have stood in for Tibet on film. It makes a good place to stretch your legs, grab a coffee or lunch and take in the wide, open views before the road climbs higher.

Puente del Inca

Puente del Inca is one of the most unusual sights on the route: a natural stone bridge arching over the river, stained in shades of orange, yellow and ochre by the mineral-rich hot springs that flow nearby. Beneath and beside it are the ruins of an old spa hotel that once drew visitors to the thermal waters.

The area sits at around 2,700 meters above sea level, so move slowly as you walk around. Stalls nearby sell souvenirs, including small objects left in the mineral waters until they are coated in a crust of orange sediment.

Aconcagua Provincial Park Viewpoint

A short distance beyond Puente del Inca is the entrance to Aconcagua Provincial Park. From the area around the Laguna de Horcones, an easy trail leads to viewpoints where, on a clear day, you can see the enormous south face of Aconcagua, which rises to nearly 7,000 meters.

Park access rules, permits and trail openings can change with the season, so check current official information before you go. Even the short walks here are at high altitude, so take them at an easy pace.

Altitude and Weather: Stay Safe

This is serious mountain terrain, and conditions can change quickly. Keep these precautions in mind:

  • Altitude — You will go from city elevation to nearly 3,000 meters in a single day. Walk slowly, stay hydrated, and go easy on alcohol. Anyone with heart or respiratory concerns should seek medical advice first.
  • Weather — It can be warm in Mendoza and freezing at the park. Bring warm layers, a windproof jacket, sunglasses and high-SPF sunscreen, even in summer.
  • Road closures — Heavy snow can close the highway, particularly in winter. Check road conditions and the status of the border crossing before setting out.
  • Border area — Heading all the way to the Chilean border involves official crossings; carry your passport and check current requirements if you plan to go that far.

Practical Wrap-Up

Start early to make the most of the daylight and the clearest mountain views, which are often best in the morning. Summer and early autumn generally offer the most reliable conditions, while winter brings snowy scenery but a higher chance of closures. A tour or driver lets you focus on the views instead of the switchbacks.

This trip fits neatly into our 3-day Mendoza itinerary, and you can find more ideas for wine, food and adventure in the full Mendoza guide.

title: How to Plan Winery Visits in Mendoza
dek: Reservations, drivers, bike tours and long lunches: a practical guide to planning Mendoza winery visits without the stress (or the hangover).
body:
Mendoza is Argentina’s wine capital, and it would be a little rude to leave without visiting a few bodegas. But with hundreds of wineries spread across several regions, a bit of planning goes a long way. Here is how to structure your tasting days so they feel indulgent rather than rushed.

Know the Wine Regions

Most visitors focus on three main areas, each with a different feel:

  • Luján de Cuyo — Close to the city and often called the heartland of Malbec, with a mix of historic estates and modern wineries.
  • Maipú — Also close to town and relatively flat, with older wineries, olive oil producers and a well-trodden bike route.
  • Uco Valley — Roughly an hour or more south of the city, with high-altitude vineyards, dramatic Andes views and many design-forward wineries.

Try to cluster your visits within one region per day. Driving between regions eats up time you would rather spend at the table.

Book Ahead — Always

Unlike some wine regions where you can simply turn up, most Mendoza wineries work on a reservation basis. Tastings and tours are usually scheduled at set times, and popular estates can book up days or even weeks ahead, especially during harvest and around the Vendimia festival.

Reserve your visits once your dates are firm, and confirm the language of the tour if you do not speak Spanish. Check each winery’s current policies directly, since formats and requirements change.

Drivers, Tours or Bikes?

Deciding how to get around is the most important logistical choice you will make:

  • Private driver — The most flexible option. You set the wineries and the pace, and nobody has to worry about drinking and driving. Ideal for the Uco Valley and for small groups.
  • Group tours — Convenient and social, with transport and bookings handled for you. The trade-off is less control over which wineries you visit and how long you stay.
  • Biking in Maipú — A classic and fun half or full day. You rent a bike and pedal between nearby wineries along mostly flat roads. Go easy on the pours, wear sunscreen, and watch for traffic on shared roads.
  • Self-driving — Possible, but Argentina has strict drink-driving rules, so it only works if someone in the group is happy to stay sober.

Pace Yourself: Two or Three a Day

It is tempting to squeeze in as many tastings as possible, but two or three wineries a day is the sweet spot. Each visit typically includes a tour and a generous tasting, and anything more starts to blur together — for your palate and your memory.

A good rhythm is one winery in the morning, a long lunch at another, and perhaps a final relaxed tasting in the late afternoon. Drink water between visits and do not skip breakfast.

Make Time for a Long Lunch

Many wineries serve multi-course lunches paired with their own wines, often on terraces overlooking the vines and mountains. These meals are a highlight of any Mendoza trip, and they are leisurely — expect to spend a good few hours at the table.

Book these lunches well in advance, and plan the rest of the day lightly around them. A siesta afterward is not a bad idea.

Bringing Wine Home

You will almost certainly find bottles you want to take with you. Some wineries may offer shipping, but availability and rules vary widely by destination country, so ask directly and check your home country’s import limits.

If you are carrying wine in checked luggage, wrap each bottle well — padded wine sleeves or clothing work — and keep in mind airline weight limits and customs allowances when you land.

Practical Wrap-Up

  • Pick one region per day and book everything in advance.
  • Plan for two or three wineries, including one long lunch.
  • Arrange a driver or tour unless you are cycling in Maipú.
  • Bring sunscreen, a hat and water — the sun is strong at altitude.

For a ready-made plan that balances wine with the rest of the city, see our 3-day Mendoza itinerary, and browse the full Mendoza guide for more ideas.

title: What to Eat in Medellín: Paisa Dishes, Snacks and Drinks
dek: From a heaping bandeja paisa to warm buñuelos and a shot of aguardiente — the paisa flavors to seek out in Medellín.
body:
Food in Medellín is generous, rustic and deeply tied to paisa identity — the culture of the Antioquia region, famous for its hospitality and its hearty mountain cooking. Come hungry, pace yourself and say yes to seconds. For everything else, head to our Medellín guide.

Bandeja Paisa: The Main Event

The region’s signature plate is less a dish than an event. A bandeja paisa typically brings together red beans, white rice, ground beef, crispy pork belly (chicharrón), chorizo, a fried egg, sweet fried plantain, avocado and an arepa, with morcilla (blood sausage) sometimes joining the party.

It was born as fuel for long days of farm work, and it shows. Order one at lunch, ideally when you have no strenuous plans afterward, and consider sharing if you want to try anything else that day.

Arepas, Paisa-Style

The everyday arepa of Antioquia is thin, round and fairly plain — made from ground white corn and designed as a side for nearly everything. Locals often eat it with a pat of butter and a slab of fresh white cheese (quesito).

For something sweeter, look for arepa de chócolo, made from fresh sweet corn and folded or topped with melting cheese. It’s a beloved street snack, especially hot off the grill. You’ll also find arepas split and stuffed with shredded meat, eggs or cheese — a full meal in your hand, and a reliable late-night fix.

Buñuelos, Empanadas and Other Snacks

  • Buñuelos — golden, fried balls of cheese and cornstarch dough, crisp outside and airy within. Best eaten warm, often with hot chocolate or coffee.
  • Empanadas — Colombian-style turnovers with a crunchy cornmeal shell, usually filled with potato and meat. Spoon on plenty of ají, the tangy, lightly spicy salsa.
  • Pandebono — chewy cheese bread, the perfect partner for a morning coffee.
  • Obleas — thin wafers sandwiched with arequipe (caramel) and other toppings, a classic street treat.

Mondongo: A Comforting Classic

Mondongo is a slow-cooked soup of tripe with pork, potatoes, vegetables and herbs, and it’s a paisa home-cooking staple. It usually comes with rice, avocado and a slice of ripe banana on the side — trust the combination. If tripe isn’t usually your thing, this is a gentle way to give it a try, and the broth alone is worth it.

Tropical Fruit and Fresh Juice

The markets and street carts of Medellín overflow with fruit, and cups of sliced mango (sometimes with lime and salt), papaya and pineapple are a constant temptation. For a deeper dive, visit a traditional market such as the Plaza Minorista, where stalls stack lulo, maracuyá, guanábana, granadilla, uchuva and more.

Try a salpicón — a juicy mix of chopped fruit in juice — or a blended jugo natural, made with water or milk. Mazamorra, a traditional drink of soft-cooked corn in its liquid, often sweetened with panela, is another paisa classic.

Coffee and Aguardiente

Antioquia is coffee country, and Medellín’s specialty scene has grown impressively, with roasters and cafés highlighting single-origin beans from farms across the region. Order a tinto for the everyday black coffee locals drink throughout the day, or explore pour-overs and tasting flights for a more nuanced cup.

After dark, the regional spirit is aguardiente — an anise-flavored cane liquor served in small shots, often shared around the table and chased with water or a bite of fruit. It’s central to paisa celebrations. Sip slowly; its easy-drinking sweetness can be deceptive.

Eating Well in Medellín

  • Look for set lunches — the menú del día or corrientazo usually includes soup, a main plate and a juice at good value.
  • Snack between meals from bakeries, where buñuelos and pandebono come fresh from the oven.
  • Drink bottled or filtered water if you’re unsure, though many locals drink tap water in the city.
  • Pace the aguardiente, particularly at altitude and in the heat of a fun night.

Build these into your plans with our 3-day Medellín itinerary, and leave room for one more buñuelo.

title: Best Time to Visit Lima: A Season-by-Season Guide
dek: Sunny summers, gray garúa winters and almost no rain. Here is how Lima’s unusual coastal climate works and when to plan your trip.
body:
Lima’s weather is unlike almost anywhere else in South America. It sits in a coastal desert where it barely ever rains, yet for months at a time the sky is a soft, stubborn gray. Knowing how the seasons work will help you decide when to go, and how to combine the capital with the rest of Peru.

Why Lima’s Climate Is So Unusual

The cold Humboldt Current runs along Peru’s coast, cooling the air above the ocean. That creates a layer of low clouds and mist that settles over the city for much of the year, while also suppressing real rainfall. The result is a mild, humid climate with few extremes: rarely truly hot, rarely truly cold, and almost never wet enough to need an umbrella.

Summer: December to April

This is Lima at its sunniest. Skies clear, temperatures climb into warm beach weather and the city turns toward the ocean. The Malecón in Miraflores fills with walkers and paragliders, surfers crowd the breaks below the cliffs and long lunches stretch into golden evenings.

  • Pros — blue skies, beach days, the city at its most energetic
  • Cons — can be hot and humid; busier around the holidays
  • Good for — coastal trips to Paracas and Huacachina

Winter: The Garúa Season, Roughly June to October

From about June through October, Lima settles under a blanket of gray. Locals call the fine, drifting mist garúa: it dampens pavements and jackets but rarely adds up to anything like rain. Temperatures are cool rather than cold, though the humidity can make it feel chillier than the thermometer suggests.

It is not the postcard version of the city, but it has its own moody charm, and it takes nothing away from what many people come for: the food. Museums, markets and restaurants are just as rewarding under a gray sky.

  • Pros — pairs perfectly with the Andes’ dry season; comfortable for sightseeing
  • Cons — weeks of overcast skies; ocean views often muted
  • Pack — layers, a light sweater and a jacket for the evenings

The Shoulder Months

May and November sit between the two moods. Skies can be mixed, crowds are often lighter and the weather is generally pleasant for walking the historic center or exploring Barranco. If you are flexible, these transition months can be a smart compromise.

Pairing Lima with the Andes

Most travelers do not visit Lima alone: they pass through on the way to Cusco, the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu. The highlands run on a different calendar. The Andes generally have a dry season from about May to September, with clearer skies for hiking, and a rainy season from roughly November to March.

That creates a neat trade-off. The Andes’ prime dry season overlaps with Lima’s gray winter, while Lima’s sunny summer coincides with the rainy months in the mountains. For many visitors, the highland weather matters more, so a trip in the May–September window, with a gray but pleasant stop in Lima, is a popular choice. If you plan to hike the Inca Trail, note that it typically closes each February for maintenance; check current official information for permits and dates.

Holidays and Busy Periods

Peru’s national holidays, Fiestas Patrias, fall on July 28 and 29, and many Peruvians travel around those dates, so transport and accommodation can fill up. The Christmas and New Year period and Easter week are also busy. If you plan to travel then, book flights and stays well ahead, and expect some businesses to keep holiday hours.

When to Go: The Wrap-Up

It comes down to what matters most to you:

  • For sunshine and beaches — December to April
  • For a combined Peru trip with hiking — May to September
  • For a balance of weather and crowds — May or November

Practical wrap-up: there is no bad time to eat your way through Lima, and the mild climate means sightseeing works year-round. Pack layers no matter the month, bring sun protection for summer and plan your highland stops around the Andes seasons. Once you have your dates, map out your days with our 3-day Lima itinerary and explore more in our Lima guide.

title: Day Trips from Lima: Paracas, Huacachina, Pachacamac and Caral
dek: From sea lions on the Ballestas Islands to desert dunes and ancient cities, these are the day trips worth taking from Lima.
body:
Lima rewards a few slow days, but the desert coast around it holds some of Peru’s most surprising scenery and oldest history. Within a few hours you can be watching sea lions, sandboarding down enormous dunes or walking through a city older than the Egyptian pyramids. Here is how to choose, and how to plan.

Paracas and the Ballestas Islands

About three and a half to four hours south of Lima by road, the small coastal town of Paracas is the gateway to the Islas Ballestas, often nicknamed the “poor man’s Galápagos.” Boat trips circle the rocky islands, which are crowded with sea lions, cormorants, boobies and, if you are lucky, Humboldt penguins. Landing on the islands is not permitted, so this is a look-from-the-water experience.

On the way out, boats pass the Candelabro, a giant geoglyph etched into a sandy hillside whose origin is still debated. Back on land, the Paracas National Reserve offers stark desert cliffs, red-sand beaches and dramatic ocean views.

  • Timing — boat tours usually run in the morning, when the sea tends to be calmer
  • Stay over? — Paracas has a relaxed seaside feel, and an overnight lets you enjoy the reserve without rushing back
  • Tip — bring sunscreen, a hat and a light jacket; spray and wind are part of the ride

Huacachina: The Desert Oasis

Near the city of Ica, roughly four and a half to five hours from Lima, Huacachina is a tiny lagoon ringed by palm trees and surrounded by towering sand dunes. It looks almost too cinematic to be real. The main event is a dune-buggy ride into the desert followed by sandboarding, ideally timed for late afternoon so you can watch the sunset over the sand.

It is technically possible as a very long day trip, but many travelers combine it with Paracas and stay overnight in one or both places. The Ica region is also Peru’s pisco heartland, so a visit to a vineyard or bodega makes a natural add-on.

Pachacamac: Ancient Ruins Close to the City

If you only have half a day, Pachacamac is the easy win. Located about 30 kilometers south of central Lima, roughly an hour’s drive depending on traffic, this vast archaeological complex was an important religious sanctuary for more than a thousand years, long before and during the Inca era.

You can walk among adobe temples and pyramids, including the Temple of the Sun, with views out to the Pacific. The on-site museum helps make sense of the layers of history. It pairs nicely with a relaxed afternoon back in Barranco or Miraflores.

Caral: A Journey to the Americas’ Oldest City

Caral is for the history devotee. The sacred city, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies in the Supe Valley roughly three to four hours north of Lima, and it is considered one of the oldest urban centers in the Americas, dating back about 5,000 years. Its stepped pyramids, sunken circular plazas and residential areas reveal a sophisticated society that flourished long before the Incas.

It is a long day, with the final stretch on a rougher road, so start early. Visits are generally guided within the site; check current access information before you go. Some travelers break up the journey with an overnight stop on the coast north of Lima rather than doing it all in one push.

Which Day Trip Should You Take?

  • Short on time — Pachacamac, easily done in a morning or afternoon
  • Wildlife and coast — Paracas and the Ballestas Islands
  • Adventure and sunsets — Huacachina, ideally with an overnight
  • Deep history — Caral, for a full and rewarding day

If you are working with a short stay, our 3-day Lima itinerary leaves room for one of these trips.

Practical Wrap-Up

Most of these destinations are reached via the Panamericana highway, and you can go by organized tour, long-distance bus or private driver. Traffic leaving and entering Lima is unpredictable, so give yourself generous buffers, especially if you have a flight the same day. Entry fees, boat schedules and site access rules change, so confirm current official details before you go. For everything else about the capital, see our Lima guide.

title: Where to Stay in Medellín: A Neighborhood Guide
dek: El Poblado, Laureles, Envigado or Manila? How to choose the Medellín neighborhood that matches your travel style.
body:
Medellín fills a long, green valley in the Andes, and its neighborhoods climb the slopes on either side. Nicknamed the City of Eternal Spring for its mild climate, it rewards visitors who pick a base that fits their pace — nightlife hub, leafy local enclave or quiet residential town. Here’s how the main options compare, with more on the city in our Medellín guide.

El Poblado and Provenza: The Classic First-Timer Base

El Poblado is the neighborhood most visitors know, and for good reason. Set on the southeastern hillside, it’s lush, upscale and packed with restaurants, cafés, bars, boutiques and accommodation at every level. Within it, Provenza is the buzziest pocket: a few tree-shaded streets lined with design-forward restaurants and cocktail spots, just uphill from the long-established nightlife around Parque Lleras.

It’s the easiest landing for a first trip — English is more widely spoken here, and everything you need is close by. The trade-offs? Prices run higher, weekend nights get loud, and the streets are steep. If you’re a light sleeper, choose a spot a few blocks away from the party zone.

Laureles: Leafy and Local

Across the river on the flat western side of the valley, Laureles has a completely different feel. Its streets curve in gentle circles around small parks, lined with low-rise homes and big shade trees. Two main corridors, known locally as La 70 and La 33, bring the energy with casual restaurants, bakeries and bars.

Laureles suits travelers who want to experience everyday Medellín, longer stays and anyone who likes to walk on level ground. It’s close to the city’s main stadium and sports complex, and it tends to offer better value than El Poblado.

Envigado: A Town of Its Own

Just south of El Poblado, Envigado is technically a separate municipality within the metropolitan area, and it has kept a proud small-town identity. Its central park, church and surrounding streets hum with local families, traditional eateries and a strong neighborhood rhythm.

It’s a great choice if you’d rather be a resident than a tourist, and it’s connected to the rest of the valley by the metro. Expect fewer international-style amenities, but more authentic day-to-day life — and a very relaxed pace.

Manila: Walkable and Low-Key

Manila is a small, flat pocket within El Poblado, near the main avenue at the bottom of the hill. It’s easier to explore on foot than the rest of the neighborhood, with cafés, bike-friendly streets, co-working spots and a scattering of small restaurants.

It’s a smart middle ground: you’re minutes from Provenza’s scene without living right in it, and you’ll spend less time trudging uphill.

Getting Around and Staying Savvy

Medellín’s metro system is clean, efficient and a point of civic pride, and its cable-car lines, the Metrocable, glide up to hillside communities with remarkable views. Ride apps and registered taxis fill in the gaps, especially after dark.

The city has transformed dramatically in recent decades, and most visits are trouble-free. Still, it’s a big city, and a local phrase sums up the best approach: no dar papaya — don’t make yourself an easy target.

  • Keep your phone tucked away on busy streets and in crowded transit.
  • Use app-based rides or registered taxis at night.
  • Be cautious meeting strangers from dating apps or social media, and meet in busy public places.
  • Watch your drink in nightlife areas and never leave it unattended.
  • Ask your hosts about the specific streets around you — current local advice beats any guidebook.

Hills, Heat and Where It Matters

Medellín sits at roughly 1,500 meters, so days are warm and nights pleasantly mild for most of the year, with rain showers that tend to arrive in the afternoon. Air-conditioning is less common than you might expect, so a room with good airflow or a fan makes a difference. On the hillsides of El Poblado, a short walk can mean a serious climb — check the terrain around your stay if you plan to explore on foot, or choose flatter Laureles or Manila.

Quick Picks

  • First trip, nightlife and dining: El Poblado or Provenza.
  • Local feel and flat, leafy walks: Laureles.
  • Small-town rhythm and longer stays: Envigado.
  • Walkable and a little quieter: Manila.

Once you’ve chosen your base, use our 3-day Medellín itinerary to plan how to spend your time across the valley.

title: Lake Chapala and Ajijic: A Day Trip from Guadalajara
dek: Mexico’s largest lake, a breezy malecón and the colorful village of Ajijic — how to plan a relaxed day trip from Guadalajara.
body:
When the city gets loud, Guadalajarans head to the lake. Lake Chapala, Mexico’s largest freshwater lake, sits roughly an hour south of the city and is ringed by mountains, lakeside promenades and small towns with a famously gentle climate — mild and sunny for much of the year. Here’s how to spend a day there, to pair with our Guadalajara guide.

Getting There

The drive from Guadalajara to Chapala usually takes about an hour, depending on traffic and where you start. From there, Ajijic is a short hop west along the shore.

  • By bus — regular buses run from Guadalajara to Chapala and Ajijic; it’s an easy, budget-friendly option.
  • By car or driver — the most flexible choice, especially if you want to visit several lakeside towns.
  • By rideshare or taxi — convenient one-way, though returning can require more planning, so confirm your ride back in advance.

Chapala: The Lakeside Town

The town of Chapala has been a weekend retreat for over a century, and you can still see stately older villas along the lakefront. Start with a stroll along the malecón, the waterfront promenade, where families gather, vendors sell snacks and the pier juts out over the water.

From the waterfront, boats can take you out onto the lake. Small islands, including Isla de los Alacranes, are popular destinations; Isla de Mezcala, farther east, is known for its role in Mexico’s independence struggle. Confirm current boat options and agree on pricing before you board.

Ajijic: Color, Art and Cobblestones

Ajijic is the charmer of the lakeshore. Its cobblestone streets are lined with brightly painted houses, murals, galleries and small boutiques, all leading down to a relaxed malecón. The village has long attracted artists and writers, and today it’s home to a large community of international retirees, which gives it a friendly, cosmopolitan feel.

Spend your time wandering the plaza, browsing local art and crafts, and watching the light change over the water from the lakefront. It’s an easy place to lose an afternoon. Look out for the village church and the plaza bandstand, and for the many murals that brighten walls around town, often celebrating local life and Indigenous heritage.

What to Eat by the Lake

Lakeside stands and casual restaurants traditionally serve charales, tiny fried fish eaten whole with lime and salsa — a classic Chapala snack. You’ll also find Jalisco staples like birria and seafood, plus cafés and bakeries in Ajijic. Grab a fresh fruit cup with chile and lime for the walk. If you’re there on a weekend, the waterfront feels like a small festival, with families picnicking and vendors selling ice cream and toys.

A Sample Day

  • Morning — leave Guadalajara early, then walk the Chapala malecón and pier while it’s still cool.
  • Late morning — take a boat ride out onto the lake if conditions are good.
  • Lunch — eat by the water in Chapala or head to Ajijic for lunch.
  • Afternoon — explore Ajijic’s streets, murals and galleries.
  • Sunset — watch the sky change over the mountains from the Ajijic malecón before heading back.

With more time, continue west to Jocotepec, a quieter town at the lake’s western end.

Prefer to linger? Many visitors stay a night or two in Ajijic, where evenings are calm and mornings by the water are especially lovely. It also makes a comfortable base for hiking in the hills above the lake — go with a local guide or a group, and check trail conditions first.

Good to Know

  • Water levels — the lake’s level can vary noticeably from year to year, which affects how the shoreline looks.
  • Swimming — the lake isn’t generally considered a swimming destination; enjoy it from the shore or a boat.
  • Weekends — Saturdays and Sundays are lively and busier; weekdays are calmer.
  • Sun — the high-altitude sun is strong, so bring sunscreen and a hat.

Lake Chapala makes a restful counterpoint to the city’s energy. Slot it into our three-day Guadalajara itinerary on a day when you’re ready to slow down.

title: Where to Stay in Lima: Miraflores vs Barranco vs San Isidro
dek: Miraflores, Barranco or San Isidro? A neighborhood-by-neighborhood guide to choosing your base in Lima, plus how to see the historic center.
body:
Lima is a sprawling city, and where you sleep shapes everything, from your morning coffee to how long you spend in traffic. Most visitors land in one of three neighboring districts along or near the Pacific cliffs: Miraflores, Barranco or San Isidro. Each has a distinct personality, and the right one depends on how you like to travel.

Miraflores: The Easy, All-Round Pick

If this is your first trip to Lima, Miraflores is the natural starting point. It sits on the clifftops above the Pacific, with the Malecón, a long ribbon of parks and walking paths, running along the edge. You can jog at sunrise, watch paragliders drift past at midday and catch the sunset over the ocean without ever getting in a car.

The district is walkable, well-lit and packed with cafés, restaurants and places to stay at every level. Parque Kennedy, at its center, is a lively hub (and home to a famously relaxed population of resident cats). It is not the most characterful corner of the city, but for convenience and ease, it is hard to beat.

  • Best for — first-timers, solo travelers, anyone who wants to walk everywhere
  • Vibe — polished, busy, ocean views
  • Trade-off — can feel more international than local

Barranco: Bohemian and Beautiful

Just south of Miraflores, Barranco is Lima’s artsy, romantic district. Pastel-colored mansions from the late 1800s and early 1900s line leafy streets, murals splash across walls, and galleries share blocks with cocktail bars. The Puente de los Suspiros, a small wooden bridge over a shaded pathway down toward the sea, is its best-known landmark and a lovely spot at golden hour.

Barranco is compact, full of personality and at its liveliest after dark. That also means it can be noisier on weekend nights, so if you are a light sleeper, choose a quieter side street. Miraflores is an easy walk or short ride away along the coast.

  • Best for — couples, creatives, nightlife and design lovers
  • Vibe — boho, colorful, a little faded in the best way
  • Trade-off — livelier at night; fewer options than Miraflores

San Isidro: Calm, Green and Upscale

San Isidro is Lima’s financial district, but it is far from all glass towers. Its standout green space, El Olivar, is a park planted with centuries-old olive trees, and the district also holds Huaca Huallamarca, a restored pre-Inca adobe pyramid rising unexpectedly among the apartment buildings.

Expect wide streets, a quieter pace and a more residential feel, especially on weekends when office workers are elsewhere. It sits a bit inland, so you will trade ocean views for tranquility, and many restaurants and sights are a short ride away rather than a stroll.

  • Best for — business travelers, return visitors, anyone craving quiet
  • Vibe — leafy, refined, residential
  • Trade-off — less walkable nightlife; you will rely more on taxis

The Historic Center: Visit by Day

Lima’s Centro Histórico is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and absolutely worth your time. The Plaza Mayor is framed by the cathedral, the Government Palace and ornate wooden balconies, and the Monastery of San Francisco is known for its catacombs and grand library.

Most travelers find it works better as a daytime excursion than a base. The center empties out in the evening, and the dining and nightlife scenes are concentrated in the coastal districts. Plan a full morning or afternoon there, then head back south for dinner. Our 3-day Lima itinerary shows how to fit it in.

How to Choose

A simple rule of thumb: pick Miraflores for convenience, Barranco for atmosphere and San Isidro for calm. All three are close enough to one another that you can easily explore the others, so there is no wrong answer, only a different first impression.

Traffic is the real variable in Lima. If you have an early flight or a day trip planned, consider how far your base is from where you need to be, and build in extra time during rush hours.

Practical Wrap-Up

  • Use registered taxis or ride-hailing apps rather than hailing cars on the street, especially at night.
  • Lima’s coast can be gray and damp for much of the year, so a room with good natural light matters more than a sea view you may not see.
  • Book further ahead for the December–April summer season and around major holidays.
  • Pair your stay with the neighborhoods, food and sights in our Lima guide.

title: Best Time to Visit Guadalajara: Weather, Seasons and Festivals
dek: Dry, sunny winters, warm springs and stormy summers — here’s how to choose the right season for your Guadalajara trip.
body:
Guadalajara sits at an elevation of roughly 1,500 meters, which gives it a mild climate much of the year — warm days, cool nights and plenty of sun. There’s no truly bad time to visit, but each season has its own personality. Here’s how to pick yours, alongside our Guadalajara guide.

The Short Answer

For most travelers, the sweet spot is the dry season, roughly November through May. You’ll get sunny days, little rain and comfortable temperatures for walking the historic center, exploring Tlaquepaque and day-tripping to Tequila or Lake Chapala.

Within that window, the late fall and winter months tend to be the most pleasant overall. Spring gets progressively hotter, and summer brings the rains. If you’re flexible, aim for November or February, when the weather is reliably pleasant and the city’s calendar is lively.

Winter (Roughly December to February)

Winter is dry, sunny and mild during the day, with crisp mornings and evenings that can feel genuinely chilly. Pack a light jacket or sweater — and don’t be surprised if your guesthouse lacks heating, which is common in this mild climate. Skies are usually clear, making it a lovely time for rooftop drinks and long walks.

The holiday period brings Christmas decorations, posadas and festive crowds, and it’s a popular time for domestic travel, so book ahead.

Spring (Roughly March to May)

Spring stays dry but heats up steadily, and April and May are typically the hottest months of the year, before the rains arrive to cool things down. Days can feel dusty and warm, especially in the afternoon, so plan outdoor sightseeing for the morning.

Holy Week (Semana Santa) is a major holiday across Mexico, bringing processions, closures and heavy domestic travel. It can be a fascinating time to visit, but reserve accommodation and transport early.

Summer Rainy Season (Roughly June to September)

The rainy season usually arrives in June and lasts into September or early October. The pattern is fairly predictable: mornings are often bright, then afternoon or evening thunderstorms roll in, sometimes heavy, occasionally causing street flooding.

The upside? Everything turns green, temperatures ease a bit and there are fewer international tourists. Plan activities for the morning, carry an umbrella and keep evenings flexible.

Summer is also when the agave fields around Tequila look their lushest, and indoor attractions — museums, markets and the murals inside the Hospicio Cabañas — make easy rainy-afternoon plans.

Fall (Roughly October to November)

As the rains taper off, fall becomes one of the most rewarding times to visit. October is a festive month in Guadalajara, with a season of celebrations and a major religious pilgrimage in neighboring Zapopan that draws huge crowds.

Then comes Día de Muertos on November 1 and 2, when altars, marigolds, sugar skulls and processions fill the city and nearby towns. It’s a beautiful, meaningful time to be in Mexico — just be respectful of family traditions and cemetery visits.

Events to Keep in Mind

  • Mariachi celebrations — Guadalajara is the heartland of mariachi, and the city has long hosted major mariachi gatherings, often in late summer.
  • International book fair — a large, well-known literary fair typically takes place in late fall.
  • Film festival — Guadalajara hosts a respected international film festival, usually in the first half of the year.
  • Día de Muertos — November 1 and 2, with celebrations building in the days before.

Dates for these events vary year to year, so check official event sites before planning around them.

Planning Tips

  • Pack layers — even warm months can have cool nights.
  • Book early around holidays — Semana Santa, Christmas and Día de Muertos are busy.
  • Stay hydrated — spring heat and altitude combine to sap your energy.

Shoulder months — late October and early November, or late May before the rains — can offer a nice balance of weather and availability. Whatever the season, Guadalajara rewards a few unhurried days. Once you’ve picked your dates, map it all out with our three-day Guadalajara itinerary.

title: What to Eat in Guadalajara: Tortas Ahogadas, Birria and Beyond
dek: Tortas ahogadas, birria, carne en su jugo, jericalla, tejuino and tequila — a tasty guide to eating in Guadalajara.
body:
Guadalajara is the capital of Jalisco — the state that gave the world mariachi and tequila — and its food is just as proud and particular. The city’s signature dishes are hearty, saucy and deeply local, many of them hard to find done quite the same way anywhere else. Here’s what to order, to pair with our Guadalajara guide.

Tortas Ahogadas: The Drowned Sandwich

If Guadalajara has one defining dish, it’s the torta ahogada. A crusty birote salado roll — a sturdy, slightly sour bread closely tied to the city — is stuffed with carnitas and then “drowned” in a mild tomato sauce, with a fiery chile de árbol sauce added to taste.

Ask for it media ahogada (half-drowned) if you’d like to keep some crunch, or bien ahogada if you’re committed. Pickled onions on top, plenty of napkins on the side. It’s classic late-morning fuel, often eaten standing up.

Locals will tell you the bread makes the dish: birote’s thick crust holds up to the sauce without collapsing, which is why the torta ahogada rarely tastes quite right outside Guadalajara.

Birria: Jalisco’s Famous Stew

Birria is Jalisco’s gift to the taco-loving world. Traditionally made with goat and slow-cooked in a rich adobo of dried chiles and spices, it’s served as a stew in a bowl of its own consommé, with onion, cilantro, lime and warm tortillas on the side. Beef and lamb versions are common too.

Birria is a weekend and celebration favorite, and many locals swear by it as a hangover cure. Don’t skip the broth — it’s the point. Many places also serve it as tacos, or quesabirria-style with melted cheese and a cup of consommé for dipping.

Carne en Su Jugo

Carne en su jugo — literally “meat in its juices” — is a Guadalajara comfort classic. Thinly sliced beef simmers in a tomatillo-based broth with crispy bacon and whole beans, then gets topped with onion, cilantro and radish. It’s savory, brothy and ideal on a cool evening. Tortillas and a squeeze of lime finish it off, and some places serve grilled green onions on the side.

Street Snacks and Local Favorites

  • Lonches — sandwiches on birote, often filled with pork leg and dressed with salsa.
  • Tacos de barbacoa and tacos al vapor — soft, steamed breakfast tacos sold from street stands.
  • Pozole — a hearty hominy soup, usually red in Jalisco, topped with cabbage, radish and oregano.
  • Mercado San Juan de Dios — the city’s enormous central market, with food stalls on the upper floor and just about everything else below.

Jericalla: The Local Custard

For dessert, look for jericalla, a Guadalajara-born custard somewhere between flan and crème brûlée. It’s made with milk, eggs, vanilla and cinnamon, and baked until the top turns a spotty, caramelized brown. Simple, creamy and wonderfully old-fashioned.

What to Drink: Tejuino, Tequila and Raicilla

Tejuino is a cold, lightly fermented corn drink sold from street carts, served with lime, salt and chile — often topped with a scoop of lime sorbet. It’s sweet, sour and incredibly refreshing on a warm afternoon.

Then there’s tequila. The town of Tequila and its blue-agave landscape, a UNESCO World Heritage site, are a short trip from the city, and bars here pour an excellent range. Sip it neat to taste the agave, or try a cantarito, a citrusy tequila cocktail served in a clay cup.

For something wilder, try raicilla, an agave spirit from Jalisco’s mountains and coast. It’s often more rustic and aromatic than tequila — a great conversation starter at any mezcal or cocktail bar.

Tips for Eating in Guadalajara

  • Tortas ahogadas and birria are often morning-to-afternoon foods; some stands sell out early.
  • Carry small bills for street stands and markets.
  • Taste salsas before pouring — Jalisco’s chile de árbol means business.
  • Visit Tlaquepaque for a stroll and a drink, but explore neighborhood spots for the best everyday food.

Hungry for more? Build these dishes into our three-day Guadalajara itinerary and leave room for a second torta.

title: What to Eat in Cusco: Andean Dishes and Drinks to Try
dek: From quinoa and alpaca to cuy, chicharrón and chicha morada, a guide to the Andean dishes and drinks worth seeking out in Cusco.
body:
Cusco’s cooking is rooted in the high Andes: hearty, warming and built on ingredients that have been grown in these mountains for centuries. Think giant-kerneled corn, countless varieties of potato, grains like quinoa and meats that suit a cold, high-altitude climate. Here is what to look for when you sit down to eat.

Andean Staples: Quinoa, Corn and Potatoes

Quinoa is everywhere, and in Cusco it is comfort food rather than a health trend. Look for sopa de quinua, a thick, soothing soup that is especially welcome on a chilly evening, as well as quinoa salads and quinoa-crusted dishes on more contemporary menus.

Then there is choclo con queso: an ear of Andean corn with huge, chewy, mildly sweet kernels, served with a slab of fresh, salty cheese. It is a classic snack sold at markets and roadside stands, especially around the Sacred Valley. Peru is also home to thousands of potato varieties, and you will find them boiled, dried, stewed and fried throughout your trip.

Meats of the Highlands

  • Alpaca — a lean, tender red meat, often served grilled as a steak or in medallions. It has a mild flavor and appears on many menus in town.
  • Cuy — guinea pig, a traditional Andean dish with deep cultural roots. In the Cusco region it is typically roasted whole until the skin crackles. It is a celebratory food for many families, and trying it is a genuine taste of local tradition.
  • Chicharrón — Cusco-style chicharrón is chunks of pork cooked in their own fat until crisp outside and tender within, often served with mote (hominy-style corn), potatoes and fresh mint.

Rocoto Relleno

The rocoto is a fiery, thick-walled red pepper, and rocoto relleno stuffs it with a savory mix of minced meat, onions, spices and often egg and olives, then tops it with melted cheese. The dish is most closely associated with Arequipa in southern Peru, but it is popular across the region and easy to find in Cusco. Kitchens usually blanch the peppers to tame the heat, but it can still bite.

Chiri Uchu: A Festival Feast

If you visit around Corpus Christi, one of Cusco’s most important festivals (usually in late May or June, following the church calendar), look for chiri uchu. The name means “cold chili” in Quechua, and the dish is served at room temperature as a grand, many-part platter.

It typically brings together roast cuy, chicken, sausage, dried meat, cheese, fish roe, seaweed, a small corn fritter and toasted corn, all arranged together. It is a dish of abundance, gathering ingredients from the mountains, the jungle and the sea, and it is very much a festival specialty rather than an everyday order.

What to Drink

  • Coca tea — mate de coca, brewed from coca leaves, is a traditional Andean infusion that many locals and travelers sip at altitude. It is widely offered in Cusco. Note that it can show up on drug tests.
  • Chicha morada — a sweet, non-alcoholic drink made from purple corn, simmered with fruit and spices such as cinnamon and clove, served cold.
  • Emoliente — a warm herbal drink sold from street carts, often made with barley, flaxseed and herbs, and sweetened to taste. A cozy choice on a crisp morning.

Eat Your Way Through San Pedro Market

The Mercado Central de San Pedro, a short walk from the Plaza de Armas, is the best place to see Cusco’s food culture up close. You will find fresh juice stalls blending fruit to order, piles of Andean potatoes and corn, cheeses, breads, herbs and simple lunch counters serving soups and set meals.

Go in the morning, when it is busiest and freshest, and keep an eye on your belongings in the crowds. It makes an easy stop on a walking day; our 4-day Cusco and Machu Picchu itinerary shows how to fit it in.

Practical Wrap-Up

At altitude, many travelers find it helps to eat lighter meals for the first day or two and save the richest dishes, like chicharrón, for once they have adjusted. Drink bottled or treated water, and approach street food with the usual common sense. For more on where to wander between meals, see our Cusco guide.

title: Altitude in Cusco: How to Acclimatize
dek: Cusco sits at about 3,400 meters. Here is how to ease into the altitude, from starting in the Sacred Valley to pacing your first days.
body:
Cusco sits at roughly 3,400 meters (about 11,150 feet) above sea level, and your body will notice. Most travelers adjust just fine with a little planning and a slower pace for the first day or two. Here is how to give yourself the best chance of feeling good.

Please note: this is general travel information, not medical advice. Talk to a doctor before your trip, especially if you have any health conditions.

What Altitude Can Feel Like

At high elevations, there is less oxygen available with each breath. Many visitors feel it in the first hours or days, even if they are young and fit. Fitness does not reliably predict who will feel the altitude most.

  • Headache
  • Shortness of breath on stairs or hills
  • Fatigue or feeling light-headed
  • Poor sleep or loss of appetite

For most people, mild symptoms ease as the body adjusts over a few days. Symptoms that are severe or worsening are a different matter; see the section on when to get help below.

Start Lower: The Sacred Valley First

One of the most popular strategies is to skip sleeping in Cusco on your first night. The Sacred Valley, a short drive away, sits noticeably lower, at roughly 2,800 to 2,900 meters around towns like Urubamba and Ollantaytambo. Spending your first nights there lets you acclimatize more gently while exploring ruins, markets and villages.

Machu Picchu is lower still, at about 2,400 meters. That means you can loop through the valley and Machu Picchu first and return to Cusco at the end, when you are better adjusted. Our 4-day Cusco and Machu Picchu itinerary is built around that kind of pacing.

Take It Slow

Your first day is for strolling, not summiting. Walk slowly, take the stairs at a relaxed pace and build in rest. Cusco’s streets are steep and cobbled, and what looks like a short walk up to San Blas can leave you breathless.

  • Plan an easy first day — save hikes and big excursions for later in your trip
  • Rest when you need to — an afternoon nap is not wasted time
  • Sleep well — extra blankets are common for a reason; nights are cold

Hydrate, Eat Light and Go Easy on Alcohol

The air at altitude is dry, so drink water steadily throughout the day. Many travelers find lighter meals easier to digest in the first day or two, so save the heaviest dishes for later. It is also widely recommended to limit alcohol at first, since it can make it harder to judge how you are feeling and affect sleep.

The Coca Tea Tradition

You will likely be offered mate de coca, a tea brewed from coca leaves, soon after you arrive. It is a long-standing Andean tradition, and many people find it soothing. Chewing coca leaves is also traditional in the highlands. Think of it as a cultural ritual rather than a cure, and note that coca products can show up on drug tests and generally should not be taken home, since they are restricted in many countries.

When to See a Doctor

Ask your doctor before your trip whether any preventive medication makes sense for you. In Cusco, seek medical attention promptly if symptoms become severe or keep getting worse, for example a headache that does not respond to rest, confusion, trouble walking, persistent vomiting or breathlessness even at rest. Descending to a lower altitude is the standard response to serious altitude illness. Many hotels can help you contact a clinic, and some keep oxygen on hand.

Practical Wrap-Up

  • Consider starting in the Sacred Valley, which is lower than Cusco.
  • Keep your first day easy and build activity gradually.
  • Drink water, eat lighter and limit alcohol early on.
  • Get travel insurance that covers medical care.
  • Talk to a doctor before you go, and seek care if symptoms are severe.

For more on planning your time in the city, head to our Cusco guide.

title: Day Trips from Buenos Aires: Tigre, Colonia, the Pampas and San Antonio de Areco
dek: Swap city bustle for river delta canals, a colonial Uruguayan town, gaucho country and a lazy estancia lunch on these easy Buenos Aires day trips.
body:
Buenos Aires is intoxicating, but a few days of late dinners and busy avenues can leave you craving open sky. The good news is that river islands, a colonial town in another country and the wide-open Pampas all sit within a couple of hours. Here are the day trips worth carving out time for.

Tigre and the Paraná Delta

About an hour north of the city by train or car, Tigre sits at the gateway to the Paraná Delta, a vast labyrinth of rivers, channels and marshy islands. Life here moves by water: wooden stilt houses, rowing clubs, grocery boats and commuter launches instead of buses.

The easiest way in is aboard one of the public river launches or a sightseeing boat that winds through the channels. Back on land, the Puerto de Frutos market is good for wicker, crafts and snacks, and the riverside promenade is lined with grand old rowing clubs. Many visitors combine the trip with the scenic coastal train line that runs along the river through the northern suburbs.

Go on a weekday if you can. Weekends bring porteños out in force for rowing, picnics and riverside lunches — fun to watch, but boats and the market get busy. Whenever you go, pack sunscreen and bug spray for the islands, and allow time to simply sit by the water with a coffee and watch the traffic drift past.

Colonia del Sacramento, Uruguay

Yes, you can pop over to another country for the day. Ferries cross the Río de la Plata from Buenos Aires to Colonia del Sacramento, with journey times ranging from roughly an hour to a few hours depending on the type of boat. Bring your passport — you will clear Argentine and Uruguayan immigration, usually at the port before boarding.

Colonia’s historic quarter is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a compact tangle of cobbled lanes, Portuguese and Spanish colonial houses and flowering bougainvillea. Walk the Calle de los Suspiros, climb the lighthouse for views over the river, and linger over a long lunch before the return crossing. The town is small enough to explore on foot in a few unhurried hours, which makes it ideal for a day trip. If it charms you, our Uruguay guide covers more of the country.

An Estancia Day in the Pampas

For a taste of rural Argentina, book a día de campo (country day) at an estancia, one of the traditional cattle ranches scattered across the flat, grassy Pampas. These days typically follow a gentle script:

  • Arrival — Empanadas and a welcome drink on the veranda.
  • Horseback riding — An easy ride across the fields, suitable for most beginners.
  • Asado — A long, generous lunch of grilled meats, salads and Argentine wine.
  • Gaucho skills — Often a show of horsemanship, folk music or dancing in the afternoon.

Most estancias arrange round-trip transport from the city, and the whole outing makes an easy, restorative break from sightseeing.

San Antonio de Areco

Roughly two hours northwest of Buenos Aires, San Antonio de Areco is often called the heartland of gaucho culture. The small town is all low colonial buildings, old-fashioned general stores and silversmith workshops producing the ornate knives, belt buckles and mate gourds associated with gaucho dress.

Stroll the leafy main square, cross the old bridge over the Areco River and visit the museum dedicated to gaucho life and literature. Each November, the town hosts a celebration of tradition with parades and horsemanship, but it is lovely any time of year. Many estancias are in the surrounding countryside, so it pairs nicely with a ranch visit.

How to Plan Your Day Trip

  • Pick your pace — Tigre is the simplest DIY option; Colonia and Areco reward an early start.
  • Check the calendar — Weekends bring more atmosphere but also more crowds, especially in Tigre.
  • Book ahead — Ferries and estancia days can fill up in peak season, so reserve in advance and check current schedules and border requirements.

Want to fit a day trip into a short stay? Our 3-day Buenos Aires itinerary leaves room for one, and the full Buenos Aires guide has everything you need back in the city.
